atoms.title: The bit — the unit of information
atoms.summary: One bit is the information in answering a single yes/no question whose two answers are equally likely.

depths.eli5: A bit is the answer to one yes-or-no question — the smallest possible piece of information. Think of guessing a number from 1 to 8. Ask 'is it 5 or higher?', then split what's left in half again, then again: three good yes/no questions always pin down the answer. Each answer is one bit, so the whole guess took three bits. 'Bit' is short for 'binary digit', meaning a single 0 or 1.
depths.core: Information is measured by how much it cuts down your uncertainty. The natural unit is the bit: the amount of information you gain from learning the result of a fair (50/50) coin flip. Picking one item out of 2^n equally likely options takes exactly n bits, because each yes/no answer halves the number of remaining possibilities. The mathematics uses the logarithm — the function that asks 'how many times must I halve N to reach 1?' — so identifying one item out of N equally likely items costs log2(N) bits.
depths.deep: The bit is dimensionless and logarithmic by necessity: information about independent events must add up, while the number of combined outcomes multiplies, and the logarithm is the unique function that turns products into sums. Using log base 2 fixes the unit as the bit; using the natural log (base e) gives 'nats', and base 10 gives 'dits' or 'hartleys' — the same quantity measured with a different ruler.

atoms.note: log2(N) bits identify one item out of N equally likely ones. Memorize: 10 bits ≈ a thousand, 20 bits ≈ a million, 30 bits ≈ a billion.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Information is not about *what* a message says but about *how much it narrows down the possibilities*. Before you learn something, several outcomes are open; afterward, fewer are. The **bit** is the unit that measures exactly that narrowing. The cleanest possible act of narrowing is answering one fair yes/no question — a question whose two answers are equally likely. Each such answer chops the field of possibilities in half. If you can pin down any answer with a sequence of these halvings, the number of halvings *is* the amount of information, measured in bits.

### Precisely

A **bit** is the information gained from observing one outcome of a source with two equally likely outcomes. More generally, identifying one item out of $N$ equally likely possibilities requires

$$\log_2 N \text{ bits.}$$

Here $\log_2 N$ answers the question "how many times must I halve $N$ to reach $1$?" The base-$2$ logarithm fixes the *unit*: base $e$ gives **nats**, base $10$ gives **hartleys** (or **dits**). All measure the same underlying quantity with a different ruler. A bit is dimensionless — it counts halvings, not meters or seconds.

### Worked example

You must identify one card from a standard 52-card deck, and each yes/no question you ask splits the remaining candidates as evenly as possible. Question 1: "Is it red?" — 52 drops to 26. Question 2: "Is it a heart or diamond, specifically a heart?" — actually, ask cleanly: "Among the remaining 26, is it in the first half (some fixed ordering)?" — 26 drops to 13. Continuing to halve: 13 → 7 → 4 → 2 → 1. That is

$$\lceil \log_2 52 \rceil = \lceil 5.70 \rceil = 6$$

well-chosen questions. The fractional part (5.70, not 6) reflects that a single card carries about 5.7 bits; the ceiling to 6 is the cost of using whole questions.

### Why it works

Why the logarithm? Because information from **independent** events must *add*, while the number of combined outcomes *multiplies*. If event A has $M$ outcomes and event B has $N$, the pair has $M\cdot N$ outcomes, but the information should be (info of A) + (info of B). The unique function turning products into sums is the logarithm: $\log(M\cdot N)=\log M + \log N$. So measuring information *forces* a logarithmic scale; choosing base 2 simply names the unit "bit."

### Where it connects

The bit is the atom on which everything else here is built. **Shannon entropy** generalizes it to outcomes that are *not* equally likely (a fair coin is exactly 1 bit; a biased coin is less). **Source coding** shows entropy is the true floor for compression. **Kolmogorov complexity** measures information in a single object rather than a distribution. A useful memory anchor: $10$ bits $\approx$ a thousand ($2^{10}=1024$), $20$ bits $\approx$ a million, $30$ bits $\approx$ a billion.

### A second angle

It helps to see the bit additively across a sequence. Asking $k$ independent fair yes/no questions distinguishes $2^k$ possibilities, and learning all $k$ answers gives exactly $k$ bits — the bits *add* because the possibility counts *multiply*. This is why file sizes, address spaces, and password strengths are all quoted in bits: a 128-bit key names one of $2^{128}\approx 3.4\times 10^{38}$ possibilities, and each added bit *doubles* the search an attacker faces. The same additivity is what makes the logarithm, not any other function, the right measure — a recurring theme you will meet again in **entropy** and **mutual information**.

### Watch out

A bit (the unit of information) is not the same as a "bit" of computer storage, though they are related: one storage bit can *hold at most* one bit of information, and exactly one bit only when its two values are equally likely. A storage bit that is almost always 0 carries far less than one bit of information. Don't equate "number of binary digits written down" with "amount of information conveyed."

atoms.title: Probability distribution and expectation
atoms.summary: A distribution assigns nonnegative weights summing to one; expectation is the weighted average of outcomes.

depths.eli5: When different outcomes can happen, each with its own chance, the 'expectation' is the average result you'd get if you repeated the whole thing a huge number of times. For a fair six-sided die the outcomes 1 through 6 are equally likely, and their average is 3.5 — even though you can never actually roll a 3.5.
depths.core: A 'random variable' X is just a quantity whose value depends on chance (like a die roll). A 'probability distribution' lists each possible value x together with its probability p(x), where every p(x) is at least 0 and all of them add up to 1 (something must happen). The 'expectation' (or expected value, or mean) E[X] = Σ x p(x) is the probability-weighted average — the long-run average value. Expectation is 'linear': E[aX+bY] = aE[X]+bE[Y], and this holds even when X and Y influence each other. Almost every quantity in information theory turns out to be the expectation of some log-probability.
depths.deep: Linearity of expectation is the workhorse of algorithm analysis precisely because it needs no independence — you can sum per-element contributions regardless of how they correlate. 'Variance' (the spread around the mean), by contrast, does require care about covariance (how variables move together).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

When outcomes depend on chance, we summarize them in two steps. First we say *how likely* each outcome is — that is the **distribution**. Then we ask, "if I repeated this forever, what would the average result be?" — that is the **expectation**. Expectation is the single most useful number for collapsing a whole random situation down to one representative value, and almost every quantity in information theory turns out to be an expectation of something.

### Precisely

A **random variable** $X$ takes values $x$ with probabilities $p(x)$. A **probability distribution** is the list of those probabilities, obeying two rules:

$$p(x)\ge 0 \quad\text{for all } x, \qquad \sum_x p(x)=1.$$

The first says probabilities are never negative; the second says *something* must happen. The **expectation** (expected value, mean) is the probability-weighted average:

$$\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_x x\,p(x).$$

A central property is **linearity of expectation**:

$$\mathbb{E}[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb{E}[X]+b\,\mathbb{E}[Y],$$

which holds *even when $X$ and $Y$ are dependent*.

### Worked example

Roll a fair six-sided die. Each face $1,\dots,6$ has probability $\tfrac16$, so

$$\mathbb{E}[X]=\tfrac16(1+2+3+4+5+6)=\tfrac{21}{6}=3.5.$$

Notice 3.5 is not a value the die can ever show — the mean is a *summary*, not a prediction of any single roll. Now suppose you roll two dice and want the expected sum. By linearity, $\mathbb{E}[X_1+X_2]=3.5+3.5=7$, and you never had to enumerate the 36 joint outcomes.

### Why it works

Linearity follows directly from the definition by regrouping the sum, with no independence assumption needed — you are just rearranging weighted terms. This is what makes it the workhorse of algorithm analysis: to find the expected number of, say, comparisons, you write it as a sum of indicator variables (one per possible comparison) and add their individual expectations, ignoring all the messy correlations between them. **Variance**, by contrast, measures spread and *does* require care about how variables move together (covariance).

### Where it connects

Expectation of a log-probability is exactly **Shannon entropy** $\mathbb{E}[-\log_2 p(X)]$. **Mutual information**, **KL divergence**, and **rate–distortion** are all expectations. In algorithms, linearity drives the analysis of **randomized algorithms**, **hashing**, and the average-case behavior of **quicksort**. **Bayes' rule** builds on the same conditional-probability machinery.

### A second angle

A second indispensable tool is the **indicator variable**: define $\mathbb{1}_A=1$ if event $A$ happens and $0$ otherwise. Then $\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_A]=P(A)$ — expectation and probability become the same operation. This lets you compute the expected *count* of many events by summing their probabilities, even highly dependent ones, via linearity. For example, the expected number of fixed points of a random permutation of $n$ items is $\sum_{i=1}^n P(\text{item } i \text{ fixed})=n\cdot\tfrac1n=1$, regardless of the tangled correlations between positions. Indicators plus linearity are the backbone of average-case algorithm analysis you will use throughout this branch.

### Watch out

Linearity of expectation does *not* require independence — that is its superpower, and forgetting it leads people to needlessly compute joint distributions. The opposite mistake is assuming the mean is "typical": for skewed distributions the mean can sit where almost no probability lies. And $\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\ne f(\mathbb{E}[X])$ in general (Jensen's inequality) — you cannot push expectation through a nonlinear function.

atoms.title: Shannon entropy
atoms.summary: Entropy is the average number of bits needed to describe an outcome — the exact amount of uncertainty in a distribution.

depths.eli5: Entropy measures how surprised you'll be, on average, by an outcome — and that surprise is exactly the amount of information the outcome carries. A coin that always lands heads has zero entropy: you already know the result, so learning it tells you nothing. A fair coin has one bit of entropy: each flip is a genuine 50/50 surprise. The more unpredictable something is, the higher its entropy.
depths.core: Shannon entropy H(X) = −Σ p(x) log2 p(x) is the average 'surprise' of an outcome, where the surprise of a single outcome with probability p is defined as −log2 p (rarer outcomes are more surprising). Measured in bits, entropy is the unique measure (up to a scaling choice) that is continuous, adds up for independent variables, and is largest for the uniform (all-equally-likely) distribution. It sets the absolute floor on lossless compression: on average you cannot encode X in fewer than H(X) bits per symbol. ('Lossless' means the original can be perfectly reconstructed.)
depths.deep: Surprise is −log2 p because rarer events carry more information, independent events' surprises must add (while their probabilities multiply), and the logarithm is the function that converts multiplication into addition. Entropy is maximized by the uniform distribution and is exactly zero when one outcome is certain. It is concave in p, which is why blending two distributions together never decreases uncertainty.

atoms.note: Joint and conditional entropy obey the chain rule H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y|X); conditioning never increases entropy: H(X|Y) ≤ H(X).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

How uncertain is a random source, in a way you can put a number on? A coin stuck on heads carries no uncertainty — you already know the answer, so observing it tells you nothing. A fair coin is maximally uncertain for two outcomes — each flip is a genuine surprise. **Entropy** measures this average surprise, and "average surprise" turns out to be exactly "average information content." High entropy means hard to predict and expensive to describe; low entropy means predictable and cheap.

### Precisely

For a random variable $X$ with distribution $p(x)$, the **Shannon entropy** is

$$H(X)=-\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x)=\mathbb{E}\big[-\log_2 p(X)\big].$$

The quantity $-\log_2 p(x)$ is the **surprise** (self-information) of outcome $x$: rare outcomes ($p$ small) are highly surprising, certain outcomes ($p=1$) carry zero surprise. Entropy is their probability-weighted average, measured in bits. It satisfies $0\le H(X)\le \log_2 |\mathcal{X}|$, hitting $0$ when one outcome is certain and the maximum $\log_2|\mathcal{X}|$ for the uniform distribution.

### Worked example

A biased coin with $P(\text{heads})=\tfrac14$, $P(\text{tails})=\tfrac34$:

$$H=-\tfrac14\log_2\tfrac14-\tfrac34\log_2\tfrac34=\tfrac14(2)+\tfrac34(0.415)\approx 0.811 \text{ bits.}$$

Less than the 1 bit of a fair coin — the bias makes outcomes partly predictable, so each flip carries less information. Push the bias to $P(\text{heads})=1$ and $H\to 0$; balance it to $\tfrac12$ and $H\to 1$.

### Why it works

Surprise must be $-\log_2 p$ for three reasons that pin it down uniquely (up to scale): rarer events should carry more information (so it decreases in $p$); a certain event should carry zero ($-\log_2 1 = 0$); and the surprises of independent events should *add* while their probabilities *multiply* — only the logarithm converts multiplication into addition. Averaging surprise gives entropy. Entropy is concave in $p$, so blending two distributions never lowers uncertainty, and it is maximized by the uniform distribution because any imbalance is a predictable hint.

### Where it connects

Entropy is the **compression floor**: the **source coding theorem** proves you cannot losslessly encode $X$ in fewer than $H(X)$ bits per symbol on average. **Conditional entropy** $H(X\mid Y)$ and the **chain rule** $H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y\mid X)$ extend it to multiple variables; **mutual information** is built from it. Through the **entropy–statistical-mechanics link**, the very same formula is the entropy of thermodynamics.

### A second angle

Entropy also has a precise **operational** meaning beyond "average surprise": it is the expected number of optimal yes/no questions to pin down the outcome. For a distribution whose probabilities are powers of $1/2$, an optimal questioning strategy uses exactly $-\log_2 p(x)$ questions for outcome $x$, and the average is $H(X)$ — connecting directly back to the **bit**. The chain rule $H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y\mid X)$ then says the information in a pair equals the information in the first plus the *remaining* information in the second once the first is known, which is exactly how you would budget questions across two stages. This operational reading is what the **source coding theorem** turns into a hard compression limit.

### Watch out

Conditioning never *increases* entropy *on average*: $H(X\mid Y)\le H(X)$. But this is an average statement — for a *specific* observed value $Y=y$, the conditional entropy $H(X\mid Y=y)$ can be larger than $H(X)$ (a surprising observation can momentarily raise your uncertainty). Also, entropy depends only on the probabilities, not on the labels of the outcomes — renaming "heads/tails" to "0/1" changes nothing.

atoms.title: Source coding theorem (and Kraft inequality)
atoms.summary: Lossless codes can compress a source down to its entropy, and no further — entropy is the compression limit.

depths.eli5: When you turn symbols into strings of 0s and 1s (a 'code'), you can give short codes to the things that show up a lot and longer codes to rare things — that's the trick Morse code uses, giving the common letter 'e' a single dot. Doing this shrinks your messages on average. But there's a hard floor: no matter how clever you are, you can't squeeze a message below its entropy, on average.
depths.core: Shannon's source coding theorem says the shortest possible average codeword length for a source equals its entropy: H(X) ≤ L̄ < H(X)+1 bits per symbol, and the leftover gap shrinks to zero when you encode long blocks of symbols at once. A 'prefix code' is one where no codeword is the start of another, so a stream of bits can be decoded with no separators ('uniquely decodable' = the bits can only be read one way). The Kraft inequality, Σ 2^(−ℓ_i) ≤ 1 (summing over codeword lengths ℓ_i), says exactly which sets of codeword lengths can form such a code.
depths.deep: The best codeword lengths are ℓ_i ≈ −log2 p_i, so the length of a codeword equals the surprise of its symbol. Huffman coding finds the optimal code when lengths must be whole numbers; arithmetic coding gets within a hair of the entropy bound by escaping the whole-number constraint. Kraft's inequality is what forbids a 'free lunch': shortening one codeword forces you to lengthen others.

sources: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (facts)

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

To store or send symbols, you turn each into a string of bits — a **code**. The trick that saves space is obvious once stated: give *short* codewords to *common* symbols and longer ones to rare symbols. Morse code does this, giving the frequent letter "e" a single dot. But there is a hard floor on how much this can save you on average: you can never beat the source's **entropy**. The source coding theorem makes both the trick and the floor exact.

### Precisely

For a uniquely decodable code with codeword lengths $\ell_i$, the achievable average length $\bar L$ obeys

$$H(X)\le \bar L < H(X)+1 \text{ bits per symbol,}$$

and the upper gap shrinks to $0$ when you encode long blocks of symbols together. A **prefix code** (no codeword is a prefix of another) is instantly decodable from a bit stream with no separators. The **Kraft inequality** says a set of lengths $\{\ell_i\}$ can form such a code *iff*

$$\sum_i 2^{-\ell_i}\le 1.$$

### Worked example

Can lengths $\{1,2,2,3\}$ form a binary prefix code? Check Kraft:

$$2^{-1}+2^{-2}+2^{-2}+2^{-3}=\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\tfrac14+\tfrac18=\tfrac98>1.$$

Since the sum exceeds 1, **no** — these lengths are impossible. Intuitively, a length-1 codeword (say "0") already "uses up" half the binary tree, leaving too little room for three more codewords this short. By contrast $\{1,2,3,3\}$ gives $\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\tfrac18+\tfrac18=1$, exactly feasible.

### Why it works

The ideal codeword length for a symbol of probability $p_i$ is $\ell_i\approx-\log_2 p_i$ — the symbol's surprise. Plugging these into $\bar L=\sum p_i\ell_i$ recovers the entropy $H(X)$, which is why entropy is the floor. Kraft's inequality is the "no free lunch" constraint: codewords correspond to leaves in a binary tree, each codeword of length $\ell$ claims a fraction $2^{-\ell}$ of the tree, and you cannot claim more than the whole tree. Shortening one codeword forces lengthening others.

### Where it connects

**Huffman coding** finds the optimal code when lengths must be whole numbers; **arithmetic coding** escapes the integer constraint to hug the entropy bound. The block-coding argument relies on the **AEP / typical sequences**. The lossy counterpart — compressing below entropy by tolerating error — is **rate–distortion theory**.

### A second angle

It is worth separating two claims people often blur. The **Kraft inequality** is a statement about *which length vectors are achievable* by a prefix code — pure combinatorics on the binary tree. The **source coding theorem** is a statement about the *best achievable average length* given the symbol probabilities — it brings in entropy. They meet at the optimal assignment $\ell_i\approx-\log_2 p_i$: Kraft says such lengths *fit* (their $2^{-\ell_i}$ sum to about 1), and plugging them into $\bar L=\sum p_i\ell_i$ *yields* $H(X)$. Huffman's algorithm finds the genuinely optimal integer lengths by repeatedly merging the two least-probable symbols, building the code tree from the leaves up.

### Watch out

Entropy is the floor *per symbol on average*, not a guarantee for every individual message: a rare symbol still gets a long codeword. Also, the "$+1$" gap is real for single-symbol coding; only by coding blocks (or using arithmetic coding) do you approach $H(X)$ closely. Finally, Kraft's inequality being satisfiable doesn't pick the code for you — it only says a code with those lengths *exists*.

atoms.title: Mutual information
atoms.summary: Mutual information is the number of bits one variable reveals about another — the reduction in uncertainty from observing it.

depths.eli5: Mutual information is how much learning one thing tells you about another. If knowing today's clouds makes you more sure whether it'll rain, clouds and rain share mutual information. If two things have nothing to do with each other — like a coin flip in Tokyo and one in Paris — their mutual information is zero.
depths.core: Mutual information I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) measures how many bits observing Y removes from your uncertainty about X (here H(X) is the entropy of X and H(X|Y) is the leftover entropy once Y is known). It is symmetric (Y tells you as much about X as X tells you about Y), never negative, and exactly zero when X and Y are 'independent' (unrelated — knowing one says nothing about the other). Equivalently it is the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the true joint distribution and the product of the separate distributions, a number measuring how far the two variables are from being independent.
depths.deep: I(X;Y) ≥ 0 follows from the convexity of KL divergence (Gibbs' inequality). The data-processing inequality says no clever post-processing of Y can increase the information it carries about X: if X→Y→Z form a 'Markov chain' (Z depends on X only through Y) then I(X;Z) ≤ I(X;Y). This is the formal reason you cannot manufacture information by computation alone.

atoms.note: Mutual information is the rate quantity behind channel capacity, feature selection, and the information bottleneck in deep learning.
sources: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (facts)
Wikipedia (facts): Mutual information; Data processing inequality

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

**Mutual information** answers: how many bits does observing one variable tell you about another? If watching the sky's clouds makes you more confident about rain, clouds and rain *share* information. If two things are unrelated — a coin flip in Tokyo and one in Paris — knowing one tells you nothing about the other, and their mutual information is zero. It is the single number quantifying "relatedness" in bits.

### Precisely

For random variables $X,Y$ with joint distribution $p(x,y)$,

$$I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X\mid Y)=\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log_2\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}.$$

Read the first form as: your uncertainty about $X$, *minus* the uncertainty that remains after seeing $Y$ — i.e., the uncertainty $Y$ removed. It is **symmetric** ($I(X;Y)=I(Y;X)$), **nonnegative** ($I\ge 0$), and **zero exactly when $X$ and $Y$ are independent**. The second form reveals it as the **KL divergence** between the true joint $p(x,y)$ and the product $p(x)p(y)$ that would hold under independence.

### Worked example

Pass $X$ through a noiseless channel so $Y=X$ exactly. Then knowing $Y$ removes *all* uncertainty about $X$: $H(X\mid Y)=0$, so $I(X;Y)=H(X)$ — the channel conveys the full entropy. At the other extreme, let $Y$ be an independent coin flip unrelated to $X$. Then $p(x,y)=p(x)p(y)$, every log term is $\log_2 1=0$, and $I(X;Y)=0$. Real channels sit between these: a noisy link conveys some but not all of $H(X)$.

### Why it works

Nonnegativity, $I(X;Y)\ge 0$, follows from **Gibbs' inequality** (KL divergence is never negative), since $I$ is a KL divergence. The deep structural fact is the **data-processing inequality**: if $X\to Y\to Z$ form a Markov chain (meaning $Z$ depends on $X$ only through $Y$), then

$$I(X;Z)\le I(X;Y).$$

No post-processing of $Y$ can manufacture information about $X$ that $Y$ didn't already carry. This is the formal reason computation alone cannot create information.

### Where it connects

Mutual information is the rate quantity inside **channel capacity** ($C=\max_{p(x)}I(X;Y)$). It underlies feature selection in statistics, the **information bottleneck** in deep learning (linked to **rate–distortion**), and independence testing. It is built directly on **Shannon entropy** and is a special case of **KL divergence**.

### A second angle

A useful picture is the **Venn diagram of entropies**. Draw $H(X)$ and $H(Y)$ as two overlapping circles; their union is the joint entropy $H(X,Y)$, the left-only crescent is $H(X\mid Y)$, the right-only crescent is $H(Y\mid X)$, and the *overlap* is the mutual information $I(X;Y)$. From this picture you can read off every identity at a glance: $I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y)$, and $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X\mid Y)$. The diagram also makes the nonnegativity intuitive — an overlap of two regions cannot be negative — and clarifies that $I(X;Y)=0$ means the circles are disjoint, i.e. the variables are independent.

### Watch out

$I(X;Y)=0$ means *statistical* independence, which is stronger than mere *zero correlation*: correlation only detects linear relationships, while mutual information catches any dependence at all. Conversely, a large $I$ does not imply a causal link — mutual information is symmetric and says nothing about which variable influences which.

atoms.title: Channel capacity and the noisy-channel coding theorem
atoms.summary: Every noisy channel has a maximum reliable rate, the capacity C, below which error can be driven to zero and above which it cannot.

depths.eli5: A 'channel' is any link that carries a message but can scramble it — a phone line with static, a scratched disc, a radio signal through interference. Shannon showed every noisy channel has a top speed (its 'capacity'): below that speed you can encode cleverly enough to be understood with essentially zero errors; push past it and mistakes become unavoidable no matter how clever you are.
depths.core: The capacity of a channel is the largest mutual information you can achieve between its input X and output Y, by choosing the best possible input distribution: C = max over p(x) of I(X;Y). Shannon's noisy-channel coding theorem says any transmission rate R below C can be achieved with arbitrarily small error using long 'block codes' (encoding many symbols together), while any rate above C is stuck with errors that never go to zero. So reliable communication and the noise floor are captured by a single number, C.
depths.deep: The proof that good codes exist is 'non-constructive': it uses random codebooks and 'typical set' decoding to prove good codes must exist, without naming one. Closing the gap to capacity with explicit, efficiently decodable codes took decades — turbo codes, LDPC codes, and polar codes (the first family proven to reach capacity on symmetric channels) finally did it. Capacity also lets you separate the two coding jobs: compress your data down to its entropy first, then protect it up to capacity, independently.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A **channel** is any link that carries a message but may corrupt it: a phone line with static, a scratched disc, radio through interference. The astonishing result is that every noisy channel has a *top speed* — its **capacity** $C$ — with a sharp threshold. Transmit below $C$ and, with clever enough coding, you can drive the error rate essentially to zero. Push above $C$ and errors become unavoidable no matter how clever you are. Noise does not force a gradual quality fade; it imposes a hard rate ceiling.

### Precisely

The **capacity** of a channel is the largest mutual information between input $X$ and output $Y$, optimized over the input distribution:

$$C=\max_{p(x)} I(X;Y).$$

Shannon's **noisy-channel coding theorem**: for any rate $R<C$ there exist block codes achieving arbitrarily small error probability as block length grows; for any $R>C$, the error probability is bounded away from zero. So one number $C$ separates "reliably achievable" from "impossible."

### Worked example

For a **binary symmetric channel** (BSC) that independently flips each transmitted bit with probability $p$, the capacity is

$$C=1-H(p),$$

where $H(p)=-p\log_2 p-(1-p)\log_2(1-p)$ is the binary entropy function. Take $p=0.11$: then $H(0.11)\approx 0.5$, so $C\approx 1-0.5=0.5$ bits per channel use. Even though only 11% of bits flip, you must "spend" about half your raw rate on redundancy to communicate reliably. At $p=0.5$ the channel is useless ($C=0$); at $p=0$ it is perfect ($C=1$).

### Why it works

The existence proof is **non-constructive** and uses the **AEP**: pick a random codebook of $2^{nR}$ long codewords; with high probability their typical noisy outputs barely overlap, so a decoder mapping each received word to the nearest typical codeword almost always recovers the right message when $R<C$. The proof shows good codes *must* exist without naming one — closing that gap with explicit, efficiently decodable codes took decades (turbo, **LDPC**, and polar codes).

### Where it connects

Capacity is built from **mutual information** and proved via **typical sequences**. It justifies the **source–channel separation** principle: compress to entropy first, then protect up to capacity, independently. **Error-correcting codes** are the practical machinery for approaching it.

### A second angle

The **separation theorem** is one of the most practically liberating consequences of capacity. It says you can split communication into two independent jobs: first compress the source down to its **entropy** (source coding), then add redundancy to protect it up to the channel **capacity** (channel coding) — and doing them separately loses nothing versus a clever joint scheme. This is why real systems have a distinct "compressor" (e.g. a codec) and "error-corrector" (e.g. an LDPC encoder) as separate modules. The theorem holds for point-to-point channels; it can *fail* in networks with multiple senders, which is part of why network information theory is harder.

### Watch out

"Below capacity, error goes to zero" requires *long* block codes — there is a latency cost; short codes pay an error penalty. Capacity is a *maximum over input distributions*, so it assumes you can shape your input optimally. And $C$ bounds *reliable* rate; you can always transmit faster, you just cannot do so reliably.

atoms.title: Error-correcting codes and Hamming distance
atoms.summary: By spreading codewords far apart in Hamming distance, a code can detect and correct a bounded number of bit errors.

depths.eli5: Suppose the only valid messages you allow are very different from one another. Then if a few bits get flipped by noise, the corrupted message is still closest to exactly one valid message — so you 'snap' it back to that one and recover the original. The 'Hamming distance' between two codewords is the number of bit positions where they differ; the smallest such distance over all pairs is d_min. A code can detect up to d_min − 1 flipped bits and correct up to t = ⌊(d_min − 1)/2⌋ of them, because any received word within t flips of a unique codeword decodes back to it. 'Linear codes' (Hamming, Reed–Solomon, LDPC) use algebra over finite number systems so that encoding and decoding stay fast.
depths.deep: Error-correcting coding is a sphere-packing problem in 'Hamming space': put non-overlapping balls of radius t around each codeword. The Hamming bound caps how many codewords fit; the Gilbert–Varshamov bound guarantees a minimum density always exists. Shannon's channel capacity is the asymptotic ceiling these combinatorial bounds approach. Reed–Solomon codes underlie CDs, QR codes, and deep-space links; LDPC and polar codes power modern wireless.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

If the only messages you allow are very *different* from each other, then when noise flips a few bits, the corrupted message is still closest to exactly one valid message. You "snap" it back and recover the original. That is the whole idea of **error correction**: deliberately build in enough difference (redundancy) that small damage is repairable. The mathematics turns "very different" into a precise, geometric notion of distance.

### Precisely

A code maps each message to a longer **codeword**. The **Hamming distance** between two equal-length strings is the number of positions where they differ. The **minimum distance** $d_{\min}$ is the smallest Hamming distance over all pairs of codewords. A code can:

- **detect** up to $d_{\min}-1$ bit errors, and
- **correct** up to $t=\big\lfloor\tfrac{d_{\min}-1}{2}\big\rfloor$ errors, because

$$d_{\min}\ge 2t+1 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{corrects } t \text{ errors.}$$

### Worked example

Suppose $d_{\min}=7$. Then $t=\lfloor (7-1)/2\rfloor=3$: the code corrects any 3-bit error. Picture each codeword as a point with a "sphere" of radius 3 around it (all words within 3 flips). If $d_{\min}=7$, these spheres don't overlap: a received word with $\le 3$ flips lands inside exactly one sphere, so nearest-codeword decoding is unambiguous. With $d_{\min}=2$ you could only *detect* a single error (a flip might land halfway between two codewords) — not correct it. The classic **Hamming(7,4)** code has $d_{\min}=3$, correcting one error per 7 bits.

### Why it works

Error correction is **sphere packing** in "Hamming space": place non-overlapping balls of radius $t$ around each codeword. Decoding = find which ball the received word fell into. Non-overlap requires the centers be at least $2t+1$ apart, which is precisely the condition $d_{\min}\ge 2t+1$. The **Hamming bound** caps how many such balls fit (limiting how many codewords you can have); the **Gilbert–Varshamov bound** guarantees a minimum achievable density. **Shannon's capacity** is the asymptotic ceiling these combinatorial bounds approach.

### Where it connects

This is the practical machinery for getting *near* **channel capacity**. **Linear codes** (Hamming, Reed–Solomon, **LDPC**) use algebra over finite fields so encoding and decoding stay fast. **Reed–Solomon** codes protect CDs, QR codes, and deep-space links; LDPC and polar codes power modern wireless and reach capacity. The notion of distance ties to **mutual information** through the geometry of distinguishable signals.

### A second angle

The parameters of a block code are written $[n,k,d]$: $n$ is the codeword length, $k$ the number of message bits, and $d=d_{\min}$ the minimum distance. The **rate** $k/n$ measures efficiency (how much of each transmitted bit carries real message), while $d$ measures protection. These pull against each other — more protection (larger $d$) usually means lower rate — and the bounds (Singleton, Hamming, Gilbert–Varshamov) chart the achievable $(n,k,d)$ region. Reed–Solomon codes meet the Singleton bound exactly ($d=n-k+1$), which is why they are "maximum distance separable" and so widely used in storage and QR codes.

### Watch out

A code cannot simultaneously correct $t$ *and* detect more than $t$ errors with the same decoder setting — there is a detect-vs-correct tradeoff you choose per use. Also, correcting $t$ errors assumes *at most* $t$ occurred; if more flips happen than the radius allows, nearest-codeword decoding can confidently return the *wrong* codeword. Redundancy also costs rate: longer codewords mean fewer message bits per transmitted bit.

atoms.title: Kolmogorov complexity
atoms.summary: The complexity of a string is the length of the shortest program that prints it — the algorithmic, per-object version of information.

depths.eli5: Ask: how short can a recipe (a computer program) be that prints out exactly this string of symbols? The string 'ababab...ab' a million times has a tiny recipe ('print ab a million times'). But a million truly random coin-flip results has no recipe shorter than just writing the whole thing out. That shortest-recipe length is the string's Kolmogorov complexity — its true, per-object amount of information.
depths.core: K(x) is the length of the shortest program that, run on a fixed 'universal Turing machine' U (an idealized general-purpose computer; see the Turing machine atom), prints x and stops. Unlike Shannon entropy, which describes a whole probability distribution, K describes one single object. The 'invariance theorem' guarantees that switching to a different universal machine changes K by at most a fixed additive constant, so K is well-defined up to that constant. A string is called 'random' or 'incompressible' when K(x) ≈ |x|, meaning it has no description shorter than itself.
depths.deep: K is not computable: no algorithm can output K(x) for every x. Chaitin's theorem sharpens this — any consistent formal system can prove statements of the form 'K(x) > c' for only finitely many x, no matter how large the true complexities get. This is Gödel's incompleteness dressed in information-theoretic clothes. The expected Kolmogorov complexity of strings drawn from a computable distribution equals that distribution's Shannon entropy up to a constant, tying the two notions of information together.

atoms.note: Most strings are incompressible by a simple counting argument: there are 2^n strings of length n but fewer than 2^n programs shorter than n, so most strings have no short description.

quiz.answer: If you could compute K, you could search for and print the first string whose complexity exceeds the length of your own program — a contradiction (the Berry-paradox/Chaitin argument), so no such algorithm exists.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Shannon entropy describes a whole *distribution*. But what is the information content of a single, specific string? Ask instead: how short can a program (a recipe) be that prints exactly this string and stops? "abababab…ab" a million times has a tiny recipe ("print 'ab' a million times"). A million genuinely random coin flips has *no* recipe shorter than writing the string out verbatim. That shortest-program length is the string's **Kolmogorov complexity** — its true, per-object amount of information.

### Precisely

Fix a **universal Turing machine** $U$. The **Kolmogorov complexity** of a string $x$ is

$$K(x)=\min\{\,|p| : U(p)=x\,\},$$

the length of the shortest program $p$ that makes $U$ output $x$ and halt. A string is **incompressible** (or "algorithmically random") when $K(x)\approx |x|$ — no description beats writing it out. The **invariance theorem** guarantees that switching to a different universal machine $U'$ changes $K$ by at most an additive constant independent of $x$, so $K$ is well-defined up to that constant.

### Worked example

Counting shows *most* strings are incompressible. There are $2^n$ strings of length $n$. How many programs are shorter than $n$ bits? At most $1+2+4+\cdots+2^{n-1}=2^n-1$ — fewer than $2^n$. So at least one length-$n$ string has no program shorter than $n$; in fact, the fraction of length-$n$ strings compressible by even $k$ bits is at most $2^{-k}$. Compressibility is the rare exception; randomness is the rule. This is why a general-purpose compressor cannot shrink *every* file — it can only exploit structure that happens to be present.

### Why it works

$K$ is **not computable**: no algorithm outputs $K(x)$ for all $x$. Suppose one did; then you could search for "the first string whose complexity exceeds the length of this very program" and print it — but printing it *with* a short program contradicts its high complexity (the **Berry paradox** made rigorous). **Chaitin's theorem** sharpens this: any consistent formal system can prove "$K(x)>c$" for only finitely many $x$ — Gödel incompleteness in information-theoretic dress.

### Where it connects

$K$ is the algorithmic, per-object counterpart of **Shannon entropy**: the expected $K$ of strings drawn from a computable distribution equals that distribution's entropy up to a constant. It depends on the **Turing machine** model, underlies **pseudorandomness** (a PRG output has low $K$ yet looks random), and ties to **Gödel incompleteness**.

### A second angle

A subtlety worth internalizing: Kolmogorov complexity is **uncomputable but upper-semicomputable**. You cannot compute $K(x)$ exactly, but you *can* compute ever-better *upper* bounds — just run all short programs in parallel ("dovetailing") and whenever one outputs $x$, you have found a description, so $K(x)$ is at most that program's length. What you can never do is *certify a lower bound* ("no shorter program exists"), because that would require solving the halting problem to know all short programs have finished. This asymmetry — upper bounds approachable, lower bounds forbidden — is the same shape as recognizability versus decidability in computability theory.

### Watch out

Because $K$ is uncomputable and defined only up to a constant, you can never *measure* it exactly — practical "complexity" estimates (like a file's gzip size) are upper bounds, not the true $K$. And "random" here means *incompressible*, a structural property of the string itself, not a statement about how it was generated.

atoms.title: Sets, functions, and relations
atoms.summary: Sets are collections; functions map each input to one output; relations are any set of input–output pairs — the vocabulary of all formal definitions.

depths.eli5: A 'set' is just a bag of distinct things (the set of vowels, the set of whole numbers). A 'function' is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input — like 'double it', which turns 3 into 6 and never into anything else. A 'relation' is looser: it can link one input to several things at once, like 'is a sibling of'.
depths.core: A set is an unordered collection of distinct elements. A function f: A→B assigns to each element of the input set A (the 'domain') exactly one element of the output set B (the 'codomain'). A 'relation' between A and B is any collection of input–output pairs, so every function is a relation but not every relation is a function. 'Cardinality' measures a set's size. A function is a 'bijection' (a perfect one-to-one pairing) when it is both 'injective' (no two inputs share an output) and 'surjective' (every output is used).
depths.deep: Whether a set is 'countable' or 'uncountable' hinges on bijection: a set is countable if its elements can be paired one-to-one with the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, …. Cantor's diagonal argument shows the real numbers (and the set of all possible languages over an alphabet) are uncountable, while the set of all computer programs is only countable — the seed of why most functions can never be computed.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Before any formal theorem can be stated, we need a vocabulary for "collections of things" and "rules connecting things." A **set** is a bag of distinct objects. A **function** is a rule giving exactly one output per input — "double it" sends 3 to 6 and never anywhere else. A **relation** is looser: it may link one input to several things, like "is a sibling of." Almost every definition in mathematics and computer science is phrased with these three.

### Precisely

A **set** is an unordered collection of distinct elements. A **function** $f:A\to B$ assigns to each element of the **domain** $A$ exactly one element of the **codomain** $B$. A **relation** between $A$ and $B$ is *any* set of pairs $(a,b)$; thus every function is a relation, but not vice versa. A function is **injective** (one-to-one) if distinct inputs give distinct outputs, **surjective** (onto) if every element of $B$ is hit, and a **bijection** if both — a perfect pairing. **Cardinality** measures a set's size via bijections.

### Worked example

Let $A=\{1,2,3\}$ and consider three rules. "$x\mapsto x^2$" into $B=\{1,4,9\}$ is a function and a bijection (each input one output, all outputs used, none repeated). "$x\mapsto$ a divisor of $x$" is a *relation but not a function*: 6 relates to 1, 2, 3, and 6 simultaneously. "$x\mapsto x \bmod 2$" into $\{0,1\}$ is a function but not injective (both 1 and 3 map to 1). Sorting these three examples is exactly the skill the definitions train.

### Why it works

The deepest payoff is **countability**. A set is **countable** if its elements pair one-to-one with $1,2,3,\dots$ The set of all finite strings (hence all *programs*) is countable. But **Cantor's diagonal argument** shows the set of all functions from naturals to $\{0,1\}$ — equivalently all *languages* over an alphabet — is **uncountable**. Pairing a countable set against an uncountable one is impossible, so *most* functions have no program. This single counting fact is the seed of uncomputability.

### Where it connects

Functions and relations are the raw material for **finite automata** (transition functions), **Turing machines** (transition relations), **logic** (predicates are relations), and **complexity** (a decision problem is a function to $\{$yes, no$\}$). The countable-vs-uncountable split directly powers the **halting problem** and **Gödel incompleteness**.

### A second angle

**Equivalence relations** deserve special mention because they appear everywhere downstream. A relation is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive; it then carves its domain into disjoint **equivalence classes**. This is the mechanism behind modular arithmetic (numbers grouped by remainder), behind the **Myhill–Nerode** characterization of regular languages (strings grouped by which futures they allow), and behind quotient constructions throughout mathematics. Recognizing when a relation is an equivalence relation — and what its classes are — is one of the most reusable moves in this whole branch, turning a messy set of pairs into a clean partition you can reason about.

### Watch out

"Relation" is strictly more general than "function" — a common slip is to assume every input–output rule is a function when it might assign several outputs (or none). Also, a bijection requires *both* injectivity and surjectivity; a map can be one without the other. Finally, two sets can have the *same* cardinality despite one "containing" the other (e.g., naturals and even naturals) — size for infinite sets is about pairing, not subset inclusion.

atoms.title: Finite automata (DFA and NFA)
atoms.summary: A finite automaton is a machine with finitely many states that reads input symbol by symbol and accepts or rejects.

depths.eli5: Picture a board game with a few squares ('states'). You read a word one letter at a time, and each letter tells you which square to hop to next. One square is where you start; some squares are marked 'win'. If you land on a win-square after reading the whole word, the machine 'accepts' that word. That little hopping game is a finite automaton.
depths.core: A 'deterministic finite automaton' (DFA) has a finite set of states, a rule ('transition function') that moves it to exactly one next state for each input symbol, a designated start state, and a set of accepting ('win') states. A 'nondeterministic finite automaton' (NFA) is allowed to branch into several states at once (or get stuck with none) and accepts a word if any branch ends in an accept state. Despite the extra freedom, DFAs and NFAs recognize exactly the same family of patterns — the 'regular languages' (the patterns describable by a finite-state machine, equivalently by a regular expression).
depths.deep: The 'subset construction' converts any NFA with n states into an equivalent DFA with up to 2^n states, proving the two models are equally powerful while exposing an exponential blowup in state count. A finite automaton has no memory beyond which single state it is currently in, which is exactly why it cannot count without limit — the limitation the pumping lemma makes precise.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Picture a board game with a few squares called **states**. You read a word one letter at a time, and each letter tells you which square to hop to next. One square is the start; some are marked "win" (accepting). If you finish the word on a win-square, the machine **accepts** that word. This little hopping game — finite squares, no scratch paper — is a **finite automaton**, the simplest model of computation with memory.

### Precisely

A **deterministic finite automaton (DFA)** is a 5-tuple $(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)$: a finite set of states $Q$, an input alphabet $\Sigma$, a **transition function** $\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q$ (exactly one next state per symbol), a start state $q_0$, and accepting states $F\subseteq Q$. A **nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA)** allows $\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to 2^Q$ — it may branch into *several* states at once (or none), and accepts if *any* branch ends in $F$. Both recognize exactly the **regular languages**.

### Worked example

Build a DFA over $\{0,1\}$ accepting strings with an even number of 1s. Two states: $E$ ("even so far," start *and* accepting) and $O$ ("odd so far"). Transitions: a 0 keeps the state; a 1 toggles $E\leftrightarrow O$. Feed "1011": $E\xrightarrow{1}O\xrightarrow{0}O\xrightarrow{1}E\xrightarrow{1}O$ — end in $O$, reject (three 1s, odd). Feed "1001": $E\to O\to O\to O\to E$ — accept. The single bit of memory (which of two states) is exactly enough to track parity.

### Why it works

The **subset construction** proves NFAs are no more powerful than DFAs: simulate an NFA by tracking the *set* of states it could currently be in. An NFA with $n$ states becomes a DFA whose states are subsets of those $n$ states — up to $2^n$ of them. So nondeterminism is a convenience, not extra power, but it can cost an exponential blowup in state count. The fundamental limit is that a finite automaton remembers only *which single state* it is in — bounded memory, no unbounded counting.

### Where it connects

DFAs, NFAs, and **regular expressions** are three faces of the same expressive power (Kleene's theorem). The bounded-memory limit is made precise by the **pumping lemma for regular languages**. Adding a stack yields **pushdown automata** (context-free); adding an unbounded tape yields the **Turing machine**. The subset construction's exponential blowup foreshadows the determinism-vs-nondeterminism theme of **P vs NP**.

### A second angle

DFAs can also be **minimized** to a unique smallest form. Two states are equivalent if they accept exactly the same set of future strings; merging all equivalent states yields the minimal DFA, which is unique up to renaming. This is the algorithmic shadow of the **Myhill–Nerode theorem**, and it gives a clean test: a language is regular iff it has finitely many such "future-equivalence" classes, and that finite number *is* the minimal DFA's state count. Minimization matters in practice — lexical analyzers and hardware controllers ship the smallest equivalent automaton to save states — and it explains why the NFA-to-DFA blowup is sometimes, but not always, unavoidable.

### Watch out

NFAs do *not* recognize more languages than DFAs — students often assume the extra "guessing" power adds capability; it only adds compactness. Also, "nondeterministic" does not mean "random": an NFA accepts if *some* path works, a kind of perfect-guess optimism, not a coin flip.

atoms.title: Regular languages and the pumping lemma
atoms.summary: Regular languages are exactly those recognized by finite automata; the pumping lemma proves some languages are not regular.

depths.eli5: A 'language' here just means a set of allowed words. Finite-memory machines can recognize lots of word-patterns, but they can't truly count, because they only remember which of a few states they're in. So a pattern like 'some number of A's followed by the exact same number of B's' is beyond them — and the 'pumping lemma' is a clever trick that proves it.
depths.core: A language is 'regular' exactly when some DFA recognizes it. The pumping lemma states that for any regular language there is a length p such that every accepted string of length ≥ p can be cut into three parts xyz — with the middle part y non-empty and sitting within the first p symbols — so that repeating that middle part any number of times, xy^i z, still gives a string in the language for every i ≥ 0. If no such p can possibly work for a language, that language is not regular. This is the standard tool for proving patterns like {0^n 1^n} (n zeros then n ones) lie outside the regular class.
depths.deep: The pumping lemma is really the pigeonhole principle applied to states: a long enough accepted string forces the automaton to revisit some state, creating a loop (the y part) that can be traversed any number of times. The lemma is a necessary but not sufficient condition for regularity, so a clean non-regularity proof must show the pumping condition fails for every possible way of cutting the string.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A **language** here just means a set of allowed words. Finite-memory machines recognize many word patterns, but they fundamentally cannot *count without bound*, because they only ever remember which of finitely many states they're in. A pattern like "some number of A's followed by *exactly the same number* of B's" requires remembering an arbitrarily large count — beyond any fixed automaton. The **pumping lemma** is the clever lever that proves such languages are not regular.

### Precisely

A language is **regular** iff some DFA recognizes it. The **pumping lemma** states: for every regular language $L$ there is a "pumping length" $p$ such that every $w\in L$ with $|w|\ge p$ can be split as $w=xyz$ with

$$|y|\ge 1,\quad |xy|\le p,\quad\text{and}\quad xy^i z\in L \text{ for all } i\ge 0.$$

That is, the middle part $y$ (non-empty, occurring within the first $p$ symbols) can be repeated any number of times — or deleted — and the result stays in $L$. If *no* such $p$ can work, $L$ is **not regular**.

### Worked example

Show $L=\{0^n1^n : n\ge 0\}$ is not regular. Suppose it were, with pumping length $p$. Take $w=0^p1^p\in L$. By the lemma $w=xyz$ with $|xy|\le p$, so $x$ and $y$ consist only of 0s; say $y=0^k$ with $k\ge 1$. Pump up: $xy^2z=0^{p+k}1^p$, which has more 0s than 1s, so it is *not* in $L$ — contradiction. Hence no valid $p$ exists and $L$ is not regular. A DFA simply cannot remember the value of $n$.

### Why it works

The lemma is the **pigeonhole principle** applied to states. A DFA with $p$ states reading a string of length $\ge p$ must visit some state twice. The piece of the string consumed *between* those two visits forms a loop — the $y$ part — that the automaton can traverse 0, 1, 2, … times while ending in the same state, so all of $xy^iz$ are accepted or rejected together. A language requiring those pumped strings to behave differently cannot be regular.

### Where it connects

This pins down the limit of **DFA/NFA** and **regular expressions**. The next rung, **context-free languages**, *can* handle $0^n1^n$ using a stack, and has its own (two-segment) pumping lemma. The **Myhill–Nerode theorem** gives an alternative, exact characterization of regularity. The pigeonhole argument recurs throughout complexity theory.

### A second angle

Regular languages enjoy strong **closure properties**, which give a second route to proving non-regularity. They are closed under union, intersection, complement, concatenation, and Kleene star. So if you suspect a language $L$ is non-regular, you can sometimes combine it with a known-regular language and derive a contradiction: e.g. if $L\cap(0^*1^*)$ equals the known-non-regular $\{0^n1^n\}$, and intersection with a regular set preserves regularity, then $L$ cannot be regular. This "closure" technique often dodges the fiddly case analysis of the pumping lemma and is worth keeping in your toolkit alongside it.

### Watch out

The pumping lemma is **necessary but not sufficient**: some non-regular languages still satisfy the pumping condition, so passing it does *not* prove regularity. A correct non-regularity proof must show the condition fails for *every* possible split — you, the prover, don't get to choose $x,y,z$; you must defeat *all* adversarial choices the lemma allows.

atoms.title: Context-free languages and grammars
atoms.summary: Context-free grammars generate nested, recursive structure (like balanced parentheses) that finite automata cannot.

depths.eli5: A 'grammar' is a set of build-rules for words. Context-free grammars allow rules like 'a sentence can contain a smaller sentence inside it', which lets you build nested structures — matching brackets ( [ { } ] ), arithmetic expressions, and the syntax of programming languages — the kind of nesting that plain finite-state machines cannot handle.
depths.core: A 'context-free grammar' (CFG) is a set of 'production rules', each rewriting a single 'nonterminal' symbol (a placeholder) into a string of 'terminals' (actual symbols) and other nonterminals. CFGs generate the 'context-free languages', which are recognized by 'pushdown automata' — finite automata equipped with a 'stack' (a last-in-first-out memory, like a stack of plates). The stack provides exactly the bounded-recursion memory needed for balanced nesting such as {0^n 1^n} (n zeros then n ones) and programming-language syntax.

Parsing a CFG can be done in polynomial time (the CYK algorithm runs in O(n^3)); deterministic CFGs admit linear-time parsers, which is why real compilers restrict their grammars to the well-behaved LL and LR subclasses.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A **grammar** is a set of build-rules for words. **Context-free grammars** allow recursive rules like "a sentence may contain a smaller sentence inside it," which lets you generate *nested* structure: matching brackets, arithmetic expressions, and programming-language syntax. This nesting is precisely what flat finite-state machines cannot do, because nesting requires remembering how deep you are — a job for a stack.

### Precisely

A **context-free grammar (CFG)** is a set of **production rules**, each rewriting a single **nonterminal** (a placeholder symbol) into a string of **terminals** (actual symbols) and nonterminals. Starting from a start symbol and applying rules generates the **context-free language (CFL)**. CFLs are exactly the languages recognized by **pushdown automata** — finite automata equipped with a **stack** (last-in-first-out memory). The stack supplies the bounded-recursion memory needed for balanced nesting.

### Worked example

A grammar for balanced parentheses, with start symbol $S$:

$$S \to (S)\,S \;\mid\; \varepsilon$$

($\varepsilon$ is the empty string). Derive the string "(())": $S\Rightarrow (S)S \Rightarrow ((S)S)S \Rightarrow (())$ by replacing inner $S$'s with $\varepsilon$. The same grammar generates $\{0^n1^n\}$ if you read open-bracket as 0 and close-bracket as 1 — note this is exactly the language the **pumping lemma** proved *non-regular*. The pushdown automaton recognizes it by pushing a marker for each open bracket and popping one for each close, accepting iff the stack empties exactly at the end.

### Why it works

The single stack is the precise extra ingredient. Each open bracket pushes; each close pops the matching one; you accept only if everything matched. There is also a **pumping lemma for context-free languages**, but with *two* pumpable segments ($uvxyz$ with $vy$ pumped together). It proves, for instance, that $\{0^n1^n2^n\}$ is *not* context-free: one stack can synchronize two counts but not three independent ones simultaneously.

### Where it connects

CFGs sit one rung above **regular languages** and one below **context-sensitive** in the **Chomsky hierarchy**. Parsing a CFG runs in polynomial time — the **CYK algorithm** in $O(n^3)$ — and deterministic subclasses (LL, LR) parse in linear time, which is why real compilers restrict their grammars to those. Adding a *second* stack jumps all the way to **Turing-machine** power.

### A second angle

Context-free languages are *not* closed under intersection or complement — a sharp contrast with regular languages. The classic witness: $\{a^nb^nc^m\}$ and $\{a^mb^nc^n\}$ are each context-free (one stack matches one pair), but their intersection is $\{a^nb^nc^n\}$, which is *not* context-free (it needs to match three counts). This failure of closure is exactly why a single pushdown stack hits a ceiling and why parsing real programming languages — which have context-sensitive aspects like declared-before-use variables — needs extra machinery layered on top of the context-free grammar. The grammar handles the nesting; a separate semantic pass handles the rest.

### Watch out

"Context-free" refers to the *form* of the rules (one nonterminal on the left), not to the language being simple — many CFLs are quite intricate. Note $\{0^n1^n\}$ is context-free but $\{0^n1^n2^n\}$ is not; the jump from two matched counts to three crosses the boundary. And passing the regular pumping test means nothing about CFLs — use the *context-free* pumping lemma for those.

atoms.title: The Chomsky hierarchy
atoms.summary: Languages stratify into four nested classes — regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ recursively enumerable — each tied to a machine model.

depths.eli5: There's a ladder of grammar power. Each rung can describe more complicated patterns than the one below it, and each needs a more powerful kind of machine to recognize it — from simple state-hopping machines at the bottom up to fully general computers at the top.
depths.core: Noam Chomsky classified grammars into four types by power: Type 3 (regular, recognized by finite automata), Type 2 (context-free, recognized by pushdown automata), Type 1 (context-sensitive, recognized by 'linear-bounded automata' — Turing machines whose tape is limited to the input length), and Type 0 (recursively enumerable, recognized by full Turing machines). The corresponding language classes are strictly nested — each inclusion is proper — so adding the right kind of memory to a machine strictly increases what it can recognize.
depths.deep: The hierarchy is really a memory ladder: no memory (finite states) → one stack (pushdown) → a tape bounded by the input length (linear-bounded) → an unbounded tape (Turing machine). The jump from Type 1 to Type 0 is the jump from 'always halts' to 'may run forever': context-sensitive languages are 'decidable' (a machine always halts with a yes/no), while recursively enumerable languages are only 'semi-decidable' (it halts and says yes on yes-instances but may loop forever otherwise).

quiz.answer: Memory: none, one stack, a tape bounded by input size, and finally an unbounded tape.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

There is a ladder of grammar power. Each rung describes more complicated patterns than the rung below, and each demands a more capable machine to recognize it — from simple state-hopping automata at the bottom to fully general computers at the top. The single resource that climbs the ladder is **memory**: none, then a stack, then a bounded tape, then an unbounded tape.

### Precisely

Noam Chomsky stratified grammars into four types, each matched to a machine model and a language class:

- **Type 3 — regular**: finite automata.
- **Type 2 — context-free**: pushdown automata (one stack).
- **Type 1 — context-sensitive**: linear-bounded automata (a Turing machine whose tape is limited to the input length).
- **Type 0 — recursively enumerable**: full Turing machines.

The language classes are *strictly* nested:

$$\text{Regular}\subsetneq\text{Context-free}\subsetneq\text{Context-sensitive}\subsetneq\text{Recursively enumerable}.$$

Each inclusion is proper, so each added memory resource strictly increases recognizing power.

### Worked example

Trace one language up the ladder. $\{a^*\}$ (any number of a's) is **regular** — a DFA handles it. $\{0^n1^n\}$ is **context-free** but not regular — a stack counts the 0s, then matches 1s. $\{0^n1^n2^n\}$ is **context-sensitive** but not context-free — a linear-bounded automaton can cross-check three counts on a bounded tape, but one stack cannot. A language encoding "this Turing machine halts on this input" is **recursively enumerable** but not decidable — only a full unbounded-tape machine even semi-recognizes it.

### Why it works

The hierarchy is a memory ladder: no memory (finite states) → one stack (pushdown) → tape bounded by input length (linear-bounded) → unbounded tape (Turing machine). The jump from Type 1 to Type 0 is the jump from "always halts" to "may run forever": context-sensitive languages are **decidable** (the machine always halts with yes/no), while recursively enumerable languages are only **semi-decidable** (the machine halts and says yes on yes-instances but may loop forever on no-instances).

### Where it connects

This unifies **DFA/NFA**, **context-free** grammars, and the **Turing machine** into one picture, and its top two rungs feed directly into **decidability** and the **halting problem**. The decidable/semi-decidable split at the top is the gateway to computability theory; the resource-as-power theme reappears quantitatively in **complexity** (time and space classes).

### A second angle

The hierarchy is not just a classification — it predicts *what tool you need*. If your pattern involves only finite lookback (validating a fixed format), reach for a **regular expression**. If it involves balanced nesting (parsing expressions, JSON, code blocks), you need a **context-free grammar** and a stack. If it involves cross-referencing unbounded counts or agreement (matching declarations to uses), you have left context-free territory and need context-sensitive power or a full general-purpose program. Reading a problem and placing it on the ladder is a practical engineering skill: it tells you immediately whether a lightweight matcher will do or whether you need a real parser or interpreter.

### Watch out

Each inclusion is *strict* — do not assume the levels collapse. Also, "recursively enumerable" (Type 0) is *not* the same as "decidable": the decidable languages sit strictly between context-sensitive and recursively enumerable and are not one of Chomsky's four named types. Finally, "context-sensitive" is a statement about grammar rule form and tape bound, not about everyday "context" in the linguistic sense.

atoms.title: The Turing machine
atoms.summary: A Turing machine is a finite controller with an unbounded tape — the standard mathematical model of any computation.

depths.eli5: Picture an endlessly long paper strip divided into cells, and a little head sitting over one cell. Following a short table of rules, the head reads the symbol under it, writes a symbol, and steps one cell left or right — over and over. That's it. This almost absurdly simple device can compute anything any real computer can; it's the standard model of what 'computing' even means.
depths.core: A Turing machine has a finite set of internal 'states', a read/write 'head', and an infinitely long 'tape' of cells. At each step it reads the symbol under the head and, according to its 'transition rule', writes a symbol, moves the head one cell left or right, and switches state — halting when it reaches an accept or reject state. Despite this simplicity it can carry out any algorithm: its unbounded tape gives it the unlimited memory that finite automata and pushdown automata lack.
depths.deep: A 'universal Turing machine' takes the description of any other Turing machine plus an input and simulates it step by step — the theoretical basis of the stored-program computer (software running on general hardware). Variations (multiple tapes, nondeterministic branching, multiple tracks) all compute exactly the same functions as the basic single-tape model, differing only by a polynomial-time overhead. The model pins down 'computable' precisely enough that we can prove certain tasks are impossible for any computer.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Picture an endlessly long paper strip divided into cells, with a small head sitting over one cell. Following a short table of rules, the head reads the symbol beneath it, writes a symbol, and steps one cell left or right — over and over. That's the whole device. Remarkably, this almost absurdly simple machine can compute anything any real computer can. It is our standard mathematical definition of what "computing" even means.

### Precisely

A **Turing machine** is $(Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,\delta,q_0,q_{\text{acc}},q_{\text{rej}})$: a finite set of states $Q$, input alphabet $\Sigma$, tape alphabet $\Gamma\supseteq\Sigma$ (including a blank), a **transition function**

$$\delta:Q\times\Gamma\to Q\times\Gamma\times\{L,R\},$$

a start state $q_0$, and halting states $q_{\text{acc}},q_{\text{rej}}$. At each step it reads the symbol under the head, then writes a symbol, moves left or right, and changes state, halting when it enters an accept or reject state. The infinitely long tape provides the unbounded memory that finite automata and pushdown automata lack.

### Worked example

A machine to decide "does the binary input contain at least one 1?" Start scanning right from the left end. Rule: in state $q_0$, on reading 0, write 0, move R, stay in $q_0$; on reading 1, move to $q_{\text{acc}}$; on reading blank (end of input), move to $q_{\text{rej}}$. On input "0010" it steps right over 0,0 then hits 1 and accepts. On "000" it walks off into blanks and rejects. The single state plus the tape scan is enough — and the *same* machine framework, with bigger rule tables, can add, multiply, or simulate any program.

### Why it works

A **universal Turing machine** takes the *description* of any other Turing machine plus an input and simulates it step by step — the theoretical basis of the stored-program computer (software running on general hardware). Crucially, all the natural variations — multiple tapes, multiple tracks, nondeterministic branching — compute exactly the same functions as the basic single-tape model, differing only by a polynomial-time overhead. This robustness is why the model so faithfully captures "computation."

### Where it connects

The Turing machine is the reference model behind the **Church–Turing thesis**, **decidability**, the **halting problem**, **Kolmogorov complexity** (which is defined via a universal machine), and all of **complexity theory** (P, NP, PSPACE are time/space classes for this machine). The **Chomsky hierarchy**'s top rung is exactly Turing-recognizable languages.

### A second angle

The number of distinct *configurations* (state + tape contents + head position) a Turing machine can occupy is the hidden quantity behind many proofs. If a machine uses $s$ tape cells, it has at most $|Q|\cdot |\Gamma|^s\cdot s$ configurations — a finite number. A machine that runs longer than its configuration count must have *repeated* a configuration, hence it is in an infinite loop. This counting argument is how space bounds turn into halting guarantees (a space-bounded machine that never repeats a configuration must halt), and it is the seed of **Savitch's theorem** and the relationship between time, space, and the **Chomsky hierarchy**'s decidable levels.

### Watch out

"Infinite tape" does not mean infinite memory *used* — any halting computation touches only finitely many cells; the tape is unbounded, not actually infinite in use. Also, the Turing machine is a model of *computability*, deliberately ignoring efficiency: that a function is Turing-computable says nothing about whether it is computable *fast* — that is what complexity theory adds.

atoms.title: The Church–Turing thesis
atoms.summary: Anything effectively computable by any mechanical procedure is computable by a Turing machine — the definition of 'computable'.

depths.eli5: Any honest, spelled-out, step-by-step method you could ever follow by hand — a recipe with no guessing or magic — can also be carried out by a Turing machine. So 'a computer can do it' and 'there's a definite procedure for it' end up meaning the same thing.
depths.core: The Church–Turing thesis claims that the everyday intuitive idea of an 'effective procedure' (a mechanical, finite, unambiguous recipe) matches exactly what Turing machines — and equivalently the lambda calculus, recursive functions, and every other model — can compute. It is not a theorem but a claim that fixes a definition, made compelling by the striking fact that every independently invented model of computation has turned out to compute the very same set of functions.
depths.deep: The thesis is empirical and conceptual rather than provable, because it equates a precise formal class with an informal human idea. The 'physical' or 'extended' Church–Turing thesis goes further, claiming nature itself can compute nothing a Turing machine cannot (its polynomial-time version is challenged by quantum computing, which may be faster but not more capable). 'Hypercomputation' models exist on paper but need physically impossible resources like infinite-precision real numbers or completed infinite processes.

quiz.prompt: Is the Church–Turing thesis a theorem? Why or why not?
quiz.answer: No — it equates the informal idea of an effective procedure with a formal class, so it cannot be proven, only supported by evidence.

quiz.answer: Every independently proposed model of computation (lambda calculus, recursive functions, register machines, etc.) defines exactly the same set of computable functions.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Any honest, fully spelled-out, step-by-step method you could ever follow by hand — a recipe with no guessing, no magic, no appeal to intuition — can also be carried out by a Turing machine. So "a computer can do it" and "there is a definite mechanical procedure for it" turn out to mean the very same thing. This is less a theorem than a decision to *define* the fuzzy idea of "computable" by the precise idea of "Turing-computable."

### Precisely

The **Church–Turing thesis** claims that the intuitive notion of an **effective procedure** (a finite, mechanical, unambiguous recipe) coincides exactly with what **Turing machines** can compute — and equivalently with the **lambda calculus**, the **general recursive functions**, register machines, and every other reasonable model. It is *not* provable, because it equates a formal class with an informal idea; it is a definitional claim, made overwhelmingly credible by evidence.

### Worked example

Consider the diverse, independently invented models of computation from the 1930s onward: Church's lambda calculus (functions as the primitive), Gödel–Herbrand's recursive functions (built from basic arithmetic operations and recursion), Turing's machines (tape and head), Post's rewriting systems, and later register machines and cellular automata. Each was defined with a completely different intuition. Yet every one was *proved* to compute exactly the same set of functions. This convergence — not any single proof — is the worked "evidence" for the thesis.

### Why it works

The thesis is **empirical and conceptual** rather than deductive: you cannot prove it, only fail to refute it, because one side ("effective procedure") has no prior formal definition. The **physical (extended) Church–Turing thesis** goes further, claiming nature itself computes nothing a Turing machine cannot. Its *polynomial-time* version is challenged by quantum computing (possibly faster, but not more *capable*). **Hypercomputation** models exist on paper but require physically impossible resources like infinite-precision reals or completed infinities.

### Where it connects

The thesis is what licenses us to prove *impossibility* results: once "computable" means "Turing-computable," the **halting problem** and **Gödel incompleteness** become statements about the limits of *all* computation, not just one machine. It underpins **decidability**, the **Chomsky hierarchy**'s top, and the entire enterprise of **complexity theory**.

### A second angle

A clarifying way to hold the thesis: it is a *bridge* between an informal world and a formal one, and bridges of this kind cannot be theorems. Compare "every continuous intuitive notion of area equals the Riemann/Lebesgue integral" — also a definitional commitment justified by how well it captures intuition, not a deduction. The thesis's credibility rests on (1) the convergence of all proposed models, and (2) the failure, across nearly a century, of anyone to exhibit a clearly "effective" procedure that no Turing machine can carry out. Proposed counterexamples invariably smuggle in non-effective resources — exactly what **hypercomputation** schemes do.

### Watch out

The thesis is about *what* is computable, not *how fast* — it says nothing about efficiency, so do not invoke it to argue about P vs NP. Also, it is widely accepted but technically *unprovable*; calling it a "theorem" is a category error. The quantum caveat concerns the *speed* (extended) version, not the basic computability version, which quantum machines do not violate.

atoms.title: Decidability and recognizability
atoms.summary: A problem is decidable if some machine always halts with the right yes/no answer; merely recognizable if it halts on the yes-instances.

depths.eli5: A problem is 'decidable' if there's a method that always finishes and gives you a definite yes or no. It's only 'recognizable' (a weaker property) if the method correctly says yes whenever the true answer is yes, but might run forever — never answering — when the true answer is no.
depths.core: A 'language' here is the set of inputs whose answer is yes. A language is 'decidable' (also called 'recursive') if some Turing machine halts on every input and correctly accepts or rejects it. It is 'recognizable' (also called 'recursively enumerable') if some machine halts and accepts on every yes-instance but is allowed to loop forever on no-instances. The key bridge: a language is decidable exactly when both it and its 'complement' (the set of no-instances) are recognizable.
depths.deep: Problems that are recognizable but not decidable are the heart of computability theory: the halting problem is recognizable (just run the machine — if it halts, accept) yet not decidable, and its complement is not even recognizable. This asymmetry — you can always confirm halting, but you can never, in general, confirm non-halting — is the source of most undecidability proofs, which proceed by 'reduction' (showing that solving the new problem would let you solve the halting problem).
