quiz.prompt: State the relationship between decidability and recognizability.
quiz.answer: A language is decidable iff both it and its complement are recognizable (recursively enumerable).

quiz.prompt: Why is the halting problem recognizable but not decidable?
quiz.answer: You can confirm a yes by simulating until it halts, but you can never be sure a non-halting machine won't eventually stop, so no machine decides it in all cases.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A problem is **decidable** if there is a method that *always finishes* and gives a definite yes or no. It is only **recognizable** — a strictly weaker property — if the method correctly says yes whenever the true answer is yes, but might run forever without answering when the true answer is no. The gap between "always halts" and "halts only on yes" is the central drama of computability theory.

### Precisely

Treat a problem as a **language** $L$ = the set of inputs whose answer is yes. $L$ is **decidable** (also **recursive**) if some Turing machine halts on *every* input and correctly accepts (input in $L$) or rejects (input not in $L$). $L$ is **recognizable** (also **recursively enumerable**, r.e.) if some machine halts and accepts on every yes-instance but is allowed to loop forever on no-instances. The bridge theorem:

$$L \text{ decidable} \iff L \text{ and its complement } \overline{L} \text{ are both recognizable.}$$

### Worked example

Consider $A=\{\langle M,x\rangle : M \text{ halts on } x\}$ (the halting language). It is **recognizable**: simulate $M$ on $x$; if it halts, accept. But you can never safely reject — a machine still running might halt next step or never. So this recognizer never loops-forever-then-says-no. Is $A$ decidable? No (that is the halting problem). And its complement $\overline{A}$ (machines that *don't* halt) is *not even recognizable* — there is no general way to confirm non-halting. So $A$ shows recognizable-but-not-decidable, and $\overline{A}$ shows not-even-recognizable.

### Why it works

The bridge theorem's forward direction is easy: a decider already halts on everything, so it recognizes both $L$ and $\overline{L}$. The reverse is the clever part: if recognizer $R_1$ for $L$ and recognizer $R_2$ for $\overline{L}$ both exist, run them *in parallel* (alternate steps). Every input is in $L$ or $\overline{L}$, so exactly one recognizer eventually accepts — and that tells you the answer with a guaranteed halt. The asymmetry "you can confirm a yes but never a no" is what blocks decidability when only one side is recognizable.

### Where it connects

This framework rests on the **Church–Turing thesis** and the **Turing machine**, and it sets up the **halting problem** (the canonical recognizable-but-undecidable language) and the proof technique of **reduction**. It mirrors the **Chomsky hierarchy**'s decidable (Type 1) vs recursively-enumerable (Type 0) split.

### A second angle

The decidable/recognizable distinction lines up exactly with the top of the **Chomsky hierarchy**: decidable languages are those a Turing machine always halts on, recognizable (recursively enumerable) languages are the Type-0 grammars where the machine may loop. There is a third tier worth naming — **co-recognizable** languages, whose *complements* are recognizable (you can confirm a "no" but maybe not a "yes"). The bridge theorem then reads cleanly: decidable = recognizable AND co-recognizable. Picturing these three overlapping classes, with the decidable languages as their common core, organizes most of computability theory and tells you in advance which direction (yes or no) you can hope to confirm.

### Watch out

"Recognizable" is genuinely weaker than "decidable" — don't conflate them. Also "recursive" here means "decidable," an old usage unrelated to recursion as a programming technique. And the parallel-simulation trick is essential: running the two recognizers *one after the other* would fail, because the first might loop forever and never let the second start.

atoms.title: The halting problem
atoms.summary: No algorithm can decide, for every program and input, whether that program eventually halts — the foundational undecidability result.

depths.eli5: You can't build a perfect 'will-this-program-eventually-finish?' checker that works for every program. Here's the catch: if such a checker existed, you could build a sneaky program that asks the checker about itself and then deliberately does the opposite of whatever the checker predicts — finishing when it's told it'll loop, looping when it's told it'll finish. Rice's theorem generalizes this: every nontrivial property of the function a program computes (its input/output behavior) is undecidable. Undecidability is therefore pervasive, not some rare exotic case.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

You cannot build a perfect "will-this-program-eventually-finish?" checker that works for *every* program. The catch is self-reference: if such a checker existed, you could build a sneaky program that asks the checker about *itself* and then deliberately does the *opposite* of the prediction — finishing when told it will loop, looping when told it will finish. That contradiction means no perfect checker can exist. This is the foundational limit on what algorithms can do.

### Precisely

The **halting problem** asks: given a program $P$ and input $x$, decide whether $P(x)$ eventually **halts** or runs forever. Turing proved this is **undecidable** — no algorithm answers correctly for all $(P,x)$. It remains **recognizable**: simulate and accept if it halts. So the halting language is the textbook example of recognizable-but-not-decidable.

### Worked example (the diagonalization proof)

Assume a perfect decider $H(P,x)$ that returns "halts" or "loops," always correctly and always halting itself. Build a program $D$ that takes one program $P$ as input and does:

$$D(P): \quad \text{if } H(P,P)=\text{"halts" then loop forever, else halt.}$$

Now run $D$ on its *own* description, $D(D)$. If $H(D,D)=$ "halts," then by its code $D(D)$ loops — contradicting $H$. If $H(D,D)=$ "loops," then $D(D)$ halts — again contradicting $H$. Either way $H$ is wrong, so no such $H$ exists.

### Why it works

The engine is **diagonalization** — the same self-reference Cantor used to show the reals are uncountable. $D$ is constructed precisely to disagree with $H$'s verdict about $D$ itself, so $H$ cannot be consistent. The argument needs only that programs can be fed their own descriptions (possible because programs are just strings) and can invoke $H$ as a subroutine.

### Where it connects

Halting is the canonical undecidable problem from which countless others are proven undecidable by **reduction**: if solving problem $A$ would let you solve halting, then $A$ is undecidable too. **Rice's theorem** generalizes massively: *every* nontrivial property of the function a program computes (e.g., "does it ever output 42?") is undecidable. The same self-reference drives **Gödel incompleteness**.

### A second angle

A vivid consequence is the impossibility of a perfect, general **infinite-loop detector** in any programming tool. No IDE, compiler, or verifier can flag *exactly* the programs that hang, for all programs — that would decide halting. This is not a gap in current technology but a permanent limit. Practical tools therefore settle for *sound but incomplete* analyses: they may prove *some* programs terminate (or warn about *some* that might not), accepting false "don't know" answers. The same reduction-from-halting pattern explains why fully general program verification, dead-code elimination, and equivalence checking are all undecidable in their unrestricted forms.

### Watch out

Undecidability is about *no single algorithm for all inputs* — it does *not* mean any particular program's halting is mysterious; many specific programs are easy to analyze. It also does not say "computers can't check halting ever," only that no method works *universally*. And recognizability (you can always confirm a halt) coexists with undecidability — they are not contradictory.

atoms.title: Asymptotic notation (big-O)
atoms.equation: f(n)=O(g(n))\iff \exists c,n_0:\ f(n)\le c\,g(n)\ \forall n\ge n_0
atoms.summary: Big-O captures how a cost grows with input size, ignoring constants and small inputs — the language of efficiency.

depths.eli5: When we judge an algorithm, we care how its work grows as the problem gets bigger — not the exact number of seconds, which depends on the machine. Doubling the input size might double the work, or quadruple it, or barely change it. Big-O is shorthand for that growth rate, like saying 'this takes about n-squared steps' while ignoring fussy details.
depths.core: Writing f(n) = O(g(n)) means: for large enough n, f grows no faster than g, ignoring constant multipliers (the formal definition: f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for some constant c once n passes some threshold). Companion notations Ω (a lower bound) and Θ (a tight bound, both upper and lower) describe matching floors and ceilings. This abstraction lets us rank algorithms by growth rate — O(log n) ≪ O(n) ≪ O(n log n) ≪ O(n^2) ≪ O(2^n) — independent of hardware and constant factors. ('log n' grows extremely slowly; '2^n' grows explosively.)
depths.deep: Asymptotic analysis can mislead when constants or lower-order terms dominate at realistic input sizes (e.g. 'galactic algorithms' with beautiful big-O but absurdly large hidden constants). Amortized and average-case analysis refine the worst-case picture; the gap between worst-case and typical-case behavior is exactly why the simplex method and quicksort thrive in practice despite poor worst cases.

atoms.note: Memorize the ladder: constant ≪ logarithmic ≪ linear ≪ n log n ≪ quadratic ≪ exponential. Crossing from polynomial to exponential is the practical wall.
atoms.art_prompt: growth curves on one axis — flat log, straight line, gentle n log n, rising parabola, exploding exponential — diverging as n increases

quiz.prompt: Is 3n^2 + 100n + 7 equal to O(n^2)? Justify briefly.
quiz.answer: Yes; for large n the n^2 term dominates and the whole expression is bounded by c·n^2 (e.g., c = 4) for n beyond some n_0.

quiz.prompt: What do Ω and Θ denote relative to O?
quiz.answer: Ω is an asymptotic lower bound and Θ is a tight bound (both upper and lower), whereas O is an upper bound.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

When judging an algorithm, we care how its work *grows* as the problem gets bigger — not the exact seconds, which depend on the machine, the language, the day. Doubling the input might double the work, quadruple it, or barely change it. **Big-O** is shorthand for that growth rate: "this takes about $n^2$ steps" while ignoring constant factors and small-input quirks. It is the common language for comparing efficiency across all hardware.

### Precisely

$$f(n)=O(g(n)) \iff \exists\, c>0,\, n_0:\ f(n)\le c\,g(n)\ \text{ for all } n\ge n_0.$$

Read: beyond some threshold $n_0$, $f$ grows no faster than a constant multiple of $g$. Companions: $\Omega(g)$ is a *lower* bound ($f\ge c\,g$ eventually), and $\Theta(g)$ is a *tight* bound (both $O$ and $\Omega$). These let us rank growth rates independent of hardware:

$$O(1)\ll O(\log n)\ll O(n)\ll O(n\log n)\ll O(n^2)\ll O(2^n).$$

### Worked example

Is $3n^2+100n+7=O(n^2)$? Yes. For $n\ge 100$, each term is bounded: $3n^2\le 3n^2$, $100n\le n^2$, $7\le n^2$, so the sum is $\le 5n^2$. Take $c=5$, $n_0=100$: the definition holds. The $100n$ term *dominates* for small $n$ (at $n=1$ it's the biggest), but asymptotically $n^2$ wins, and big-O cares only about the asymptote. The constant 3 and the lower-order $100n+7$ are simply discarded.

### Why it works

The logarithmic and polynomial ladder is robust because it survives changes of machine and constant factor — exactly what the **Cobham–Edmonds** view of tractability needs. Constants and lower-order terms wash out as $n\to\infty$, so the leading term's *order* is what determines scalability. Crossing from polynomial to exponential is the practical wall: $2^n$ overtakes any polynomial and quickly becomes astronomically large.

### Where it connects

Big-O is the measuring stick for **divide and conquer**, **dynamic programming**, **graph algorithms**, **hashing**, **greedy** and **amortized** analysis, and it formalizes the class **P** (polynomial time) and the **time hierarchy**. The whole edifice of **complexity theory** is phrased in it.

### A second angle

Beware of comparing growth rates by plugging in one input size — asymptotics are about the *trend*, not a single point. At $n=10$, an $O(n^2)$ algorithm (100 steps) beats an $O(n\log n)$ one only if constants align; the ordering $n\log n\ll n^2$ is a promise about *large* $n$. A practical habit: identify the single dominant term, drop constants and lower-order terms, and only then compare. Also keep the three notations straight by their role — $O$ for "no worse than" (upper bound, for guarantees), $\Omega$ for "no better than" (lower bound, for impossibility), and $\Theta$ for "exactly this order" (a matched claim).

### Watch out

Asymptotics can mislead at realistic sizes: a "galactic" algorithm with beautiful $O(n)$ but a hidden constant of $10^{100}$ is useless in practice. Big-O is an *upper* bound, so saying an algorithm is "$O(n^2)$" doesn't forbid it from also being $O(n)$ — use $\Theta$ when you mean a tight bound. And worst-case big-O can differ wildly from typical behavior (quicksort, simplex).

atoms.title: Divide and conquer
atoms.summary: Split a problem into smaller subproblems, solve them recursively, and combine — the recipe behind mergesort and fast multiplication.

depths.eli5: Take a big job, cut it into smaller pieces, solve each piece the exact same way (cutting those further until they're trivial), then stitch the partial answers back together. Sorting a shuffled deck by splitting it in half, sorting each half, then merging the two sorted halves is the classic example ('mergesort').
depths.core: A divide-and-conquer algorithm breaks an input of size n into 'a' subproblems each of size n/b, solves them by 'recursion' (calling itself on the smaller pieces), and spends f(n) extra work combining the results — giving the recurrence (self-referential cost formula) T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n). The 'Master Theorem' solves such recurrences by comparing the combine cost f(n) to n^(log_b a); whichever term is bigger sets the overall running time. Mergesort (a=2, b=2, f(n)=n) comes out to Θ(n log n).
depths.deep: Divide and conquer wins when the subproblems are independent and recombining is cheap compared to the split. Karatsuba multiplication beats grade-school O(n^2) by cleverly reducing four sub-multiplications to three (T(n)=3T(n/2)+O(n) → O(n^1.585)); the Fast Fourier Transform pushes the idea to O(n log n) polynomial multiplication. When the subproblems overlap and get re-solved, divide and conquer wastes work and dynamic programming is the right tool instead.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Take a big job, cut it into smaller pieces, solve each piece *the exact same way* (cutting further until trivial), then stitch the partial answers back together. Sorting a shuffled deck by splitting it in half, sorting each half, then merging the two sorted halves — **mergesort** — is the classic example. The power comes from recursion doing the heavy lifting and a cheap "combine" step assembling the result.

### Precisely

A divide-and-conquer algorithm splits an input of size $n$ into $a$ subproblems each of size $n/b$, solves them recursively, and spends $f(n)$ extra work combining, giving the recurrence

$$T(n)=a\,T(n/b)+f(n).$$

The **Master Theorem** solves such recurrences by comparing $f(n)$ to $n^{\log_b a}$: whichever grows faster sets $T(n)$. The three cases are (i) $f(n)$ smaller $\Rightarrow T=\Theta(n^{\log_b a})$, (ii) comparable $\Rightarrow T=\Theta(n^{\log_b a}\log n)$, (iii) $f(n)$ larger (with a regularity condition) $\Rightarrow T=\Theta(f(n))$.

### Worked example

Mergesort: split the array in two ($a=2$, $b=2$) and merge in linear time ($f(n)=n$). The recurrence is $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n$. Compute $n^{\log_b a}=n^{\log_2 2}=n^1=n$, which is *comparable* to $f(n)=n$ — Master Theorem case (ii) — giving

$$T(n)=\Theta(n\log n).$$

You can also see this directly: the recursion tree has $\log_2 n$ levels, each doing $\Theta(n)$ total merging work, so $n\log n$ overall.

### Why it works

Divide and conquer wins when subproblems are **independent** and recombining is **cheap** relative to the split. The Master Theorem just bookkeeps the recursion tree: level $i$ has $a^i$ nodes of size $n/b^i$; summing $f$ over all nodes and levels reduces to comparing the per-level work against a geometric series, whose dominant term gives the answer.

### Where it connects

The same recipe yields **Karatsuba** multiplication ($T(n)=3T(n/2)+O(n)=O(n^{1.585})$, beating grade-school $O(n^2)$) and the **FFT** ($O(n\log n)$). When subproblems *overlap* and get re-solved, divide and conquer wastes work — that is exactly when **dynamic programming** takes over by caching results. Built on **big-O** analysis.

### A second angle

Reading a recursion via its **recursion tree** demystifies the Master Theorem. Each level $i$ has $a^i$ subproblems of size $n/b^i$, doing $a^i f(n/b^i)$ work. Three regimes emerge: if the per-level work *shrinks* down the tree, the root dominates and $T=\Theta(f(n))$; if it *grows*, the leaves dominate and $T=\Theta(n^{\log_b a})$; if it is *constant* across $\log_b n$ levels, you get the extra $\log n$ factor, $T=\Theta(n^{\log_b a}\log n)$. Mergesort is the balanced middle case. Drawing the tree once for an unfamiliar recurrence is faster and safer than memorizing the three formal cases.

### Watch out

The Master Theorem covers only recurrences of the form $aT(n/b)+f(n)$ with the standard cases — uneven splits or $f$ that doesn't fit need other tools (Akra–Bazzi, recursion-tree, substitution). Case (iii) also requires a regularity condition, easy to forget. And don't apply divide and conquer when subproblems overlap; you'll get exponential blowup.

atoms.title: Dynamic programming
atoms.summary: Solve overlapping subproblems once and reuse the answers, turning exponential brute force into polynomial time.

depths.eli5: If the same small subproblem keeps coming up while you work, solve it just once and jot the answer down — then look it up instead of redoing the work a thousand times. That bookkeeping is dynamic programming, and it can turn a hopelessly slow brute-force approach into a fast one.
depths.core: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has two features: 'optimal substructure' (the best overall answer is built out of best answers to subproblems) and 'overlapping subproblems' (the same subproblems come up again and again). You write a 'recurrence' (a formula expressing each case in terms of smaller cases) over a set of 'states', then either fill a table bottom-up or 'memoize' top-down (cache each result the first time you compute it) so every state is solved exactly once. Computing Fibonacci numbers, shortest paths, edit distance between strings, and the knapsack problem are canonical examples.
depths.deep: The art is choosing the right 'state space' so the recurrence is both correct and small; the running time is roughly (number of states) × (work per transition). Bellman's principle of optimality justifies the recurrence, and for shortest paths it yields the Bellman–Ford and Floyd–Warshall algorithms. Many dynamic programs can be sped up further with monotonicity tricks (convex-hull, Knuth, and divide-and-conquer optimization).

atoms.note: Two ingredients are mandatory: optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. Without overlap, plain divide and conquer suffices; without optimal substructure, DP is invalid.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

If the same small subproblem keeps coming up while you work, solve it *once*, jot the answer down, and look it up instead of redoing the work a thousand times. That bookkeeping is **dynamic programming (DP)**, and it can turn a hopelessly slow brute-force approach into a fast one — often from exponential to polynomial time. The art is recognizing the repeated subproblems and naming them cleanly.

### Precisely

DP applies when a problem has two features:

- **Optimal substructure**: an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to subproblems.
- **Overlapping subproblems**: the same subproblems recur many times.

You write a **recurrence** over a set of **states** (subproblem identities), then solve each state once — either bottom-up (fill a table) or top-down with **memoization** (cache on first computation). Total time $\approx$ (number of states) $\times$ (work per transition).

### Worked example

Fibonacci. The naive recursion $F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2)$ recomputes $F(k)$ exponentially many times — $\Theta(\varphi^n)$ calls. The states here are just $F(0),F(1),\dots,F(n)$: only $n+1$ distinct subproblems. Memoize: compute each $F(k)$ once, store it, reuse it. Now there are $n+1$ states with $O(1)$ work each, giving $O(n)$ time. The exponential blowup was *entirely* redundant recomputation, which the cache eliminates.

### Why it works

**Bellman's principle of optimality** justifies the recurrence: if the global optimum passes through a subproblem, the portion within that subproblem must itself be optimal — otherwise you could swap in a better sub-solution and improve the whole, a contradiction. Overlap is what makes caching pay off: without it, every subproblem is unique and plain **divide and conquer** suffices. The running time follows because each state is solved exactly once.

### Where it connects

DP solves shortest paths (**Bellman–Ford**, **Floyd–Warshall**), edit distance, knapsack, and sequence alignment. **Backpropagation** in neural networks is DP over the computation graph (reusing the chain rule). It sits one step beyond **divide and conquer** and underlies many **graph algorithms**.

### A second angle

A reliable recipe for designing a DP: (1) define the **state** — the minimal information identifying a subproblem; (2) write the **recurrence** expressing each state via smaller states; (3) identify **base cases**; (4) choose an **evaluation order** (bottom-up table or top-down memoization) so every state is ready when needed; (5) read the answer from the final state, optionally reconstructing the choices. For edit distance, the state is "(prefix of string A, prefix of string B)", the recurrence picks the cheapest of insert/delete/substitute, and the table is filled row by row. Most DP "aha" difficulty is entirely in step (1) — naming the right state.

### Watch out

Both ingredients are mandatory. Without **overlapping subproblems**, DP gives no speedup over divide and conquer. Without **optimal substructure**, DP is simply *incorrect* — greedy-looking recurrences can give wrong answers. Also, a sloppy state definition can blow up the state space or miss cases; choosing the *right*, minimal state is the real skill.

atoms.title: Graphs and graph search
atoms.summary: Graphs model relationships as vertices and edges; BFS and DFS explore them, underpinning shortest paths, connectivity, and ordering.

depths.eli5: A 'graph' (in this sense, not a chart) is just dots connected by lines — cities joined by roads, people joined by friendships. The dots are 'vertices' and the lines are 'edges'. To explore a graph you either fan out level by level from a starting dot (breadth-first search, BFS) or plunge deep down one path and back up when stuck (depth-first search, DFS).
depths.core: A graph G = (V, E) is a set of vertices V and a set of edges E; edges can be 'directed' (one-way) or 'undirected' (two-way), and 'weighted' (each edge has a cost) or not. Breadth-first search explores outward in layers and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; depth-first search recurses along edges and reveals connectivity, cycles, and 'topological order' (a valid ordering of tasks that respects all dependencies). Dijkstra's algorithm extends BFS to graphs with non-negative edge weights using a 'priority queue' (a structure that always hands back the smallest pending item), running in O((V+E) log V).
depths.deep: Graph problems span the whole difficulty spectrum: shortest path and minimum spanning tree are solvable in polynomial time, while Hamiltonian cycle and graph coloring are NP-complete (believed intractable). The same graph can pose an easy or a hard question — finding an Eulerian circuit (use every edge exactly once) is linear-time, but finding a Hamiltonian cycle (visit every vertex exactly once) is NP-complete, despite how similar the two sound.

quiz.answer: BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS yields topological order (on a DAG).

quiz.answer: BFS counts edges, not weights, so a path with more low-weight edges can be cheaper than a few heavy ones; Dijkstra's priority queue handles weights.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A **graph** here is dots connected by lines — cities joined by roads, people joined by friendships, web pages joined by links. The dots are **vertices**, the lines **edges**. To explore a graph you either fan out level by level from a starting dot (**breadth-first search**, BFS) or plunge deep down one path, backtracking when stuck (**depth-first search**, DFS). These two traversals underlie an enormous fraction of practical algorithms.

### Precisely

A graph is $G=(V,E)$: a set of vertices $V$ and edges $E\subseteq V\times V$. Edges may be **directed** (one-way) or **undirected**, **weighted** (a cost per edge) or not. **BFS** explores outward in layers and finds shortest paths in *unweighted* graphs. **DFS** recurses along edges and reveals connectivity, cycles, and **topological order** (an ordering of vertices respecting all directed dependencies, on a DAG). **Dijkstra's algorithm** extends shortest paths to non-negative weights using a **priority queue**, running in $O((V+E)\log V)$.

### Worked example

Find the fewest hops from vertex $A$ in an unweighted graph with edges $A\!-\!B$, $A\!-\!C$, $B\!-\!D$, $C\!-\!D$, $D\!-\!E$. BFS from $A$: layer 0 = $\{A\}$; layer 1 = $\{B,C\}$ (neighbors of $A$); layer 2 = $\{D\}$ (reached from $B$ and $C$); layer 3 = $\{E\}$. So distances are $A$:0, $B$:1, $C$:1, $D$:2, $E$:3. BFS discovers each vertex at its shortest hop-distance because it never visits a layer-$k$ vertex before exhausting layer $k\!-\!1$.

### Why it works

BFS uses a FIFO queue, guaranteeing vertices come out in nondecreasing distance order — that ordering *is* the shortest-path proof for unweighted graphs. DFS uses recursion (a stack), and finishing-times of that recursion yield topological order. Dijkstra generalizes BFS: instead of a plain queue it uses a priority queue keyed by accumulated weight, always finalizing the closest unfinished vertex, which is correct precisely because edge weights are non-negative (no shorter path can arrive later).

### Where it connects

Graph problems span the whole difficulty spectrum. Shortest path and **minimum spanning tree** are polynomial (the latter solved by **greedy** algorithms). But Hamiltonian cycle and graph coloring are **NP-complete**. Strikingly, finding an *Eulerian* circuit (use every edge once) is linear-time, while a *Hamiltonian* cycle (visit every vertex once) is NP-complete — nearly identical-sounding problems on opposite sides of the tractability line. Built on **big-O**.

### A second angle

Representation choice quietly drives performance. An **adjacency list** stores, per vertex, its neighbors — using $O(V+E)$ space and making "iterate over a vertex's neighbors" fast, ideal for the sparse graphs ($E\ll V^2$) that dominate practice. An **adjacency matrix** uses $O(V^2)$ space but answers "is there an edge $u\!-\!v$?" in $O(1)$, useful for dense graphs or algorithms like Floyd–Warshall. BFS and DFS run in $O(V+E)$ on adjacency lists — linear in the graph's size — which is why they scale to graphs with millions of vertices. Picking the representation before coding the algorithm is half the battle.

### Watch out

Plain BFS fails for *weighted* shortest paths: it counts edges, not weights, so a many-small-edges path can beat a few-heavy-edges path — use Dijkstra. Dijkstra in turn fails with *negative* edges (use Bellman–Ford). And "graph" in this sense (vertices and edges) is unrelated to a "graph" of a function — a frequent terminology collision.

atoms.title: Hashing and core data structures
atoms.summary: Data structures trade memory for speed; hash tables give expected O(1) lookup by scattering keys across buckets.

depths.eli5: A 'data structure' is a way of organizing information so certain operations are fast. A hash table is like a coat-check counter: a quick formula turns your ticket number into a specific hook, so the attendant grabs your coat instantly instead of checking every hook. The formula that turns a key into a slot is the 'hash function'.
depths.core: Choosing a data structure means choosing which operations you want to be fast. Arrays give O(1) lookup by position; balanced search trees give O(log n) ordered queries (find, range, sort); heaps give O(log n) access to the smallest or largest item; and hash tables give expected O(1) insert and lookup by mapping each key to a 'bucket' (slot) through a hash function. When two keys land in the same bucket — a 'collision' — it is resolved by 'chaining' (keep a small list in that bucket) or 'open addressing' (probe for the next free slot).
depths.deep: A hash table's speed guarantees are probabilistic and depend on the hash function spreading keys roughly evenly. With 'universal hashing' (picking the hash function at random from a carefully designed family) the expected number of collisions stays O(1) for any input, defeating an adversary who would otherwise craft inputs forcing the O(n) worst case. The space–time tradeoff is fundamental: Bloom filters shrink memory in exchange for occasional false positives, while cuckoo and perfect hashing buy guaranteed worst-case O(1) lookups at extra construction cost.

atoms.note: Worst-case for a naive hash table is O(n) per operation; universal/randomized hashing restores expected O(1) even against adversarial inputs.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A **data structure** organizes information so that certain operations are fast. A **hash table** is like a coat-check counter: a quick formula turns your ticket number into a specific hook, so the attendant grabs your coat instantly instead of scanning every hook. The formula mapping a key to a slot is the **hash function**. Choosing a data structure is really choosing *which operations* you want to be cheap.

### Precisely

Common structures and their costs: **arrays** give $O(1)$ lookup by index; **balanced search trees** give $O(\log n)$ ordered queries (find, range, successor); **heaps** give $O(\log n)$ access to the min or max; **hash tables** give *expected* $O(1)$ insert and lookup by mapping each key through a hash function to a **bucket**. When two keys map to the same bucket — a **collision** — it is resolved by **chaining** (a small list per bucket) or **open addressing** (probe for the next free slot).

### Worked example

Hash 12 keys into a table of 16 buckets with $h(k)=k \bmod 16$. Keys 7, 23, 39 all give $7,7,7$ — a collision chain of length 3 in bucket 7. Lookup of 23: compute $h(23)=7$, then walk that bucket's short chain comparing keys. If the hash spreads keys evenly, chains stay length $O(1)$ on average and lookup is $O(1)$. If an adversary deliberately sends keys that all hash to bucket 7, the chain grows to length $n$ and lookup degrades to $O(n)$ — the worst case.

### Why it works

Hash-table speed is **probabilistic** and depends on the hash spreading keys roughly uniformly. **Universal hashing** picks the hash function at *random* from a carefully designed family, so that for *any* fixed input the expected collisions stay $O(1)$ — defeating an adversary, because they cannot predict which function you chose. The space–time tradeoff is fundamental: **Bloom filters** shrink memory at the cost of occasional false positives; **cuckoo** and **perfect hashing** buy worst-case $O(1)$ lookups at extra construction cost.

### Where it connects

Built on **big-O** and **probability** (expectation analyzes collision counts). Hash tables power dictionaries, sets, database indexes, and caches. **Cryptographic** hash functions add the one-way property used in signatures and integrity checks (related to **one-way functions**). The expected-vs-worst-case distinction echoes the themes of **randomized algorithms**.

### A second angle

The **load factor** $\alpha=n/m$ (items over buckets) is the dial controlling a hash table's speed. With chaining, the expected chain length is $\alpha$, so lookups cost $O(1+\alpha)$ — kept $O(1)$ by *resizing* (rehashing into a bigger table) whenever $\alpha$ exceeds a threshold, an operation analyzed by **amortized** analysis exactly like the doubling dynamic array. With open addressing, performance degrades sharply as $\alpha\to 1$ (probes pile up), so those tables resize earlier. Understanding the load factor explains both why hash tables are fast in practice and why their occasional resize spikes are nonetheless cheap when averaged.

### Watch out

"Expected $O(1)$" is not "guaranteed $O(1)$" — a naive fixed hash has a real $O(n)$ worst case on adversarial input; universal/randomized hashing is what restores the guarantee. Also, hash tables give up *order*: they cannot do range queries or sorted traversal efficiently — when you need those, a balanced tree's $O(\log n)$ is the right choice despite being slower per single lookup.

atoms.title: The class P (efficient computation)
atoms.summary: P is the class of problems a deterministic machine solves in polynomial time — the standard formal notion of 'tractable'.

depths.eli5: P is the collection of problems a computer can solve reasonably fast. 'Fast' here means the work grows like the input size raised to some fixed power (n, n-squared, n-cubed…) rather than exploding. A 'decision problem' is one with a yes/no answer, like 'is this number prime?'.
depths.core: A decision problem is in P if some deterministic Turing machine decides it in time O(n^k) for some constant power k ('polynomial time'). Polynomial time is the robust dividing line between 'tractable' (practically solvable) and 'intractable': it is closed under composition (plugging one efficient algorithm into another stays efficient) and stays the same across all reasonable machine models (the Cobham–Edmonds thesis), so 'polynomial' means the same thing whether you count tape steps or laptop operations.
depths.deep: Polynomial time is a deliberate idealization — an O(n^100) algorithm is 'efficient' in theory but useless in practice, while a few exponential-time algorithms run fine on real inputs. Yet the polynomial/exponential boundary stays the right theoretical cut because it is model-independent and composition-stable, which finer constant-sensitive definitions are not. Sorting, shortest paths, and primality testing all sit comfortably inside P.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

**P** is the collection of problems a computer can solve *reasonably fast*. "Fast" here means the work grows like the input size raised to some fixed power — $n$, $n^2$, $n^3$ — rather than exploding exponentially. P is the standard formal stand-in for "tractable," the dividing line between problems we can realistically solve and those we (probably) cannot.

### Precisely

A **decision problem** (yes/no answer) is in **P** if some *deterministic* Turing machine decides it in time $O(n^k)$ for some constant $k$ — **polynomial time**. Formally,

$$\text{P}=\bigcup_{k\ge 1}\text{DTIME}(n^k).$$

Polynomial time is robust: it is **closed under composition** (an efficient algorithm calling another stays efficient) and is **model-independent** — the same problems are in P whether you count Turing-machine steps or laptop operations (the **Cobham–Edmonds thesis**).

### Worked example

Is a number prime? Decision form: "given $n$ in binary, is it prime?" The input size is the number of *digits*, about $\log n$ bits. Trial division up to $\sqrt n$ takes about $\sqrt n=2^{(\log n)/2}$ steps — *exponential* in the input size, so that algorithm is *not* polynomial. Yet primality *is* in P: the AKS algorithm (2002) decides it in time polynomial in the number of digits. The lesson: "polynomial" is measured against *input length* (digits), not the numeric value.

### Why it works

Polynomial time is the *right* theoretical cut precisely because of its robustness. Compose two polynomial algorithms and the result is still polynomial ($n^a$ fed into $n^b$ gives $n^{ab}$). Switch machine models and polynomials map to polynomials. Constant-sensitive definitions (like "$\le 100n$ steps") lack both properties and so make poor theoretical boundaries. The polynomial/exponential gap is stable under all these transformations.

### Where it connects

P is the baseline for **NP**, **PSPACE**, **NP-completeness**, and the famous **P vs NP** question. Sorting, shortest paths (**graph algorithms**), and primality all live comfortably in P. The **time hierarchy theorem** proves $\text{P}\subsetneq\text{EXP}$. Built on the **Turing machine** and **big-O**.

### A second angle

A common confusion is *what counts as "input size."* For graph and string problems it is the obvious length, but for *number* problems it is the number of **bits**, not the magnitude. An algorithm running in time proportional to the numeric value $N$ is **pseudo-polynomial**, not polynomial, because $N$ is exponential in its bit-length $\log N$. This is exactly the gap between the knapsack problem's $O(nW)$ dynamic program (pseudo-polynomial, since $W$ is a value) and genuine polynomial time, and it is why knapsack is NP-hard despite that "fast-looking" DP. Always anchor "polynomial" to input *length* in bits.

### Watch out

Polynomial is a *deliberate idealization*: an $O(n^{100})$ algorithm is "in P" yet useless in practice, while a few exponential algorithms run fine on real inputs. "In P" means "tractable in principle," not "fast for your data." Also, P is defined for *decision* problems; optimization problems are handled by their decision versions. And always measure complexity against *input length*, not numeric magnitude.

atoms.title: The class NP and verification
atoms.summary: NP is the class of problems whose 'yes' answers have short certificates checkable in polynomial time.

depths.eli5: NP problems are ones where finding the answer might be very hard, but checking a proposed answer is fast — like a completed jigsaw puzzle: hard to assemble from scratch, but you can glance at a finished one and instantly see it's right.
depths.core: A problem is in NP if every yes-instance comes with a 'certificate' (also called a 'witness') — a short piece of evidence, polynomial in size — that a deterministic 'verifier' can check in polynomial time. Equivalently, NP is the set of problems a nondeterministic Turing machine (one allowed to 'guess' and explore many paths at once) can decide in polynomial time. P ⊆ NP, because if you can solve a problem outright you can certainly verify a claimed answer; whether that inclusion is strict (whether some NP problems truly cannot be solved as fast as they can be checked) is the famous P vs NP question.
depths.deep: NP is fundamentally about the asymmetry between finding a solution and checking one. The complementary class co-NP concerns short certificates for no-instances; whether NP = co-NP is open and tied to whether short proofs of unsatisfiability always exist. Most natural search problems whose solutions are easy to recognize but seemingly require search — Boolean satisfiability (SAT), finding a large clique, scheduling — live in NP.

atoms.note: P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXP. Each inclusion is believed strict; only P ⊊ EXP is currently proven (by the time hierarchy theorem).

quiz.prompt: Give the verifier-based definition of NP.
quiz.answer: Problems whose yes-instances have polynomial-size certificates checkable by a deterministic verifier in polynomial time.

quiz.prompt: Why is P ⊆ NP immediate?
quiz.answer: If you can solve a problem in polynomial time, you can verify any claimed answer in polynomial time (just re-solve), so every P problem is in NP.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

**NP** problems are ones where *finding* an answer might be very hard, but *checking* a proposed answer is fast — like a completed jigsaw puzzle: brutal to assemble from scratch, but you can glance at a finished one and instantly confirm it's correct. This asymmetry between solving and verifying is the heart of NP and of the most famous open question in computer science.

### Precisely

A problem is in **NP** if every yes-instance has a **certificate** (a **witness**) — a piece of evidence polynomial in size — that a deterministic **verifier** checks in polynomial time. Equivalently, NP is what a *nondeterministic* Turing machine (one that may "guess" and explore many paths at once) decides in polynomial time. Clearly

$$\text{P}\subseteq\text{NP},$$

since if you can *solve* a problem fast you can certainly *verify* a claimed answer fast. Whether the inclusion is strict is the **P vs NP** question.

### Worked example

Boolean satisfiability (**SAT**): given a logical formula, is there an assignment of true/false to its variables making it true? Finding such an assignment may require searching $2^n$ possibilities. But if someone *hands* you an assignment, you just plug it in and evaluate the formula — linear time. The assignment is the polynomial-size certificate; the evaluator is the verifier. So SAT is in NP. Same pattern for "does this graph have a clique of size $k$?" — hand over the $k$ vertices, check all pairs are connected.

### Why it works

$\text{P}\subseteq\text{NP}$ is immediate: a P-algorithm *is* a verifier that ignores the certificate and re-solves the problem. The two definitions of NP (certificate-checking vs nondeterministic guessing) coincide because a nondeterministic machine's accepting *path* is exactly a certificate, and a verifier reading a certificate simulates choosing that path. NP captures "easy to recognize a solution, seemingly hard to find one."

### Where it connects

NP sets up **reductions**, **NP-completeness** (the hardest problems in NP), and **co-NP** (certificates for *no*-instances). The chain $\text{P}\subseteq\text{NP}\subseteq\text{PSPACE}\subseteq\text{EXP}$ places it among the **space-complexity** classes. Cryptography's **one-way functions** rely on a related (but stronger, average-case) hardness.

### A second angle

The relationship $\text{P}\subseteq\text{NP}\subseteq\text{PSPACE}$ has an intuitive reading. A P problem you can *solve* outright. An NP problem you can *check* a guessed solution to — equivalently, a nondeterministic machine *guesses* the certificate then verifies. A PSPACE problem you can solve by *systematically trying all* guesses while reusing memory, which is why NP (one round of guessing) sits inside PSPACE (exhaustive bounded-memory search). This "solve / verify a guess / exhaust all guesses" ladder is the cleanest mental model of the lower complexity hierarchy, and it foreshadows why **space-complexity** treats nondeterminism so much more gently than time does.

### Watch out

NP does *not* mean "non-polynomial" — it means *nondeterministic* polynomial, and P problems are a subset of NP. Also, NP is about *short, checkable certificates for yes-instances*; there is no symmetric guarantee for no-instances (that's co-NP, possibly different). Finally, "NP-hard" and "in NP" are distinct — a problem can be NP-hard without being in NP.

atoms.title: Polynomial-time reductions
atoms.summary: A reduction transforms one problem into another in polynomial time, transferring tractability and hardness between them.

depths.eli5: A 'reduction' is a way of rewriting one problem as another. If you can quickly rewrite every instance of problem A as an instance of problem B, then any solver for B automatically solves A too — just translate, solve, and translate back. That means A is 'no harder than' B.
depths.core: A polynomial-time 'many-one reduction' from A to B is a polynomial-time function f that converts each instance of A into an instance of B with the very same yes/no answer, written A ≤_p B. It certifies that A is no harder than B up to polynomial factors: if B ∈ P then A ∈ P, and (taking the contrapositive) if A is known to be hard then B must be hard too. Reductions are, in effect, the algebra of computational difficulty.
depths.deep: Reductions are 'transitive' — A ≤_p B and B ≤_p C together give A ≤_p C — which is what lets a single hard problem certify the hardness of thousands of others. The direction matters: to prove B is hard you reduce a known-hard A to B (A ≤_p B), not the reverse, a very common student pitfall. 'Turing reductions' (which allow repeated oracle calls to B) are more permissive than many-one reductions and define different notions of completeness.

quiz.answer: Reduce a known-hard problem A to B (A ≤_p B): if B were easy, A would be too, contradicting A's hardness — so B must be hard.

quiz.prompt: If A ≤_p B and B ∈ P, what follows about A?
quiz.answer: A ∈ P — tractability transfers from B back to A through the reduction.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A **reduction** rewrites one problem as another. If you can *quickly* rewrite every instance of problem $A$ as an instance of problem $B$ with the same answer, then any solver for $B$ automatically solves $A$ — just translate, solve, translate back. That means "$A$ is no harder than $B$." Reductions are the algebra of computational difficulty: they let one hard problem certify the hardness of thousands of others.

### Precisely

A **polynomial-time many-one reduction** from $A$ to $B$, written $A\le_p B$, is a polynomial-time computable function $f$ such that for every instance $w$,

$$w\in A \iff f(w)\in B.$$

It certifies $A$ is no harder than $B$ up to polynomial factors: if $B\in\text{P}$ then $A\in\text{P}$; contrapositively, if $A$ is hard then $B$ is hard. Reductions are **transitive**: $A\le_p B$ and $B\le_p C$ give $A\le_p C$.

### Worked example

Reduce SAT to 3-SAT (clauses of exactly three literals). Given any clause with more than three literals, say $(x_1\lor x_2\lor x_3\lor x_4)$, introduce a fresh variable $y$ and replace it with two clauses $(x_1\lor x_2\lor y)\land(\bar y\lor x_3\lor x_4)$. A satisfying assignment of the original extends to one of the new (pick $y$ to absorb the split), and vice versa. The rewriting is linear-time and answer-preserving — exactly a $\le_p$ reduction showing SAT $\le_p$ 3-SAT.

### Why it works

If $f$ runs in polynomial time and preserves yes/no answers, then composing $f$ with any polynomial solver for $B$ yields a polynomial solver for $A$ — polynomials compose to polynomials. Transitivity follows by composing the two reduction functions; the composite is still polynomial. This composability is precisely what lets a *single* seed problem (SAT) spread hardness across an entire web of problems.

### Where it connects

Reductions are the engine of **NP-completeness** (every NP problem reduces to an NP-complete one) and of undecidability proofs (reduce the **halting problem** to a new problem to prove *it* undecidable). They also define **approximation**-hardness. Built on **P** and **NP**.

### A second angle

Reductions also transfer *algorithms*, not just hardness — the optimistic direction. If you have a fast solver for a well-studied problem $B$ (say linear programming or 2-SAT), and you can reduce your new problem $A$ to $B$, you instantly inherit $B$'s solver and all its engineering. Much of practical problem-solving is exactly this: recognize that your scheduling or matching task *is* a max-flow or shortest-path problem in disguise, reduce to it, and reuse decades of optimized code. So $A\le_p B$ reads two ways — "A is no harder than B" for theory, and "B's toolbox now solves A" for practice.

### Watch out

**Direction matters**, and it is the most common student error. To prove $B$ is *hard*, reduce a known-*hard* $A$ *to* $B$ ($A\le_p B$) — not the reverse. Reducing $B$ to something easy proves nothing about $B$'s hardness. Also, **Turing reductions** (allowing repeated oracle calls to $B$) are more permissive than many-one reductions and yield different notions of completeness — don't mix them.

atoms.title: NP-completeness and Cook–Levin
atoms.summary: The NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP; Boolean satisfiability was the first, and a fast algorithm for any one would crack them all.

depths.eli5: Some NP problems are universal keys: solve any one of them quickly and you'd automatically solve every NP problem quickly. SAT — deciding whether a logical formula full of ANDs, ORs, and NOTs can be made true by some setting of its variables — was the very first such universal problem found.
depths.core: A problem is 'NP-complete' if it is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time (this second condition alone is called 'NP-hard'). The Cook–Levin theorem proved Boolean satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete by encoding the entire run of a nondeterministic machine as one big Boolean formula. Karp then showed dozens of natural problems — 3-SAT, clique, vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle, knapsack — are NP-complete by reducing SAT to them. A polynomial-time algorithm for any single NP-complete problem would place all of NP inside P.
depths.deep: NP-completeness explains why thousands of practically important problems all resist efficient solution: they are really the 'same' problem in disguise, linked by a web of reductions tracing back to SAT. This is why P vs NP is the central open question — proving P ≠ NP would confirm these problems are genuinely intractable, while proving P = NP would collapse the distinction and break most modern cryptography. In practice, discovering a problem is NP-hard is the signal to switch to approximation algorithms, heuristics, or special tractable cases.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Some NP problems are *universal keys*: solve any one of them quickly and you would automatically solve *every* NP problem quickly. These are the **NP-complete** problems — the hardest in NP, all secretly the same problem wearing different costumes, linked by a web of reductions. **SAT** was the first such universal key discovered.

### Precisely

A problem is **NP-complete** if (1) it is in NP, and (2) *every* problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time. Condition (2) alone is called **NP-hard**. The **Cook–Levin theorem** proved Boolean satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete by encoding the entire computation of an arbitrary nondeterministic polynomial-time machine as one large Boolean formula that is satisfiable iff the machine accepts. A polynomial-time algorithm for *any single* NP-complete problem would put all of NP into P:

$$\exists\text{ NP-complete } X\in\text{P}\implies\text{P}=\text{NP}.$$

### Worked example

After Cook–Levin gave us SAT, Karp showed many problems NP-complete by *reducing SAT (or 3-SAT) to them*. For Independent Set: from a 3-SAT formula, build a graph with a triangle per clause (one vertex per literal) plus edges joining contradictory literals ($x$ to $\bar x$). The formula is satisfiable iff the graph has an independent set of size = number of clauses. Since 3-SAT $\le_p$ Independent Set and Independent Set is in NP, it is NP-complete. This pattern — reduce from a known NP-complete problem — proved clique, vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle, and knapsack all NP-complete.

### Why it works

Condition (2) is inherited through **transitivity** of reductions: once SAT is NP-complete, proving SAT $\le_p X$ for a new $X\in\text{NP}$ makes $X$ NP-complete too, because *every* NP problem reaches $X$ via SAT. So a single hardness anchor (SAT) plus a chain of reductions certifies thousands of problems as equally hard. If one of them were easy, the whole chain — all of NP — would collapse into P.

### Where it connects

This is the payoff of **reductions**, **P**, and **NP**. **P vs NP** asks whether these problems are truly intractable; almost all experts believe $\text{P}\ne\text{NP}$, but it carries a \$1M Clay Millennium Prize and no proof. When a problem is shown NP-hard, the practical response is **approximation algorithms**, heuristics, or special tractable cases.

### A second angle

NP-completeness is, paradoxically, *good news* for the practitioner. Once you prove your problem NP-complete, you stop hunting for an efficient exact algorithm (almost certainly hopeless) and pivot to productive alternatives: **approximation algorithms** with provable ratios, heuristics like SAT solvers and branch-and-bound that are fast on real instances, fixed-parameter algorithms that are efficient when some parameter is small, or restricting to a tractable special case. The Cook–Levin/Karp web also means a fast solver for *any* one of these problems (a SAT solver, say) can be reused for *all* of them via reduction — which is precisely why industrial SAT solvers are such valuable general-purpose tools.

### Watch out

NP-hard is *not* the same as NP-complete: NP-hard needs only condition (2), so an NP-hard problem need not even be in NP (it could be harder, e.g. undecidable). Also, NP-completeness is about *worst-case* hardness — many NP-complete instances are easy in practice, which is why SAT *solvers* work despite the theory.

atoms.title: Space complexity and PSPACE
atoms.summary: Measuring memory instead of time gives the classes L, PSPACE, and the theorem that nondeterministic and deterministic space coincide up to squaring.

depths.eli5: Besides 'how long does it take?', we can ask 'how much scratch paper does it need?'. That's space complexity. Some problems are gentle on memory but slow to run, and others are quick but memory-hungry — time and space are two different costs.
depths.core: Space complexity counts how many work-tape cells (scratch memory) a machine uses, regardless of how long it runs. 'PSPACE' is the class of problems solvable in polynomial space (with no limit on time); it contains NP and exactly matches the difficulty of polynomial-space games and 'quantified Boolean formulas' (the problem TQBF is PSPACE-complete). Savitch's theorem shows that for space, nondeterminism barely helps: nondeterministic space s can be simulated in deterministic space s^2 (NSPACE(s) ⊆ DSPACE(s^2)), so PSPACE = NPSPACE.
depths.deep: Memory is reusable (you can overwrite scratch paper) in a way that elapsed time is not, which is why nondeterminism is far weaker for space (Savitch) than it is believed to be for time (P vs NP). The chain L ⊆ NL ⊆ P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXP has every inclusion conjectured to be strict, yet only L ⊊ PSPACE and P ⊊ EXP are actually proven (via the space and time hierarchy theorems). The huge gaps we still cannot separate are the frontier of complexity theory.

quiz.prompt: What does Savitch's theorem say about nondeterministic vs deterministic space?
quiz.answer: NSPACE(s) ⊆ DSPACE(s^2): nondeterminism saves at most a squaring in space, so PSPACE = NPSPACE.

quiz.prompt: Why is nondeterminism much less powerful for space than it seems to be for time?
quiz.answer: Space can be reused/overwritten, so a deterministic machine can systematically search all nondeterministic paths with only quadratic extra space — no analogous trick is known for time.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Besides "how long does it take?", we can ask "how much scratch paper does it need?" — that is **space complexity**. Time and space are *different* costs: some problems are gentle on memory but slow, others quick but memory-hungry. Studying memory reveals a surprise: for space, the gap between deterministic and nondeterministic computation almost vanishes, unlike the (believed) chasm for time.

### Precisely

Space complexity counts the work-tape cells a machine uses, ignoring running time. **PSPACE** is the class of problems solvable in *polynomial space* (with unlimited time); it contains NP. The chain is

$$\text{L}\subseteq\text{NL}\subseteq\text{P}\subseteq\text{NP}\subseteq\text{PSPACE}\subseteq\text{EXP}.$$

**Savitch's theorem**: nondeterministic space $s$ can be simulated in deterministic space $s^2$, i.e. $\text{NSPACE}(s)\subseteq\text{DSPACE}(s^2)$, so $\text{PSPACE}=\text{NPSPACE}$. Polynomial-space-complete problems include **TQBF** (true quantified Boolean formulas) and the solvability of many two-player games.

### Worked example

Consider TQBF: a SAT formula wrapped in quantifiers, e.g. $\forall x\,\exists y\,(x\lor y)\land(\bar x\lor \bar y)$. To decide it, recursively try both values of the outermost variable, reusing the *same* memory for each branch since they run one at a time. The recursion depth is the number of variables $n$, and each level stores $O(1)$ extra, so total space is $O(n)$ — polynomial — even though the implicit game tree has $2^n$ leaves and the running time is exponential. This is why TQBF is in PSPACE: *memory is reusable*, time is not.

### Why it works

The key asymmetry: **space can be overwritten and reused**, elapsed time cannot. Savitch's theorem exploits this — to check whether a nondeterministic machine can get from configuration $A$ to $B$ in $2^s$ steps, recursively ask "is there a midpoint $M$ reachable from $A$ in half the steps and reaching $B$ in half?", reusing memory across the two halves. The recursion costs only $s^2$ space. No analogous time-saving trick is known, which is why nondeterminism seems far more powerful for time (P vs NP) than for space.

### Where it connects

This extends **complexity-P** and **complexity-NP** into the memory dimension and connects to the **time hierarchy theorem** (the analogous space hierarchy gives the few proven strict separations). PSPACE-complete games tie back to **reductions**.

### A second angle

The very smallest space classes are surprisingly rich. **L** (logarithmic space) allows only $O(\log n)$ work cells — enough to hold a constant number of pointers into the input, but not to copy it. Remarkably, undirected graph connectivity is in L (Reingold's theorem), while directed connectivity sits in **NL** and is NL-complete. Because $\log^2 n$ space suffices for directed connectivity by **Savitch's theorem**, and NL is closed under complement (Immerman–Szelepcsényi), the low end of the hierarchy has clean, proven structure — a refreshing contrast to the wide-open questions (like P vs NP) one rung up.

### Watch out

Every inclusion in the chain is *conjectured strict*, but only $\text{L}\subsetneq\text{PSPACE}$ and $\text{P}\subsetneq\text{EXP}$ are actually *proven* (via hierarchy theorems). The big gaps — including P vs NP — remain open. Don't assume the chain collapses or that any particular inclusion is known strict; almost none are.

atoms.title: Propositional logic

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Take simple statements that are each either true or false, and glue them together with AND, OR, NOT, and "if…then." A **truth table** lists every possible true/false combination of the parts and shows when the whole glued statement comes out true. Propositional logic is the algebra of such yes/no statements — the foundation under digital circuits, SAT solvers, and all of formal reasoning.

### Precisely

Formulas are built from **atomic propositions** (basic true/false variables) and **connectives**: $\lnot$ (not), $\land$ (and), $\lor$ (or), $\to$ (implies), $\leftrightarrow$ (iff). An **assignment** sets each atom true or false. A formula is **satisfiable** if *some* assignment makes it true, **valid** (a **tautology**) if *every* assignment does, and a **contradiction** if *none* does. Truth tables settle all of these by brute force over $2^n$ rows for $n$ atoms.

### Worked example

Is $(P\to Q)\lor(Q\to P)$ a tautology? Build the truth table over the four assignments of $(P,Q)$. Recall $P\to Q$ is false *only* when $P$ is true and $Q$ false. If $P$ is true and $Q$ false, then $P\to Q$ is false but $Q\to P$ is true (false antecedent), so the OR is true. In every other row at least one implication holds. All four rows give true — so yes, it is a tautology. The brute-force enumeration is the proof.

### Why it works

Propositional logic is **sound and complete**: a formula is provable in a proper proof system iff it is a tautology — syntactic provability and semantic truth coincide exactly. It is also **decidable**, since truth tables always terminate (finitely many rows). This decidability is precisely the property that *predicate* (first-order) logic loses. **Normal forms** — CNF (an AND of ORs) and DNF (an OR of ANDs) — standardize formulas, and converting to CNF is the front door to **SAT solvers** and the resolution proof method.

### Where it connects

Deciding satisfiability of propositional formulas *is* the **SAT** problem at the root of **NP-completeness** (Cook–Levin). Propositional logic underlies **proof systems**, digital circuit design, and is the base case beneath **predicate logic**. Truth-table reasoning connects to **probability** when truth values become probabilities.

### A second angle

Propositional logic is the mathematics of **digital circuits**. Every combinational circuit computes a Boolean function, and every Boolean function can be written as a formula over AND, OR, NOT — indeed in CNF or DNF. Minimizing such formulas (Karnaugh maps, Quine–McCluskey) is literally circuit optimization. Two functionally complete sets are worth knowing: $\{\text{AND, OR, NOT}\}$, and the single gate **NAND** (or NOR), from which every other connective can be built — which is why chip fabs can implement any logic with one repeated gate type. This bridge from truth tables to silicon is why propositional logic is foundational to computer engineering, not just to proofs.

### Watch out

Don't confuse **satisfiable** (true under *at least one* assignment) with **valid** (true under *every* assignment) — a formula can be satisfiable without being a tautology. Also, $\to$ (material implication) is true whenever the antecedent is false, which often surprises people: "if the moon is cheese, then 2+2=5" is *true* propositionally. And while truth tables always work, they take exponential time — which is exactly why SAT is hard.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Propositional logic only handles whole true/false statements. **First-order (predicate) logic** adds the power to say "for all $x$…" and "there exists an $x$…", and to talk about *properties* of objects and *relationships* between them. That extra expressiveness is enough to write down essentially all of mathematics — arithmetic, set theory, geometry — in a single formal language.

### Precisely

First-order logic extends propositional logic with: **variables** ranging over a **domain** of objects; **predicates** (properties and relations, e.g. $\text{Even}(x)$ or $x<y$); **functions**; and the **quantifiers** $\forall$ ("for all") and $\exists$ ("there exists"). A **model** is an interpretation assigning meaning to the symbols. **Gödel's completeness theorem** states the proof system is sound and complete:

$$\vdash \varphi \iff \varphi \text{ is true in every model.}$$

Provability and universal semantic truth coincide.

### Worked example

Express "every number has a successor that is greater": $\forall x\,\exists y\,(y>x)$. The quantifier *order* is load-bearing. Compare $\forall x\,\exists y\,(y>x)$ ("for each $x$ there is *some* larger $y$" — true of the integers) with $\exists y\,\forall x\,(y>x)$ ("there is *one* $y$ bigger than *every* $x$" — false, no largest integer). Same atoms, swapped quantifiers, opposite truth. This sensitivity to quantifier nesting is exactly the expressive power propositional logic lacks.

### Why it works

Validity in first-order logic is **undecidable** (Church and Turing) but **recursively enumerable**: you can mechanically *list all proofs* and so eventually confirm any valid sentence, yet you cannot always decide that a *non*-valid sentence is non-valid. This is the precise boundary — propositional logic is fully decidable, first-order logic only semi-decidable. The completeness theorem guarantees a proof *exists* for every validity; undecidability says no algorithm finds it (or its absence) for all inputs in bounded time.

### Where it connects

It builds on **propositional logic** and **sets/functions/relations**, and grounds **proof systems** and **Gödel's incompleteness theorems**. Its undecidability is a cousin of the **halting problem**; the proof-enumeration view connects to **decidability** (validity is recognizable but not decidable).

### A second angle

First-order logic has expressive *limits* worth knowing alongside its power. It cannot, in a single sentence, say "the domain is finite" or pin down the natural numbers up to isomorphism — by the **Löwenheim–Skolem** theorems, any theory with an infinite model has models of every infinite size, and **compactness** guarantees "nonstandard" models slip in. Capturing notions like "finitely many" or "the *least* set closed under…" requires second-order logic (quantifying over *sets* of objects), which buys expressiveness but *loses* the completeness theorem. This trade — first-order is complete but limited, second-order is expressive but incomplete — is a recurring tension at the foundations.

### Watch out

Do **not** conflate Gödel's *completeness* theorem (about first-order logic's proof system being able to prove all validities) with his *incompleteness* theorems (about specific strong theories like arithmetic being unable to prove all their own truths) — they point in opposite directions and are easily confused. Also, quantifier order matters enormously; $\forall\exists$ and $\exists\forall$ generally mean different things.

atoms.title: Proof systems and soundness/completeness
atoms.summary: A proof system is a set of axioms and inference rules; soundness means it proves only truths, completeness that it proves all of them.

depths.eli5: A proof system is a rulebook for deriving new true statements from ones you already accept. A good rulebook has two virtues: it never lets you derive something false ('sound'), and it can eventually reach every truth in its world ('complete').

'Soundness' means every provable statement is actually true (no false theorems can be derived); 'completeness' means every true statement can be proved. Natural deduction, sequent calculus, and resolution are different but equivalent proof systems for first-order logic, all sound and complete for it.

The Curry–Howard correspondence reveals a deep identity — proofs are programs and propositions are types — unifying logic and computation, so that constructing a proof is literally the same act as writing a program.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A **proof system** is a rulebook for deriving new true statements from ones you already accept. A good rulebook has two virtues: it never lets you derive something false (**sound**), and it can eventually reach every truth in its world (**complete**). Formalizing "proof" this way turns reasoning into something a machine can check mechanically, line by line.

### Precisely

A formal proof system specifies **axioms** (statements taken as given) and **inference rules** (e.g. *modus ponens*: from $A$ and $A\to B$, conclude $B$) that mechanically generate **theorems**. Two key properties:

- **Soundness**: everything provable is true ($\vdash\varphi \Rightarrow \models\varphi$) — no false theorems.
- **Completeness**: everything true is provable ($\models\varphi \Rightarrow \vdash\varphi$).

Natural deduction, sequent calculus, and resolution are different but equivalent systems, all sound and complete for first-order logic.

### Worked example

A two-line natural-deduction proof that $A\land B$ entails $A$: assume $A\land B$; apply the $\land$-elimination rule, which says "from $A\land B$ infer $A$"; conclude $A$. Each step cites an explicit rule, so a checker needs no creativity — just verify each line follows from earlier lines by a named rule. This mechanical checkability is the whole point: *finding* a proof may demand insight, but *verifying* one is routine. (Note the parallel to **NP**: proofs are short certificates, easy to check, sometimes hard to find.)

### Why it works

Soundness is proved by checking each rule preserves truth (if the premises are true in a model, so is the conclusion); chaining truth-preserving steps keeps every theorem true. Completeness (for first-order logic, Gödel's theorem) is the deep direction: it shows the chosen rules are *enough* to reach every validity, via a model-construction argument. **Proof complexity** then asks not *whether* a proof exists but *how long* it must be — resolution needs exponentially long proofs for some formulas (e.g. the pigeonhole principle).

### Where it connects

Builds on **predicate logic**. The **Curry–Howard correspondence** identifies *proofs with programs* and *propositions with types* — constructing a proof literally *is* writing a program of that type, unifying logic and computation. Proof length connects to **NP vs co-NP**. **Gödel's incompleteness** shows completeness fails for strong arithmetic theories.

### A second angle

**Resolution** is the proof system that powers automated reasoning, so it is worth seeing concretely. Working with clauses (ORs of literals), the single resolution rule combines two clauses sharing a complementary literal: from $(A\lor x)$ and $(B\lor\lnot x)$ derive $(A\lor B)$, cancelling $x$. A formula is *unsatisfiable* exactly when repeated resolution can derive the empty clause (a contradiction). This one rule is complete for *refutation*, and it is the engine inside SAT solvers and logic-programming languages like Prolog. Its weakness — some unsatisfiable formulas (pigeonhole instances) need exponentially many resolution steps — is a headline result in **proof complexity**.

### Watch out

Soundness and completeness are *different* directions and a system can have one without the other — an unsound system "proves" falsehoods; an incomplete one misses some truths. Also, first-order logic's *completeness* (every validity is provable) does **not** contradict arithmetic's *incompleteness* (some arithmetic truths are unprovable in a given theory): the former is about logical validity, the latter about a fixed axiom set's truths.

atoms.title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
atoms.summary: Any consistent, sufficiently strong formal system cannot prove all true statements about arithmetic, nor prove its own consistency.

depths.eli5: Any logical rulebook powerful enough to do ordinary arithmetic contains true statements it can never prove from its own rules. Worse, such a rulebook can't even prove that it will never contradict itself. Truth, it turns out, always reaches a little beyond what any fixed set of rules can capture.
depths.core: Gödel's first incompleteness theorem: any 'consistent' (never proves a contradiction), 'effectively axiomatized' (its axioms can be mechanically listed) theory strong enough to encode arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. The construction uses 'Gödel numbering' (assigning numbers to statements) to encode the sentence 'this very statement is unprovable' as a statement about arithmetic — a self-reference that is true precisely because it is unprovable. The second theorem says such a system cannot prove its own consistency, unless it is in fact inconsistent.
depths.deep: The incompleteness theorems are tightly tied to undecidability: the unprovability of certain truths mirrors the halting problem's undecidability, and Chaitin recast incompleteness using Kolmogorov complexity (no formal system can prove that a specific string's complexity exceeds the system's own size). The lesson is not that mathematics is broken but that truth outruns proof in any fixed formal system — there is no finite set of axioms that captures every arithmetic truth.

atoms.note: First theorem: truth > provability. Second theorem: a consistent system can't certify its own consistency. Both require the system to be strong enough to do arithmetic.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Any logical rulebook powerful enough to do ordinary arithmetic contains *true* statements it can never *prove* from its own rules. Worse, such a rulebook cannot even prove that it will never contradict itself. Truth, it turns out, always reaches a little beyond what any fixed set of rules can capture. This is not a flaw in mathematics — it is a permanent feature of formal systems.

### Precisely

**First incompleteness theorem**: any **consistent** (never proves a contradiction), **effectively axiomatized** (axioms mechanically listable) theory strong enough to encode arithmetic contains a true sentence it cannot prove. **Second incompleteness theorem**: such a system cannot prove its own **consistency** (unless it is in fact inconsistent). The construction uses **Gödel numbering** to assign numbers to statements, letting a sentence talk about provability of statements — including itself.

### Worked example

Build the Gödel sentence $G$ that effectively asserts "$G$ is not provable in this system." Now reason: if the system *proved* $G$, then $G$ would be false (it says it's unprovable), so the system would prove a falsehood — violating consistency. Hence, *if the system is consistent*, it cannot prove $G$. But that is exactly what $G$ asserts — so $G$ is **true**. We have a true statement the system cannot prove: incompleteness. (For the second theorem, the system *can* prove "if I'm consistent then $G$ is unprovable," so proving its own consistency would let it prove $G$ — impossible.)

### Why it works

The mechanism is **self-reference via the diagonal lemma**, the same engine behind the **halting problem**. Gödel numbering makes "provability" an arithmetic predicate, so a sentence can encode a claim about itself. Consistency is what blocks proving $G$; truth then follows because $G$'s claim is exactly its own unprovability. Chaitin recast this with **Kolmogorov complexity**: no system of size $c$ can prove "$K(x)>c$" for any specific $x$ — truth outruns proof, quantitatively.

### Where it connects

Builds on **proof systems** and the **halting problem**, and is deeply tied to **decidability** and **Kolmogorov complexity**. It clarifies the limit that **predicate logic**'s completeness theorem does *not* contradict: logical validity is complete, but arithmetic *truth within a theory* is not.

### A second angle

A frequent misreading is to think incompleteness lets you "step outside" a system and *see* the truth of $G$ by magic. What actually happens is more disciplined: *from the meta-level assumption that the system is consistent*, you deduce $G$ is unprovable, and since $G$ asserts exactly that, $G$ is true. You can then *add* $G$ as a new axiom — but the strengthened system has its *own* new Gödel sentence, and so on forever. There is no final system that proves all arithmetic truths. This endless tower, not any mystical insight, is the real content: truth permanently outruns any single effective axiomatization.

### Watch out

The theorems require the system to be (1) consistent, (2) effectively axiomatized, and (3) strong enough for arithmetic — drop any condition and they don't apply (e.g. true arithmetic with *all* truths as axioms is complete but not effectively axiomatized). Also, "incompleteness" does *not* mean mathematics is broken or that specific theorems are in doubt; it means no single finite axiom set captures *every* arithmetic truth. And don't confuse it with the *completeness* theorem of first-order logic.

atoms.title: One-way functions
atoms.summary: A one-way function is easy to compute but computationally hard to invert — the conjectured bedrock of modern cryptography.

depths.eli5: Some operations are like scrambling an egg: easy to do, practically impossible to undo. A 'one-way function' is the mathematical version — quick to compute forwards, but so hard to reverse that nobody can in any reasonable time. Cryptography is built on functions like that.
depths.core: A one-way function f can be computed in polynomial time, but no efficient algorithm can find a 'preimage' (an input x that produces a given output f(x)) for random x, except with negligible probability. Whether such functions even exist is unproven, and their existence would imply P ≠ NP — yet they are both necessary and sufficient for most of cryptography: secure encryption, digital signatures, and pseudorandom generators all rest on them. Leading candidates are built on integer factoring and the discrete-logarithm problem.
depths.deep: Cryptography depends on 'average-case' hardness, not merely 'worst-case': NP-hardness only guarantees that some instances are hard, but cryptography needs a function that is hard on typical, randomly chosen inputs. One-way functions formalize exactly that. They also connect to pseudorandomness — a function whose output no efficient test can tell apart from random is the engine behind stream ciphers — and to Shannon's distinction between 'unconditional' (information-theoretic) and 'computational' security: a one-time pad is unbreakable in principle, while practical crypto trades that ideal for keys you can actually distribute.

atoms.note: The existence of one-way functions is the single most important open assumption in cryptography; it implies P ≠ NP but is believed to be strictly stronger.
