atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Some operations are like scrambling an egg: easy to do, practically impossible to undo. A **one-way function** is the mathematical version — quick to compute forward, but so hard to reverse that nobody can in any reasonable time. Modern cryptography is built on functions like this: anyone can lock, only the holder of a secret can unlock.

### Precisely

A function $f$ is **one-way** if it is computable in polynomial time, but no efficient (polynomial-time) algorithm can find a **preimage** — an $x'$ with $f(x')=f(x)$ — for randomly chosen $x$, except with negligible probability. Whether one-way functions *exist* is unproven; their existence would imply $\text{P}\ne\text{NP}$ (and is believed strictly stronger). They are both **necessary and sufficient** for most of cryptography: secure encryption, signatures, and pseudorandom generators all reduce to them.

### Worked example

Multiplication vs factoring. Computing $f(p,q)=p\cdot q$ for two large primes is fast — schoolbook multiplication is polynomial in the number of digits. But given only the product $N=p\cdot q$ (say a 2048-bit number), *recovering* the factors $p,q$ is believed intractable; the best known algorithms run in time super-polynomial in the digit count. So "multiply two primes" is a candidate one-way function, and it is exactly the hardness underpinning **RSA**. The discrete-logarithm problem gives another candidate.

### Why it works

Cryptography needs **average-case** hardness, not merely **worst-case**. NP-hardness only guarantees that *some* instances are hard — useless if a random key is usually easy. A one-way function must be hard on *typical, randomly chosen* inputs, which is a strictly stronger demand. This is why one-way functions sit *above* P≠NP in assumption strength. They also yield **pseudorandomness**: an output no efficient test distinguishes from random.

### Where it connects

Built on **complexity-NP** (the find-vs-verify asymmetry) and **Shannon entropy** (the security/uncertainty link). They are the foundation of **public-key cryptography**, **pseudorandom generators**, and digital signatures. The worst-case/average-case distinction connects to **PAC learning** and to the structure of NP.

### A second angle

It is illuminating that one-way functions sit in a precise spot in the assumption hierarchy. Their existence *implies* $\text{P}\ne\text{NP}$ (inverting could otherwise be done by guessing-and-checking in P), but is believed *strictly stronger* — $\text{P}\ne\text{NP}$ alone gives only *worst-case* hard problems, whereas crypto needs *average-case* hardness with an efficiently *samplable* hard distribution. Impagliazzo's famous "five worlds" thought experiment charts the possibilities between these: worlds where NP is hard but crypto still impossible. So even a proof that $\text{P}\ne\text{NP}$ would not automatically secure cryptography — a sobering point about how much of modern security rests on conjecture.

### Watch out

NP-hardness alone does *not* give a one-way function — worst-case hardness is too weak; you need *average-case* hardness on random inputs. Also, the *existence* of one-way functions is unproven (the biggest open assumption in cryptography); all of practical crypto rests on conjectured, not proven, hardness. "Hard to invert" means computationally, not information-theoretically — the preimage exists, it's just infeasible to find.

atoms.title: Public-key cryptography
atoms.summary: Public-key systems use a publishable encryption key and a secret decryption key, enabling secure communication without sharing secrets first.

depths.eli5: Imagine handing out copies of an open padlock to everyone, while keeping the only key for yourself. Anyone can snap a box shut with your padlock, but only you can open it. That's public-key cryptography: strangers can send you secrets without ever meeting to agree on a shared password first.
depths.core: Public-key (also called 'asymmetric') cryptography gives each person two matched keys: a 'public key' shared openly and a 'private key' kept secret. Anyone can encrypt a message with your public key, but only you, holding the private key, can decrypt it; swapping the roles produces 'digital signatures' (proof a message came from you). RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring large integers; Diffie–Hellman and elliptic-curve systems rely on the discrete-logarithm problem — these are 'trapdoor one-way functions' (one-way unless you hold the secret trapdoor).
depths.deep: The breakthrough (Diffie–Hellman in 1976, then RSA) solved the key-distribution problem that had crippled older 'symmetric' crypto: two parties can now agree on a shared secret over a fully public channel. The security is computational and conditional — Shor's algorithm can factor integers and compute discrete logs in polynomial time on a large quantum computer, threatening RSA and elliptic-curve crypto (ECC) and driving the shift to 'post-quantum cryptography' based on lattice problems believed hard even for quantum machines.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Imagine handing out copies of an *open padlock* to everyone, while keeping the only key for yourself. Anyone can snap a box shut with your padlock, but only you can open it. That is **public-key cryptography**: strangers can send you secrets without ever meeting first to agree on a shared password. It solved the problem that had crippled all earlier cryptography — how to share a key securely *before* you have a secure channel.

### Precisely

Public-key (**asymmetric**) cryptography gives each person two matched keys: a **public key** shared openly and a **private key** kept secret. Anyone encrypts with your public key; only you, holding the private key, can decrypt. Swapping the roles (sign with private, verify with public) yields **digital signatures**. **RSA** relies on the hardness of factoring large integers; **Diffie–Hellman** and elliptic-curve systems rely on the discrete-logarithm problem. These are **trapdoor one-way functions** — one-way unless you hold the secret trapdoor.

### Worked example

Diffie–Hellman key exchange over a public channel. Both parties agree on public numbers $g$ and prime $p$. Alice picks secret $a$, sends $g^a \bmod p$; Bob picks secret $b$, sends $g^b \bmod p$. Alice computes $(g^b)^a=g^{ab}$; Bob computes $(g^a)^b=g^{ab}$ — the *same* shared secret. An eavesdropper sees $g$, $p$, $g^a$, $g^b$ but cannot get $g^{ab}$ without solving the discrete logarithm (recovering $a$ or $b$), believed intractable. Two strangers thus agree on a secret in full public view.

### Why it works

The security is **computational and conditional**: encryption uses a trapdoor function easy to compute forward but infeasible to invert *without* the private key, which is the trapdoor. The 1976 Diffie–Hellman breakthrough (then RSA in 1978) solved the **key-distribution problem** — no prior shared secret needed. The whole scheme stands on the *conjectured* hardness of factoring / discrete log.

### Where it connects

Directly built on **one-way functions** (specifically trapdoor variants). It enables TLS/HTTPS, signed software, and cryptocurrencies. It connects to **complexity** (security rests on problems believed outside P) and is threatened by quantum computing.

### A second angle

In practice public-key crypto is almost never used to encrypt bulk data directly — it is too slow and constrained. Instead, real protocols use **hybrid encryption**: the public-key system encrypts a freshly generated short *symmetric* key, and that fast symmetric cipher (like AES) encrypts the actual message. TLS, the protocol behind HTTPS, does exactly this on every connection — a public-key handshake to agree on session keys, then symmetric encryption for the data stream. So the padlock metaphor describes the *key exchange* step; the heavy lifting of confidentiality is handed to symmetric primitives once the secret is shared.

### Watch out

The security is *conditional*, not absolute: **Shor's algorithm** factors integers and solves discrete logs in polynomial time on a large quantum computer, breaking RSA and elliptic-curve crypto — driving the shift to **post-quantum** (lattice-based) schemes. Also, public-key crypto is slow, so in practice it's used to exchange a key for fast *symmetric* encryption, not to encrypt bulk data directly.

atoms.title: Pseudorandomness
atoms.summary: A pseudorandom generator stretches a short seed into a long string no efficient test can distinguish from true randomness.

depths.eli5: Start with a tiny bit of genuine randomness (a 'seed'), then run it through a clever recipe that spits out a long stream of bits. To anyone without unlimited computing power, that stream looks completely random — even though it's totally determined by the seed. It isn't truly random, but no fast test can catch the difference.
depths.core: A 'pseudorandom generator' (PRG) is an algorithm that turns a short truly-random seed into a much longer output that is 'computationally indistinguishable' from genuinely uniform random bits — meaning no efficient (polynomial-time) test can tell the two apart with any meaningful advantage. PRGs are known to exist if one-way functions do (the Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby theorem). They power stream ciphers, simulations, and 'derandomization', letting you replace scarce true randomness with cheap pseudorandom bits.
depths.deep: Pseudorandomness is randomness relative to an observer's computational power: a PRG's output has low Kolmogorov complexity (a short program generates it) yet is operationally random to any bounded adversary — showing that 'random' is not absolute but resource-relative. The derandomization conjectures (that BPP = P, assuming strong circuit lower bounds) suggest true randomness may give no extra computational power at all, only convenience.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Start with a tiny bit of genuine randomness — a short **seed** — then run it through a clever recipe that spits out a long stream of bits. To anyone without unlimited computing power, that stream looks completely random, even though it is *totally determined* by the seed. It isn't truly random, but no fast test can catch the difference. This lets us replace scarce true randomness with cheap, reproducible pseudorandom bits.

### Precisely

A **pseudorandom generator (PRG)** is an algorithm $G$ that stretches a short uniform seed into a much longer output that is **computationally indistinguishable** from genuinely uniform bits: for every efficient (polynomial-time) test $D$,

$$\big|\Pr[D(G(\text{seed}))=1]-\Pr[D(\text{uniform})=1]\big| \le \text{negligible}.$$

PRGs exist *if and only if* one-way functions exist (the **Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby theorem**). They power stream ciphers, simulations, and **derandomization**.

### Worked example

A stream cipher takes a short key (the seed), expands it via a PRG into a long keystream, and XORs that keystream with the plaintext — a one-time-pad lookalike using a *short* key instead of a key as long as the message. Security rests entirely on the keystream being pseudorandom: if an attacker could distinguish it from random with non-negligible advantage, they could break the cipher; the PRG guarantee says no efficient attacker can. The convenience is enormous — you ship a 256-bit key, not a gigabyte pad.

### Why it works

Pseudorandomness is **randomness relative to an observer's computational power**. A PRG output has *low* **Kolmogorov complexity** (a short program — the seed plus $G$ — generates it), yet it is operationally random to any *bounded* adversary. So "random" is not absolute but *resource-relative*. The HILL theorem builds a PRG from any one-way function: the hardness of inverting $f$ is converted into bits no efficient test can predict.

### Where it connects

Built on **one-way functions** and **Kolmogorov complexity**. It underlies **public-key** and symmetric crypto, Monte Carlo **randomized algorithms**, and the derandomization program: the conjecture $\text{BPP}=\text{P}$ (under strong circuit lower bounds) says true randomness gives no extra *computational power*, only convenience.

### A second angle

There is a beautiful equivalence between **unpredictability** and **indistinguishability** (Yao's theorem): a bit-generator is pseudorandom iff no efficient algorithm can predict its *next* bit from the previous ones better than chance. The two notions sound different — "looks random to any test" versus "you can't guess what comes next" — yet they coincide. This gives a practical security target: a stream cipher is secure exactly when its keystream's next bit is unpredictable. It also clarifies what breaks a PRG: any efficient next-bit predictor *is* a distinguisher, and finding one is precisely what cryptanalysts hunt for.

### Watch out

Pseudorandom output is *deterministic and low-complexity* — it only *looks* random to a *computationally bounded* tester; an unbounded adversary (or one who learns the seed) sees right through it. So PRGs are useless against information-theoretic attacks (use a true **one-time pad** for that). And the whole guarantee is conditional on one-way functions existing, which is unproven.

atoms.title: PAC learning
atoms.summary: PAC learning formalizes learning from examples: with high probability, output a hypothesis that is approximately correct on unseen data.

depths.eli5: Learning from examples works like this: you see a pile of labeled examples (this photo is a cat, that one isn't), then you guess a rule. A good rule is mostly right on brand-new examples you've never seen — and you want to be confident that it really is mostly right. PAC learning makes that intuition precise.
depths.core: In Valiant's 'Probably Approximately Correct' (PAC) framework, a 'concept class' (a family of possible rules) is PAC-learnable if some algorithm can, for any target rule and any unknown distribution of examples, draw a polynomial number of samples and output — with probability at least 1 − δ — a 'hypothesis' (its guessed rule) whose error is at most ε. The two knobs separate accuracy (ε, the 'approximately') from confidence (δ, the 'probably'). The whole point is generalizing from finite data, not memorizing it.
depths.deep: PAC makes a 'distribution-free' demand: the learner must succeed no matter what distribution generates the examples, which is what makes the guarantee meaningful. The key insight is that generalization is possible only if the hypothesis class is restricted — an unrestricted learner can always fit the training data perfectly yet behave arbitrarily on new points ('overfitting'). Exactly how much restriction is needed is captured by the VC dimension.

quiz.prompt: Why must the hypothesis class be restricted for learning to generalize?
quiz.answer: An unrestricted class can always fit the training data exactly while behaving arbitrarily on unseen points, giving no generalization guarantee; restriction limits this overfitting.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Learning from examples works like this: you see a pile of labeled examples (this photo is a cat, that one isn't), then you guess a rule. A *good* rule is mostly right on *brand-new* examples you've never seen — and you want to be *confident* it really is mostly right. **PAC learning** ("Probably Approximately Correct") makes that double demand precise.

### Precisely

In Valiant's framework, a **concept class** $\mathcal{C}$ (a family of possible rules) is **PAC-learnable** if there is an algorithm that, for any target concept and any unknown distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over examples, draws a *polynomial* number of samples and outputs a **hypothesis** $h$ such that, with probability at least $1-\delta$,

$$\text{error}(h)=\Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[h(x)\ne\text{target}(x)]\le \epsilon.$$

The two knobs separate **accuracy** ($\epsilon$, the "approximately") from **confidence** ($\delta$, the "probably").

### Worked example

Learn an unknown threshold on the line: points below some cutoff $\theta^*$ are labeled "−", above are "+", but you don't know $\theta^*$. Draw $m$ labeled samples; output the hypothesis threshold $\hat\theta$ sitting between the largest "−" and smallest "+" you saw. The only way $\hat\theta$ has error $>\epsilon$ is if no sample landed in the $\epsilon$-probability gap around $\theta^*$ — and the chance of *missing* an $\epsilon$-mass region across $m$ samples is at most $(1-\epsilon)^m\le e^{-\epsilon m}$. Choosing $m\ge\frac1\epsilon\ln\frac1\delta$ drives that below $\delta$. So thresholds are PAC-learnable with few samples.

### Why it works

PAC makes a **distribution-free** demand: the learner must succeed *no matter what* distribution generates the examples — that is what makes the guarantee meaningful rather than rigged to a convenient data source. The crucial insight is that generalization is possible *only if the hypothesis class is restricted*: an unrestricted learner can always fit the training data perfectly yet behave arbitrarily on new points (**overfitting**). How much restriction suffices is captured by the **VC dimension**.

### Where it connects

Built on **complexity-P** (efficient learning) and **probability**. It is the theoretical backbone of supervised machine learning, leads directly to **VC dimension**, and its worst-case/average-case themes echo **one-way functions**. **Neural network learning** both uses and strains this theory.

### A second angle

The clean special case to anchor PAC intuition is **finite hypothesis classes**. If your class $\mathcal{H}$ has $|\mathcal{H}|$ candidate rules and *some* rule perfectly fits the data (the realizable case), then any consistent hypothesis has error $\le\epsilon$ with probability $\ge 1-\delta$ once you draw

$$m\ge\frac1\epsilon\Big(\ln|\mathcal{H}|+\ln\tfrac1\delta\Big)$$

examples. Read it: sample complexity grows only *logarithmically* in the number of hypotheses, so even a huge-but-finite class is learnable from modest data. This bound is the finite-class shadow of the **VC dimension** result, and the $\ln|\mathcal{H}|$ term is a precise, computable stand-in for "model capacity."

### Watch out

"Probably approximately correct" is a *double* guarantee — both $\epsilon$ (allowed error) and $\delta$ (allowed failure probability) are non-zero; PAC never promises a perfect rule with certainty. Also, the guarantee is *distribution-free over the unknown $\mathcal{D}$* but assumes train and test come from the *same* $\mathcal{D}$ — it says nothing if the test distribution shifts.

atoms.title: VC dimension
atoms.summary: The VC dimension measures a model's capacity by the largest set of points it can label in every possible way — it sets the sample size needed to learn.

depths.eli5: A model's 'power' (its capacity) is the size of the biggest set of points it can fit perfectly no matter how you label them — every yes/no combination. More power sounds good, but it means you need more examples before you can trust the model on data it hasn't seen. The VC dimension is the number that measures this power.
depths.core: A hypothesis class 'shatters' a set of points if, for every possible way of labeling them (every assignment of yes/no), some hypothesis in the class produces exactly that labeling. The 'VC dimension' (named for Vapnik and Chervonenkis) is the size of the largest set the class can shatter. A class is PAC-learnable if and only if its VC dimension is finite, and the number of examples needed (the 'sample complexity') scales roughly as Θ((d/ε) + (1/ε)log(1/δ)) where d is the VC dimension — capacity directly sets how much data you need.
depths.deep: VC dimension quantifies the 'bias–variance tradeoff': high capacity can fit almost anything (low bias) but demands far more data to generalize (high variance), formalizing Occam's razor — simpler classes generalize from fewer examples. Concretely, axis-aligned half-lines on the number line have VC dimension 1, intervals 2, and straight-line ('linear') separators in d-dimensional space have VC dimension d+1. A class that can shatter arbitrarily large sets (infinite VC dimension) is not PAC-learnable at all.

atoms.note: Finite VC dimension is exactly the condition for distribution-free PAC learnability — the fundamental theorem of statistical learning.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A model's "power" (its **capacity**) is the size of the biggest set of points it can fit *perfectly no matter how you label them* — every yes/no combination. More power sounds good, but it means you need *more examples* before you can trust the model on data it hasn't seen. The **VC dimension** is the single number that measures this power, and it pins down exactly how much data learning requires.

### Precisely

A hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ **shatters** a set of points if, for *every* possible labeling of them, some $h\in\mathcal{H}$ realizes exactly that labeling. The **VC dimension** $d$ is the size of the *largest* set $\mathcal{H}$ can shatter. The **fundamental theorem of statistical learning**: $\mathcal{H}$ is (distribution-free) PAC-learnable iff $d<\infty$, with sample complexity

$$m=\Theta\!\left(\frac{d}{\epsilon}+\frac1\epsilon\log\frac1\delta\right).$$

### Worked example

Linear separators (lines) in the plane have VC dimension 3. Three points in general position can be shattered: for any of the $2^3=8$ labelings, some line separates the "+" from the "−". But *no* set of 4 points can be shattered — the XOR-like labeling (two diagonal points "+", the other two "−") cannot be split by any single straight line. So you can shatter 3 but not 4, giving VC dimension exactly 3 ($=d+1$ for $d=2$ dimensions). Intervals on the line have VC dimension 2; half-lines, 1.

### Why it works

VC dimension quantifies the **bias–variance tradeoff**: high capacity fits almost anything (low bias) but demands far more data to generalize (high variance) — a formal **Occam's razor**, since simpler classes generalize from fewer examples. The sample-complexity formula shows data needed grows *linearly* in $d$. The reason finiteness is *necessary*: a class with infinite VC dimension can shatter arbitrarily large samples, so it can always fit the training set while behaving arbitrarily on new points — no generalization guarantee is possible.

### Where it connects

It completes **PAC learning** by characterizing exactly which classes are learnable. The **Sauer–Shelah lemma** bounds how many labelings a finite-VC class can produce. It underlies generalization bounds in classical machine learning — and the fact that hugely over-parameterized **neural networks** generalize *despite* enormous VC dimension is a central modern puzzle.

### A second angle

The **Sauer–Shelah lemma** explains *why* finite VC dimension tames learning. Although a class might in principle label $n$ points in $2^n$ ways, a class of VC dimension $d$ can produce at most $O(n^d)$ distinct labelings on any $n$ points — *polynomial*, not exponential. This polynomial "growth function" is what makes uniform convergence (training error tracking true error) possible: there are too few effectively-different hypotheses to overfit by luck. So the abstract shattering definition cashes out as a concrete counting bound, and that bound is the technical heart of every classical generalization guarantee in machine learning.

### Watch out

VC dimension is the size of the *largest shatterable* set — you only need *one* set of size $d$ that *can* be shattered, but *every* set of size $d+1$ must fail. A common error is thinking you must shatter *all* sets of size $d$. Also, finite VC dimension guarantees learnability *in principle* (sample complexity), not computational efficiency — finding the hypothesis may still be hard.

atoms.title: Entropy bridges information and statistical mechanics
atoms.summary: Shannon's information entropy and Boltzmann/Gibbs thermodynamic entropy are the same functional, linking bits to physical energy.

depths.eli5: Physicists measure 'disorder' in a box of gas; information theorists measure 'uncertainty' in a message. It turns out these are the very same formula, just written with different units. The bits in your phone and the heat in a gas are governed by one shared idea — entropy.
depths.core: The 'Gibbs entropy' of physics, S = −k_B Σ p_i ln p_i (where k_B is Boltzmann's constant and ln is the natural log), and the Shannon entropy H = −Σ p_i log2 p_i of information theory are the same function, differing only by the constant k_B and the choice of logarithm base. Jaynes recast statistical mechanics as 'inference': the equilibrium state of a physical system is the maximum-entropy probability distribution consistent with what you know (such as the average energy), recovering the famous Boltzmann distribution as the least-biased guess. Landauer's principle then attaches a real physical energy cost, k_B T ln 2, to erasing a single bit.
depths.deep: This identification turns thermodynamics into a special case of information theory: temperature plays the role of a Lagrange multiplier on the energy constraint, and the partition function is just a normalizer. Landauer's bound — together with Bennett's resolution of the Maxwell's-demon paradox — shows that information is physical: logically irreversible erasure must dissipate heat, closing the loop between computation, entropy, and the second law of thermodynamics. The same maximum-entropy principle reappears in machine learning as the logistic/softmax model and in statistics as the exponential families.

atoms.note: Landauer's principle: erasing one bit costs at least k_B T ln 2 ≈ 0.018 eV of dissipated energy at room temperature — the thermodynamic price of forgetting.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Physicists measure "disorder" in a box of gas; information theorists measure "uncertainty" in a message. It turns out these are the *very same formula*, written with different units. The bits in your phone and the heat in a gas are governed by one shared idea — **entropy**. This is not a loose analogy: it is a mathematical identity, and it attaches a real energy cost to information.

### Precisely

The **Gibbs entropy** of physics and the **Shannon entropy** of information are the same function:

$$S=-k_B\sum_i p_i\ln p_i \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad H=-\sum_i p_i\log_2 p_i,$$

differing only by Boltzmann's constant $k_B$ and the log base. **Jaynes** recast statistical mechanics as *inference*: a system's equilibrium state is the **maximum-entropy** distribution consistent with what you know (e.g. average energy), which recovers the **Boltzmann distribution** as the least-biased guess. **Landauer's principle** attaches a physical cost $k_B T\ln 2$ to *erasing* one bit.

### Worked example

Landauer's bound, numerically. Erasing a single bit at room temperature ($T\approx 300$ K) dissipates at least

$$k_B T\ln 2 \approx (1.38\times 10^{-23}\,\text{J/K})(300\,\text{K})(0.693)\approx 2.9\times 10^{-21}\,\text{J}\approx 0.018\,\text{eV}.$$

Tiny per bit, but it is a *floor* no technology can beat: logically irreversible erasure *must* release at least this much heat. Reversible computation, which never erases, can in principle avoid the cost — the loophole Bennett used to resolve Maxwell's demon.

### Why it works

Jaynes' maximum-entropy principle says: among all distributions matching your known constraints (like fixed average energy), pick the one with the *highest* entropy — the least presumptuous. Maximizing $-\sum p_i\ln p_i$ subject to fixed $\langle E\rangle$ via a Lagrange multiplier yields exactly $p_i\propto e^{-\beta E_i}$, the Boltzmann distribution, with the multiplier $\beta=1/k_BT$ playing the role of inverse temperature. Thermodynamics thus becomes a *special case of inference*. Landauer + Bennett close the loop: information is physical, and erasing it obeys the second law.

### Where it connects

Built on **Shannon entropy** and **mutual information**. The maximum-entropy principle reappears in machine learning as the **softmax/logistic** model and in statistics as **exponential families**. It links the **05-biophysics** and **02-physics** canon branches to information, and Landauer's bound connects computation to thermodynamics.

### A second angle

The maximum-entropy principle is a general *recipe*, not a physics-only trick. Whenever you must choose a distribution given only some average constraints, picking the maximum-entropy distribution consistent with them is the least-presumptuous choice — and it always yields an **exponential family**: $p(x)\propto\exp(\sum_k\lambda_k f_k(x))$, where the $f_k$ are the constrained quantities and the $\lambda_k$ are Lagrange multipliers. Fix the mean and variance, you get the Gaussian; fix the mean of a positive quantity, the exponential distribution; fix average energy, the Boltzmann distribution. This single principle unifies thermodynamics, the **softmax** in machine learning, and much of statistical modeling.

### Watch out

The identity is *formal* — Shannon and thermodynamic entropy share the same functional form, but you must keep units straight ($k_B$ and log base) to convert bits to joules. Also, Landauer's cost applies to *irreversible erasure*, not to computation in general; reversible operations can sidestep it. "Entropy = disorder" is a loose slogan; the precise meaning is "uncertainty / number of accessible microstates."

atoms.title: Modern machine learning — a glimpse
atoms.summary: Deep networks fit huge parametric functions by gradient descent, and their surprising generalization stretches classical learning theory.

depths.eli5: A neural network is a giant adjustable function with millions of little knobs ('parameters'). Training nudges those knobs a tiny bit at a time to reduce its mistakes on example data. Remarkably, after enough nudging it can handle brand-new examples it never saw during training. Nobody fully understands why this works as well as it does.
depths.core: A neural network stacks layers, each a 'linear map' (a weighted sum) followed by a simple 'nonlinearity' (a bending function), into one huge function with millions or billions of parameters. Training minimizes a 'loss' (a mistake score) by 'gradient descent' — repeatedly stepping the parameters in the direction that lowers the loss. The needed gradients are computed efficiently by 'backpropagation', which is really dynamic programming reusing the calculus chain rule across layers. Classical VC theory predicts such hugely 'over-parameterized' models should overfit badly, yet they generalize well — a puzzle modern theory (implicit regularization, the 'double descent' curve) is still working to explain.
depths.deep: Backpropagation is exactly dynamic programming over the network's computation graph: each intermediate derivative is computed once and reused, so the total gradient cost is linear in network size rather than exponential. The frontier puzzle is generalization when parameters vastly outnumber the training data — classical uniform-convergence bounds (VC dimension, Rademacher complexity) become vacuous there, so model capacity alone no longer explains why learning succeeds. The information-bottleneck view and links back to statistical mechanics (energy landscapes, phase transitions in learning) are active attempts to rebuild the theory.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A neural network is a giant adjustable function with millions of little knobs (**parameters**). Training nudges those knobs a tiny bit at a time to reduce its mistakes on example data. Remarkably, after enough nudging it handles brand-new examples it never saw during training. Even more remarkably, nobody fully understands *why* it generalizes as well as it does — classical theory predicts it should fail.

### Precisely

A network stacks **layers**, each a **linear map** (weighted sum) followed by a **nonlinearity** (a bending function), into one huge function with millions–billions of parameters. Training minimizes a **loss** $\mathcal{L}$ (a mistake score) by **gradient descent**: repeatedly step parameters $\theta$ opposite the gradient,

$$\theta \leftarrow \theta-\eta\,\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}.$$

The gradients are computed efficiently by **backpropagation** — reverse-mode automatic differentiation, which is dynamic programming over the calculus chain rule across layers.

### Worked example

Backprop as dynamic programming. Consider a chain $x\to h_1\to h_2\to \mathcal{L}$. The chain rule gives $\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial h_2}\cdot\frac{\partial h_2}{\partial h_1}\cdot\frac{\partial h_1}{\partial x}$. Naively recomputing these products for every parameter is exponential in depth. Backprop instead computes $\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial h_2}$ *once*, reuses it to get $\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial h_1}$, and so on backward — each intermediate derivative computed once and cached, exactly like **dynamic programming**. Total gradient cost is *linear* in network size, not exponential.

### Why it works

Backpropagation = reverse-mode autodiff = DP over the computation graph: store each node's partial derivative and reuse it, so cost stays linear in the number of operations. The deep *puzzle* is **generalization**: classical **VC** / uniform-convergence bounds predict that vastly **over-parameterized** models (more parameters than data) should overfit catastrophically — yet they generalize well. The **double descent** curve (test error dips, rises, then dips *again* past the interpolation point) shows the classical bias–variance picture is incomplete.

### Where it connects

Built on **VC dimension** (which it strains), **dynamic programming** (backprop), and **mutual information** (the information-bottleneck view of why hidden layers generalize). Modern theory reaches back to **statistical mechanics** (energy landscapes, phase transitions in learning) to rebuild the account of generalization.

### A second angle

A concrete handle on the generalization mystery is **implicit regularization**. Gradient descent does not just find *any* zero-loss solution among the many an over-parameterized network admits — it is *biased* toward particular ones (e.g. minimum-norm or maximum-margin solutions) by the dynamics of the optimization itself, with no explicit penalty added. This hidden preference, rather than any capacity limit, may be what curbs overfitting. It reframes the puzzle: the question is less "why doesn't huge capacity overfit?" and more "which of the infinitely many fitting solutions does gradient descent prefer, and why does that one generalize?" — an active research frontier.

### Watch out

Backprop computes *gradients*; it is not the learning algorithm itself — gradient descent (with all its variants and tricks) is. Also, "it generalizes" is empirical, not yet fully explained: don't assume classical VC bounds account for deep-network success — in the over-parameterized regime those bounds become *vacuous*, which is precisely the open frontier.

atoms.title: Randomized algorithms
atoms.summary: Algorithms that flip coins can be simpler and faster than deterministic ones, trading certainty for high-probability correctness or speed.

depths.eli5: Sometimes letting an algorithm flip coins and make random choices makes it faster or simpler, while still being almost always right. For example, quicksort runs fast on average when it picks a random item to split the list around, side-stepping the bad cases that trip up a fixed choice.
depths.core: Randomized algorithms consume random bits while running. 'Las Vegas' algorithms (like randomized quicksort) always return the correct answer but have a random running time; 'Monte Carlo' algorithms (like the Miller–Rabin primality test) run in a fixed time but may give a wrong answer with a small, controllable probability. Randomness often dodges worst-case 'adversarial' inputs and simplifies design. The corresponding complexity class is BPP ('bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time') — problems solvable fast with a small error chance.
depths.deep: The true power of randomness is subtle: under widely believed circuit lower bounds, BPP = P, meaning randomness buys convenience and speed but not fundamentally more solvable problems ('derandomization' via pseudorandom generators). Yet in other models randomization is provably essential — distributed consensus, communication complexity, and cryptography rely on it irreducibly. The gap between 'random helps' and 'random is necessary' depends on the model.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Sometimes letting an algorithm *flip coins* makes it faster or simpler while still being almost always right. Randomized quicksort picks a random pivot, side-stepping the adversarial inputs that wreck a fixed-pivot choice. Randomness can dodge worst cases, break symmetry, and simplify design — trading a sliver of certainty for a lot of practical robustness.

### Precisely

A **randomized algorithm** consumes random bits while running. Two flavors:

- **Las Vegas** (e.g. randomized quicksort): *always* correct, but running time is a random variable.
- **Monte Carlo** (e.g. Miller–Rabin primality): *fixed* running time, but a small, controllable probability of a wrong answer.

The associated complexity class is **BPP** ("bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time"): problems solvable in polynomial time with error probability $\le 1/3$ on every input (boostable to negligible by repetition).

### Worked example

Miller–Rabin primality testing (Monte Carlo). To test if $n$ is prime, pick a random base $a$ and check an algebraic identity that *all* primes satisfy. A composite $n$ fails the identity for at least 3/4 of bases — so a random $a$ "catches" a composite with probability $\ge 3/4$. One round might be fooled, but run $k$ independent rounds: the chance a composite survives all $k$ is $\le (1/4)^k$. With $k=50$ that is below $10^{-30}$ — vastly less than a hardware glitch. Fast, simple, and as reliable as you like.

### Why it works

Randomness defeats *adversarial structure*: an adversary who could engineer a bad input for a *deterministic* choice cannot predict your *random* choice, so the bad case becomes vanishingly unlikely. Error is driven down geometrically by independent repetition (a Chernoff/union-bound argument). The expectation analysis leans on **linearity of expectation** and **probability** basics.

### Where it connects

Built on **probability** and **big-O**. Randomization is central to **hashing** (universal hashing), cryptography (**pseudorandomness**, key generation), distributed consensus, and sampling. The class **BPP** sits beside P and NP in the complexity landscape.

### A second angle

A clean lens on Las Vegas vs Monte Carlo: you can *convert* between them. Run a Las Vegas algorithm but cut it off after a time budget — you get a Monte Carlo algorithm (fixed time, small chance of no/incorrect answer). Conversely, a Monte Carlo algorithm whose answers you can *verify* becomes Las Vegas by re-running until the check passes. This interconvertibility, plus **probability amplification** (repeat $k$ times, error drops geometrically), means the two flavors are two settings of one dial — correctness-certainty versus time-certainty — and you choose which to fix based on whether wrong answers or long runtimes are more costly in your application.

### Watch out

The deep subtlety: under widely believed circuit lower bounds, **BPP = P** — randomness buys *convenience and speed*, not fundamentally more solvable problems (derandomization via **PRGs**). Yet in *other* models (distributed, communication, cryptographic) randomness is provably *essential*. So "does randomness help?" has different answers depending on the setting — don't overgeneralize either way. Also, Monte Carlo error is real, however tiny; for correctness-critical uses, prefer Las Vegas or heavy repetition.

atoms.title: Kullback–Leibler divergence
atoms.summary: KL divergence measures the extra bits wasted when you encode data from p using a code optimized for q.

depths.eli5: Suppose you build your data compression assuming the world behaves like distribution q, but the world is actually distribution p. You'll waste some bits because your code was tuned to the wrong guess. KL divergence is exactly the count of how many extra bits you waste, on average.
depths.core: The Kullback–Leibler divergence D_KL(p‖q) is the average number of extra bits you spend by coding data from the true distribution p with a code that was optimized for a different distribution q. It is never negative (Gibbs' inequality), is zero exactly when p = q, but is 'asymmetric' (D_KL(p‖q) ≠ D_KL(q‖p)) so it is not a true distance metric. Mutual information is the special case D_KL(joint distribution ‖ product of the separate distributions), and 'cross-entropy' equals entropy plus KL divergence.
depths.deep: KL divergence is the natural 'distance' from a model to reality in 'information geometry', and minimizing it is exactly maximum-likelihood estimation — fitting a model to data minimizes D_KL(empirical data ‖ model). Its asymmetry encodes a real modeling choice: D_KL(p‖q) punishes q for assigning low probability where p is high ('mode-covering'), while D_KL(q‖p) does the reverse ('mode-seeking') — a distinction that shapes variational inference and generative models.

atoms.note: Cross-entropy loss, ubiquitous in machine learning, is entropy plus KL divergence — minimizing it fits the model distribution to the data distribution.

atoms.art_prompt: two distribution curves p and q with the shaded gap between them metered as wasted bits, an arrow noting the asymmetry p‖q ≠ q‖p

quiz.prompt: Why is KL divergence not a true distance metric?
quiz.answer: It is asymmetric (D_KL(p‖q) ≠ D_KL(q‖p)) and violates the triangle inequality, though it is nonnegative and zero iff p = q.

quiz.prompt: How is minimizing KL divergence related to maximum-likelihood estimation?
quiz.answer: Minimizing D_KL(empirical data ‖ model) over the model's parameters is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood of the data under the model.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Suppose you build your data compression assuming the world behaves like distribution $q$, but the world is *actually* distribution $p$. You'll waste some bits because your code was tuned to the wrong guess. **KL divergence** is exactly the count of how many *extra* bits you waste, on average. It measures how far a model $q$ is from reality $p$ — in the natural currency of information, bits.

### Precisely

$$D_{KL}(p\,\|\,q)=\sum_x p(x)\log_2\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}.$$

It is the average excess bits from coding true-distribution-$p$ data with a code optimized for $q$. Properties: $D_{KL}\ge 0$ (**Gibbs' inequality**), with equality iff $p=q$; but it is **asymmetric** ($D_{KL}(p\|q)\ne D_{KL}(q\|p)$), so it is *not* a true distance metric. **Mutual information** is the special case $D_{KL}\big(p(x,y)\,\|\,p(x)p(y)\big)$, and **cross-entropy** equals entropy plus KL: $H(p,q)=H(p)+D_{KL}(p\|q)$.

### Worked example

Let true $p=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ but your model $q=(\tfrac14,\tfrac34)$. Then

$$D_{KL}(p\|q)=\tfrac12\log_2\tfrac{1/2}{1/4}+\tfrac12\log_2\tfrac{1/2}{3/4}=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(\log_2\tfrac23)\approx 0.5-0.29=0.21\text{ bits.}$$

So coding fair-coin data with a code built for the 1:3 model wastes about 0.21 bits per symbol. Reverse it: $D_{KL}(q\|p)$ gives a *different* number — concrete proof of asymmetry.

### Why it works

Nonnegativity is **Gibbs' inequality**, a consequence of the concavity of the logarithm (Jensen). The asymmetry encodes a real modeling choice: $D_{KL}(p\|q)$ heavily punishes $q$ for assigning *low* probability where $p$ is high (**mode-covering** — $q$ must cover all of $p$'s mass), while $D_{KL}(q\|p)$ does the reverse (**mode-seeking** — $q$ may concentrate on one peak of $p$). This distinction shapes variational inference and generative models.

### Where it connects

Built on **Shannon entropy**. **Cross-entropy loss**, ubiquitous in machine-learning classifiers, is entropy plus KL — minimizing it fits model to data. Minimizing $D_{KL}(\text{empirical}\,\|\,\text{model})$ *is* maximum-likelihood estimation. KL is the local distance of **information geometry** and underlies **mutual information** and **rate–distortion**.

### A second angle

KL divergence's two directions power two famous algorithm families. Minimizing $D_{KL}(\text{data}\,\|\,\text{model})$ over parameters is **maximum-likelihood estimation** — the workhorse of statistics and the cross-entropy loss of classifiers. Minimizing the *reverse*, $D_{KL}(\text{approx}\,\|\,\text{target})$, is **variational inference**, where a tractable distribution is fit to an intractable one. The mode-covering vs mode-seeking asymmetry then has visible consequences: maximum-likelihood spreads probability to cover all the data (avoiding zeros), while reverse-KL variational methods tend to lock onto a single mode and underestimate spread. Knowing *which* KL you are minimizing predicts the qualitative behavior of the fitted model. A final practical note: because $D_{KL}$ is unbounded and blows up when the model assigns near-zero probability to observed data, real systems often optimize a smoothed or symmetrized surrogate — for instance the bounded, symmetric **Jensen–Shannon divergence**, which averages the two directions against their midpoint distribution and stays finite even when the two supports differ.

### Watch out

KL is *not symmetric* and violates the triangle inequality — it is a *divergence*, not a metric, so "distance from $p$ to $q$" $\ne$ "distance from $q$ to $p$." Also, $D_{KL}(p\|q)$ is *infinite* if $q(x)=0$ where $p(x)>0$ (you'd need infinitely many bits for an event your model deemed impossible) — a real pitfall when a model assigns zero probability to observed data.

atoms.title: Conditional probability and Bayes' rule
atoms.summary: Bayes' rule inverts conditional probabilities, updating a prior belief into a posterior in light of evidence.

depths.eli5: Bayes' rule flips a 'how likely is the evidence?' question into a 'how likely is the cause?' question. If you know how often a test beeps when someone truly has a disease, Bayes lets you compute how likely they actually have the disease once the test beeps — combining the test with how rare the disease is to begin with.
depths.core: 'Conditional probability' P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) is the probability that A happens given that B has occurred (P(A∩B) is the chance both happen). Bayes' rule rearranges this into P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(A)/P(B), letting you invert a known 'likelihood' P(B|A) into the 'posterior' P(A|B) you want, using your 'prior' belief P(A). It is the engine of all probabilistic inference, from spam filters to medical diagnosis.
depths.deep: The 'base-rate fallacy' is Bayes' rule ignored: a rare condition (small prior) combined with an imperfect test makes most positive results false positives, no matter how 'accurate' the test sounds. Bayesian updating is also the discrete cousin of the maximum-entropy / inference view of statistical mechanics — both treat probability as a state of knowledge updated by constraints, not as a property of the world alone.

atoms.note: P(B) in the denominator is the normalizer, expandable via the law of total probability: P(B) = Σ_A P(B|A)P(A).

quiz.prompt: In Bayes' rule, name the prior, likelihood, and posterior.
quiz.answer: Prior P(A), likelihood P(B|A), posterior P(A|B); P(B) is the normalizing evidence.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

**Bayes' rule** flips a "how likely is the evidence given the cause?" question into a "how likely is the cause given the evidence?" question. If you know how often a test beeps when someone truly has a disease, Bayes lets you compute how likely they *actually* have the disease once the test beeps — by combining the test's accuracy with how *rare* the disease is to begin with. That second ingredient, the base rate, is the part people forget.

### Precisely

**Conditional probability**: $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$ — the probability of $A$ given that $B$ occurred. Rearranging gives **Bayes' rule**:

$$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}.$$

Here $P(A)$ is the **prior** (belief before evidence), $P(B\mid A)$ the **likelihood** (how the evidence behaves under $A$), $P(A\mid B)$ the **posterior** (updated belief), and $P(B)$ the normalizer, expandable by the **law of total probability**: $P(B)=\sum_A P(B\mid A)P(A)$.

### Worked example

A disease affects 1 in 10,000; a test is 99% accurate (1% false-positive rate, catches all true cases). You test positive — do you have it? Out of 1,000,000 people: 100 are sick (all test positive); of the 999,900 healthy, 1% = 9,999 falsely test positive. So among ~10,099 positives, only 100 are truly sick:

$$P(\text{sick}\mid +)=\frac{100}{100+9{,}999}\approx 0.0099\approx 1\%.$$

Despite a "99% accurate" test, a lone positive is ~99% likely to be a *false* alarm — the **base-rate fallacy**.

### Why it works

Bayes' rule is just algebra on the definition of conditional probability ($P(A\cap B)$ computed two ways), but its power is conceptual: it forces the prior $P(A)$ into the calculation. When the prior is tiny, even an accurate test produces mostly false positives, because the huge healthy population's small error rate still outnumbers the small sick population's true positives. Ignoring the base rate is the single most common probabilistic mistake.

### Where it connects

Built on **probability** basics. It is the engine of all probabilistic inference: spam filters, medical diagnosis, **PAC**-adjacent Bayesian learning. It is the discrete cousin of the maximum-entropy/inference view in the **entropy–statistical-mechanics link** — both treat probability as a state of *knowledge* updated by evidence.

### A second angle

Bayesian updating composes cleanly, which is its quiet superpower. Yesterday's **posterior** becomes today's **prior**: after observing evidence $E_1$ then $E_2$, the final belief is the same whether you update once with both or sequentially, one piece at a time. In log-odds form the update is even simpler — each piece of evidence *adds* a fixed "weight of evidence" $\log\frac{P(E\mid A)}{P(E\mid\lnot A)}$ to the running log-odds. This additive, order-independent accumulation is exactly how spam filters, medical risk scores, and sensor-fusion systems combine many weak signals into one calibrated belief, and it ties Bayes back to the additive nature of information in **bits**.

### Watch out

The **base-rate fallacy**: never judge a positive result by the test's accuracy alone — the prior (base rate) can dominate. Also, $P(A\mid B)\ne P(B\mid A)$ in general ("prosecutor's fallacy" — confusing "probability of evidence given innocence" with "probability of innocence given evidence"). And $P(B)$ must be the *total* probability of the evidence across all hypotheses, not just under $A$.

atoms.title: Regular expressions
atoms.summary: Regular expressions are an algebraic notation for patterns, exactly as expressive as finite automata.

depths.eli5: A 'regular expression' (regex) is a compact written pattern — like 'one or more digits' or 'a word starting with cat' — that a machine can test text against. It can describe exactly the same patterns that a simple state-hopping machine (a finite automaton) can recognize.
depths.core: Regular expressions are built from three operations on patterns: 'union' (written |, meaning 'this or that'), 'concatenation' (one pattern followed by another), and the 'Kleene star' (zero-or-more repetitions), starting from single symbols and the empty string. Kleene's theorem proves they describe exactly the 'regular languages' — every regex can be converted into an equivalent NFA, and every DFA back into a regex. They are the everyday practical front-end to finite automata in text processing.
depths.deep: The Kleene star is what lets a finite written pattern match strings of unbounded length, and it corresponds precisely to a loop (a revisited state) in the automaton. Real-world regex engines often add 'backreferences' (matching a repeat of something matched earlier), which push them beyond truly regular into a strictly more powerful — and worst-case exponential — regime, a frequent source of 'catastrophic backtracking' denial-of-service bugs (ReDoS).

quiz.answer: Kleene's theorem: regular expressions describe exactly the regular languages, equivalently those recognized by finite automata.

quiz.prompt: Why can a regex engine with backreferences behave worse than linear time?
quiz.answer: Backreferences exceed regular expressiveness, forcing backtracking search that can blow up exponentially — the catastrophic-backtracking ReDoS pitfall.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A **regular expression** (regex) is a compact written pattern — "one or more digits," "a word starting with cat" — that a machine tests text against. The beautiful fact: regexes describe *exactly* the same patterns a simple state-hopping machine (a finite automaton) can recognize. They are the everyday, practical front-end to the theory of **regular languages**.

### Precisely

Regular expressions are built from three operations on patterns, starting from single symbols and the empty string:

- **union** ($a\mid b$): "this or that,"
- **concatenation** ($ab$): one pattern then another,
- **Kleene star** ($a^*$): zero or more repetitions.

**Kleene's theorem** proves they describe *exactly* the regular languages: every regex converts to an equivalent NFA, and every DFA converts back to a regex. So regex, DFA, and NFA are three notations for one class of patterns.

### Worked example

The regex $(0\mid 1)^*\,1$ matches all binary strings ending in 1. Read it: $(0\mid 1)^*$ means "any number of 0s and 1s in any order," then the final $1$ pins the last symbol. Compile it to an NFA: a loop state consuming any symbol (the star), with a transition on $1$ to an accepting state. Feed "1011": the loop absorbs "101," then the final "1" reaches accept. The **Kleene star** in the pattern corresponds precisely to the *loop* (revisited state) in the automaton.

### Why it works

The Kleene star is what lets a *finite* written pattern match strings of *unbounded* length — and it corresponds exactly to a loop in the automaton (a revisited state, per the **pumping lemma** intuition). Kleene's theorem's two conversions (regex→NFA via Thompson's construction, DFA→regex via state elimination) establish the equivalence constructively, so the three formalisms are interchangeable.

### Where it connects

Built directly on **DFA/NFA** and characterizes **regular languages**. Regexes are the workhorse of text processing, lexical analysis in compilers, and search. The loop-equals-star insight ties to the **pumping lemma**.

### A second angle

Knowing the regex–automaton equivalence makes you a better engineer. A *true* regular expression compiles to a finite automaton that scans text in guaranteed **linear time**, with no backtracking — which is why tools like RE2 and the classic grep are immune to catastrophic blowup. The trouble starts when convenience features (backreferences, lookaround) push beyond regular and force a backtracking matcher. The practical rule: if your pattern is genuinely regular (no backreferences), prefer an automaton-based engine for predictable performance; reserve backtracking engines for patterns that truly need the extra power, and audit those for **ReDoS** exposure on untrusted input.

### Watch out

Real-world regex engines often add **backreferences** (matching a repeat of something matched earlier, e.g. $(.+)\backslash 1$). These push the engine *beyond* truly regular into a strictly more powerful — and worst-case *exponential* — regime, causing **catastrophic backtracking** denial-of-service bugs (**ReDoS**). So "regex" in practice is *not* always "regular." Don't assume engine features map to the clean theory.

atoms.title: Greedy algorithms
atoms.summary: Greedy algorithms make the locally best choice at each step, which yields a global optimum only when the problem has matroid-like structure.

depths.eli5: A greedy algorithm always grabs the best-looking option right now and never reconsiders. Sometimes that string of locally-best choices happens to land you the best overall answer; other times it walks you into a dead end. The trick is knowing which problems it's safe on.
depths.core: A greedy algorithm builds a solution one step at a time, each step taking whatever choice looks best at that moment. This is guaranteed correct only when the problem has the 'greedy-choice property' (a locally best choice can always be extended to a globally best solution) and 'optimal substructure'. Minimum spanning tree (Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms), Huffman coding, and interval scheduling are classic greedy successes; the general 0/1 knapsack problem is the classic failure.
depths.deep: The deep reason greedy works for minimum spanning tree but not knapsack is 'matroid theory': greedy is provably optimal exactly on problems whose feasible solutions form a matroid (an abstract structure capturing 'independence'). When greedy fails, dynamic programming or exchange arguments are needed. Even when greedy is not optimal, it often guarantees a fixed 'approximation ratio', making it a workhorse for NP-hard problems.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A **greedy algorithm** always grabs the best-looking option *right now* and never reconsiders. Sometimes that string of locally-best choices lands the best overall answer; other times it walks you into a dead end. The whole skill is knowing *which problems* greedy is safe on — and there is a precise mathematical answer.

### Precisely

A greedy algorithm builds a solution one step at a time, each step taking whatever choice looks best at that moment. It is guaranteed optimal only when the problem has:

- the **greedy-choice property** — a locally optimal choice can always be extended to a globally optimal solution, and
- **optimal substructure** — optimal solutions contain optimal sub-solutions.

Formally, greedy is provably optimal exactly when the feasible solutions form a **matroid** (an abstract structure capturing "independence").

### Worked example

Interval scheduling: pick the most non-overlapping meetings from a set with fixed start/end times. Greedy rule: always pick the meeting that *finishes earliest* among those still compatible. Sort by finish time; repeatedly take the next interval whose start is after the last chosen finish. This is optimal — an *exchange argument* shows any optimal schedule can be transformed, swap by swap, into the greedy one without losing meetings, because the earliest-finishing choice leaves the most room for the rest. Contrast the 0/1 knapsack, where greedily taking the best value-per-weight item can preclude a better combination — greedy *fails* there.

### Why it works

The deep reason greedy works for **minimum spanning tree** (Kruskal's, Prim's) but *not* knapsack is **matroid theory**: greedy is optimal precisely on problems whose feasible sets form a matroid, where the exchange property guarantees local choices extend globally. The interval-scheduling exchange argument is a concrete instance. When greedy fails, **dynamic programming** or explicit exchange arguments are needed instead.

### Where it connects

Built on **big-O**. Greedy successes: MST, **Huffman coding** (optimal prefix codes), interval scheduling. The contrast with **dynamic programming** is central — both need optimal substructure, but DP also handles overlapping subproblems where greedy's single-pass commitment fails. Even when not optimal, greedy often gives a guaranteed **approximation** ratio for NP-hard problems.

### A second angle

The standard way to *prove* a greedy algorithm correct is the **exchange argument**, and it is worth internalizing as a template. Assume an optimal solution differs from the greedy one; locate the first place they diverge; show you can "exchange" the optimal's choice there for the greedy choice *without* making the solution worse (often: making it no worse and no shorter). Repeat, transforming the optimal step by step into the greedy solution while preserving optimality — so the greedy solution is optimal too. The "greedy stays ahead" variant argues instead that after each step the greedy partial solution is at least as good as any other's. Master one of these and most greedy proofs become routine.

### Watch out

Greedy is **only sometimes correct** — never assume it without proving the greedy-choice property (or matroid structure). The 0/1 knapsack is the canonical trap: highest value-per-weight first is *not* optimal. Also, a greedy heuristic that lacks a proof may still be useful as an *approximation*, but don't claim optimality without the matroid/exchange justification.

atoms.title: Amortized analysis
atoms.summary: Amortized analysis bounds the average cost per operation over a sequence, even when individual operations are occasionally expensive.

depths.eli5: Some operations are usually cheap but every so often very expensive. Instead of judging by the rare expensive one, amortized analysis spreads that big cost across all the cheap ones to find the true average cost per operation over a whole run.
depths.core: Amortized analysis measures the average cost of an operation across a worst-case sequence of operations, rather than the cost of the single worst operation. For example, a 'dynamic array' that doubles its capacity when full costs O(n) on the rare resize but only O(1) 'amortized' per insertion, because resizes happen rarely enough that their total cost is spread thin. The three standard proof techniques are the aggregate method, the accounting (banker's) method, and the potential method.
depths.deep: Amortized is not the same as average-case: it makes no probabilistic assumption and holds for every worst-case sequence. The 'potential method' assigns the data structure a 'stored energy' Φ; the amortized cost of an operation is its actual cost plus the change ΔΦ, so cheap operations bank potential that expensive ones later spend. This makes data structures like splay trees and Fibonacci heaps analyzable despite wild swings in their per-operation cost.

atoms.note: Amortized O(1) per op over n ops means total O(n) — distinct from, and stronger than, an average-case probabilistic claim.

quiz.prompt: How does amortized analysis differ from average-case analysis?
quiz.answer: Amortized analysis averages over a worst-case sequence with no probabilistic assumptions; average-case assumes a distribution over inputs.

quiz.prompt: Why is insertion into a doubling dynamic array O(1) amortized despite O(n) resizes?
quiz.answer: Resizes happen only when the array is full and double its size, so the total resize work over n insertions is O(n), giving O(1) per insertion on average.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Some operations are usually cheap but every so often very expensive. Instead of judging a data structure by its rare worst single operation, **amortized analysis** spreads that big cost across all the cheap ones to find the *true average cost per operation over a whole run*. It answers "what does a typical operation really cost in the long run?" — without any probabilistic assumption.

### Precisely

Amortized analysis bounds the *average cost per operation across a worst-case sequence* of operations, rather than the cost of the single worst operation. Three standard techniques: the **aggregate method** (total cost / number of ops), the **accounting (banker's) method** (overcharge cheap ops to bank credit for expensive ones), and the **potential method** (assign the structure a "stored energy" $\Phi$; amortized cost = actual cost + $\Delta\Phi$).

### Worked example

A **dynamic array** that *doubles* its capacity when full. Most insertions are $O(1)$ (just write a slot). But when the array fills, an insertion triggers an $O(n)$ copy to a new array of double size. Is insertion expensive? Over $n$ insertions starting from size 1, the resizes copy $1+2+4+\cdots+n<2n$ elements *total*. Adding the $n$ cheap writes, total work is $O(n)$, so the **amortized** cost per insertion is

$$\frac{O(n)}{n}=O(1).$$

The rare $O(n)$ resize is paid for by the many cheap insertions before it.

### Why it works

The **potential method** makes this rigorous: define $\Phi$ = (number of elements) − (half the capacity), so $\Phi$ grows with each cheap insertion (banking potential) and *drops* sharply at a resize (spending it). The amortized cost = actual cost + $\Delta\Phi$ stays $O(1)$ every step, because each expensive resize is exactly funded by potential the cheap operations banked. Cheap operations *prepay* for the expensive ones.

### Where it connects

Built on **big-O**. Amortization is what makes **splay trees**, **Fibonacci heaps**, union-find, and dynamic arrays analyzable despite wild per-operation swings. It complements worst-case and average-case analysis as a third lens on cost.

### A second angle

The **accounting (banker's) method** is often the most intuitive of the three techniques. You assign each operation an *amortized charge* that may exceed or undershoot its real cost; the surplus is stored as "credit" on the data structure, and later expensive operations spend that credit. The rule for correctness: the bank balance must never go negative, so stored credit always covers future spending. For the doubling array, charge each insertion 3 units — 1 to write the new element, and 2 banked so that when a resize copies an old element, the 2 units it deposited earlier pay for moving it. The balance stays non-negative, proving $O(1)$ amortized.

### Watch out

Amortized is **not** average-case: it makes *no probabilistic assumption* and holds for *every* worst-case sequence — it is a stronger, deterministic guarantee. Don't conflate "amortized $O(1)$" with "expected $O(1)$." Also, an amortized bound describes a *sequence*: a single operation can still take $O(n)$; you are promised only that such spikes are rare enough to average out.

atoms.title: The time hierarchy theorem
atoms.summary: More time strictly buys more computational power: there are problems solvable in O(n^3) time but not in O(n^2).

depths.eli5: Give a computer genuinely more running time and it can genuinely solve more problems — no surprise, but here it's actually proven, not just assumed. It's one of the few clean, settled facts in complexity theory, where most of the big questions are still open.
depths.core: The time hierarchy theorem says that if you allow a time budget f that grows enough faster than another budget g (for well-behaved 'time-constructible' bounds), then DTIME(g) ⊊ DTIME(f): strictly more time lets you decide strictly more problems. The proof uses 'diagonalization' — it builds a machine that, given the extra time, deliberately disagrees with the output of every machine confined to less time, so it can't be in the smaller class. This is exactly why P ⊊ EXP (problems solvable in polynomial time are a strict subset of those solvable in exponential time) is a proven theorem, not merely a conjecture.
depths.deep: The hierarchy theorems are among the rare 'unconditional' separations in complexity theory, and they work because the diagonalization can be carried out within the allotted time/space budget. Crucially, diagonalization alone cannot resolve P vs NP: the 'relativization' barrier (the Baker–Gill–Solovay result) shows that any proof technique blind to a machine's internals fails on P vs NP, which is why that question stays open while the hierarchy theorems are settled.

atoms.note: Hierarchy theorems give us our only proven separations (P ⊊ EXP, L ⊊ PSPACE); the famous open separations (P vs NP) provably need non-relativizing techniques.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Give a computer genuinely *more running time* and it can genuinely solve *more* problems — no surprise intuitively, but here it is actually *proven*, not merely assumed. The **time hierarchy theorem** is one of the few clean, settled separations in complexity theory, where almost every other big question (P vs NP foremost) remains open.

### Precisely

For "well-behaved" (**time-constructible**) bounds where $f$ grows sufficiently faster than $g$ (specifically $g(n)\log g(n)=o(f(n))$),

$$\text{DTIME}(g)\subsetneq\text{DTIME}(f):$$

strictly more time decides strictly more problems. As a corollary, $\text{P}\subsetneq\text{EXP}$ — polynomial time is a *proper* subset of exponential time — is a **theorem**, not a conjecture.

### Worked example

The proof builds a **diagonalizing** machine $D$ with time budget $f$ that deliberately *disagrees* with every machine confined to budget $g$. $D$ on input $\langle M\rangle$ simulates $M$ on $\langle M\rangle$ for up to $f(n)$ steps; if $M$ halts within that budget and accepts, $D$ rejects, and vice versa. Then $D$'s language cannot be decided by *any* $g$-time machine $M$ — because $D$ was engineered to differ from each such $M$ on the input $\langle M\rangle$ itself. Yet $D$ runs in time $f$. So $\text{DTIME}(f)$ contains a language $\text{DTIME}(g)$ does not. The extra $\log$ factor in the condition is the simulation overhead.

### Why it works

The hierarchy theorems are rare **unconditional** separations, working because the diagonalization fits *within* the allotted time budget (the $\log$ factor accounts for simulation cost). Crucially, diagonalization alone *cannot* settle P vs NP: the **relativization barrier** (**Baker–Gill–Solovay**) shows there are oracles making P=NP and others making P≠NP, so any proof technique that works identically with any oracle — and diagonalization does — must fail on P vs NP.

### Where it connects

Built on the **Turing machine** and **complexity-P**. It supplies the *only* proven strict separations in the standard hierarchy ($\text{P}\subsetneq\text{EXP}$; the analogous space hierarchy gives $\text{L}\subsetneq\text{PSPACE}$). The relativization barrier explains *why* **P vs NP** and the **space-complexity** inclusions stay open.

### A second angle

The hierarchy theorems sit inside a bigger story about *why some questions are hard to prove*. Complexity theory has identified **barriers** — proof techniques that provably cannot resolve certain questions. **Relativization** (Baker–Gill–Solovay) blocks diagonalization from settling P vs NP; **natural proofs** (Razborov–Rudich) block a wide class of circuit-lower-bound arguments (assuming strong one-way functions exist); and **algebrization** blocks algebraic extensions of diagonalization. The time hierarchy theorem succeeds precisely because it stays *within* a single uniform model and relativizes harmlessly. Knowing which barrier a question runs into tells you what kind of genuinely new technique a proof would require — which is why P vs NP remains open.

### Watch out

The theorem needs the bounds to be **time-constructible** and the gap large enough (the $\log$ factor matters) — it doesn't separate arbitrarily close budgets. And the headline limitation: this technique *relativizes*, so however powerful diagonalization feels, it provably cannot resolve P vs NP — non-relativizing methods are required there.

atoms.title: Lossy compression and rate–distortion
atoms.equation: R(D)=\min_{p(\hat x\mid x):\,\mathbb{E}[d]\le D} I(X;\hat X)
atoms.summary: Rate–distortion theory gives the minimum number of bits needed to represent a source within an allowed level of distortion.

depths.eli5: Perfect, lossless compression can only shrink a file so far. But if you're willing to lose a little quality — a slightly blurrier photo, a slightly rougher song — you can use far fewer bits. Rate–distortion theory tells you the best possible trade between file size and faithfulness.
depths.core: Lossless coding is bounded below by entropy, but allowing some 'distortion' D (a measured amount of error in the reconstruction) lets you compress further. The 'rate–distortion function' R(D) is the smallest bit rate you can achieve while keeping the average distortion at or below D. Formally it is the minimum mutual information I(X;X̂) between the source X and its reconstruction X̂, over all reconstructions meeting the distortion limit. It is the 'lossy' counterpart of the source coding theorem and the theoretical floor underneath JPEG, MP3, and video codecs.
depths.deep: R(D) is convex and decreasing: R(0) recovers the entropy (perfect, lossless reconstruction), and R climbs steeply as you demand near-perfect fidelity. The curve formalizes the universal engineering trade-off between file size and quality. Rate–distortion is also the conceptual ancestor of the 'information bottleneck' in deep learning, which compresses an input while preserving the information relevant to a target — relevance-constrained lossy coding.

sources: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (facts)
Wikipedia (facts): Rate–distortion theory; Information bottleneck method
atoms.art_prompt: a convex R(D) curve falling from the entropy at zero distortion, with codec quality knobs sliding along it trading size for fidelity

quiz.prompt: What does the rate–distortion function R(D) give, and what is R(0)?
quiz.answer: The minimum bit rate to represent a source within expected distortion D; R(0) equals the source entropy (lossless).

quiz.prompt: How does lossy compression beat the entropy bound?
quiz.answer: It does not reconstruct the source exactly — by tolerating bounded distortion it discards information the entropy bound assumed must be preserved, so fewer bits suffice.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Perfect, *lossless* compression can only shrink a file so far — down to its entropy. But if you're willing to lose a little quality — a slightly blurrier photo, a slightly rougher song — you can use *far* fewer bits. **Rate–distortion theory** tells you the best possible trade between file size and faithfulness: the minimum bits needed to represent a source within an allowed amount of error.

### Precisely

Allowing average **distortion** $D$ (a measured reconstruction error) lets you compress below entropy. The **rate–distortion function** is the smallest achievable bit rate at distortion $\le D$:

$$R(D)=\min_{p(\hat x\mid x):\,\mathbb{E}[d(x,\hat x)]\le D} I(X;\hat X),$$

the minimum **mutual information** between source $X$ and reconstruction $\hat X$ over all reconstruction schemes meeting the distortion budget. It is the *lossy* counterpart of the source coding theorem.

### Worked example

The curve $R(D)$ is convex and decreasing. At $D=0$ (demand perfect reconstruction) it returns the entropy: $R(0)=H(X)$ — you cannot do better than lossless. As you *relax* the fidelity requirement (allow larger $D$), $R(D)$ falls, often steeply at first: tolerating a little blur saves a lot of bits. Eventually, at the maximum tolerable distortion, $R$ reaches 0 (send nothing, just guess the average). A JPEG quality slider literally moves you along this curve, trading file size for image fidelity.

### Why it works

The result extends Shannon's coding machinery via **typical sequences**: instead of coding the source exactly, you code a *reconstruction* $\hat X$ that stays within distortion $D$, and the cheapest such coding costs $I(X;\hat X)$ bits per symbol. Minimizing that mutual information over all valid reconstructions gives the floor $R(D)$. Convexity and monotonicity formalize the universal "size vs quality" engineering trade-off.

### Where it connects

Built on **source coding** (the lossless floor it generalizes) and **mutual information** (the quantity it minimizes). It is the theory underneath **JPEG**, **MP3**, and video codecs. It is also the conceptual ancestor of the **information bottleneck** in deep learning — compress an input while preserving information relevant to a target, i.e. relevance-constrained lossy coding (linking to **neural network learning**).

### A second angle

For a concrete feel, the rate–distortion function of a **Gaussian source** has a clean closed form: a source with variance $\sigma^2$, under squared-error distortion $D$, requires

$$R(D)=\tfrac12\log_2\frac{\sigma^2}{D}\quad\text{bits (for }0<D\le\sigma^2\text{), and }0\text{ beyond.}$$

Read it: halving the allowed distortion $D$ adds exactly half a bit per sample, and once $D\ge\sigma^2$ you need zero bits (just output the mean). This logarithmic law is the quantitative backbone of audio and image codec design, and the "**reverse water-filling**" solution generalizes it to many frequency components — spend bits on the high-variance components, ignore the ones quieter than your distortion budget.

### Watch out

Lossy compression beats the entropy bound *only because it does not reconstruct the source exactly* — by tolerating distortion it discards information the entropy floor assumed must be preserved. Don't expect $R(D)<H(X)$ with *zero* error; $R(0)=H(X)$ exactly. Also, $R(D)$ depends on the chosen distortion measure $d$ — "quality" is defined by whatever metric you picked, and a perceptually wrong metric gives a misleading curve.

atoms.title: Approximation algorithms
atoms.summary: When a problem is NP-hard, approximation algorithms find provably near-optimal solutions in polynomial time.

depths.eli5: When finding the perfect answer is too slow to be practical, settle for one that's guaranteed to be close — say, provably never worse than twice the best possible — but that you can find quickly. That guarantee of closeness is what separates an approximation algorithm from a random guess.
depths.core: An α-approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time and always returns a solution within a factor of α of the optimal value (for example, a 2-approximation is never more than twice as costly as the best answer). For NP-hard optimization problems this is the practical response to intractability: vertex cover has a simple 2-approximation, set cover a (ln n)-approximation, and some problems admit a PTAS (a polynomial-time approximation scheme, getting arbitrarily close to optimal). The best achievable α is itself a deep question, tied to 'hardness of approximation'.
depths.deep: The PCP theorem reveals that for some problems even approximating is NP-hard: there is a threshold ratio below which no polynomial-time algorithm can go unless P = NP (e.g., MAX-3SAT is hard to approximate beyond 7/8). So NP-hardness comes in grades — some problems approximate arbitrarily well (PTAS), some to a fixed constant, and some not at all — refining the coarse P-vs-NP picture into a rich landscape of approximability.

atoms.note: Hardness of approximation (via the PCP theorem) shows some problems are not just hard to solve exactly but provably hard to even approximate beyond a fixed ratio.

quiz.answer: It runs in polynomial time and always returns a solution within a factor α of the optimal value.
