quiz.answer: For some NP-hard problems, even approximating beyond a fixed ratio is itself NP-hard, so they cannot be approximated arbitrarily well unless P = NP.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

When finding the *perfect* answer is too slow to be practical (an NP-hard problem), settle for one *guaranteed to be close* — say, provably never worse than twice the best possible — but findable quickly. That guarantee of closeness is exactly what separates an **approximation algorithm** from a random guess or an unprincipled heuristic.

### Precisely

An **$\alpha$-approximation algorithm** runs in polynomial time and *always* returns a solution within a factor $\alpha$ of the optimal value (for a minimization problem, cost $\le \alpha\cdot\text{OPT}$). Examples: vertex cover has a simple **2-approximation**; set cover a $(\ln n)$-approximation; some problems admit a **PTAS** (polynomial-time approximation scheme), getting within $(1+\epsilon)$ of optimal for *any* $\epsilon>0$. The best achievable $\alpha$ is itself a deep question.

### Worked example

A 2-approximation for vertex cover (find a small set of vertices touching every edge). Algorithm: repeatedly pick *any* uncovered edge $(u,v)$ and add *both* endpoints to the cover; remove all edges they touch; repeat. The edges you picked are pairwise disjoint (a matching), so the optimal cover must include at least one endpoint of each — at least (number of picked edges) vertices. You used *two* per picked edge, so your cover is at most twice optimal: a guaranteed 2-approximation, in linear time. No exponential search needed.

### Why it works

The guarantee comes from a *lower bound on OPT* you can compute cheaply (here, the matching size), against which you bound your solution. The deeper story: the **PCP theorem** shows that for some problems *even approximating* is NP-hard — there is a threshold ratio below which no polynomial algorithm can go unless P=NP (e.g. MAX-3SAT is hard to approximate beyond 7/8). So NP-hardness comes in *grades* — some problems approximate arbitrarily well (PTAS), some to a fixed constant, some not at all.

### Where it connects

Built on **NP-completeness** (the intractability that motivates approximation) and **greedy algorithms** (a common design technique). The PCP theorem refines the coarse **P vs NP** picture into a rich landscape of *approximability*. This is the practical response when a problem is shown NP-hard.

### A second angle

It is worth knowing the hierarchy of approximability classes, since "NP-hard" hides large differences. At the friendly end, **FPTAS/PTAS** problems (like the knapsack problem) approximate to within any $(1+\epsilon)$ in polynomial time. Next, **APX** problems (like vertex cover, metric TSP) admit a *fixed* constant-factor approximation but no PTAS unless P=NP. At the hard end, problems like general TSP or max-clique cannot be approximated within *any* constant (clique is hard to approximate within $n^{1-\epsilon}$). Placing a problem in this ladder tells you the *best guarantee you can even hope for* before you design anything — a planning tool as much as a classification.

### Watch out

An $\alpha$-approximation is a *worst-case* guarantee, not typical performance — a 2-approximation never exceeds twice optimal but is often much better in practice. Conversely, "approximation" without a proven ratio is just a heuristic, with *no* guarantee. And **hardness of approximation** (via PCP) means some problems cannot be approximated beyond a fixed ratio at all — don't assume every NP-hard problem has a good approximation.

atoms.title: Typical sequences and the AEP
atoms.summary: For long sequences of i.i.d. symbols, almost all probability concentrates on roughly 2^{nH} nearly-equiprobable 'typical' sequences.

depths.eli5: Flip a biased coin a million times and the exact sequence you get is almost certainly one of a fairly predictable family — the 'typical' outcomes, the ones with roughly the expected mix of heads and tails. There are about 2 raised to the power (length × entropy) of these typical sequences, and nearly all the probability lives among them.
depths.core: The 'asymptotic equipartition property' (AEP) is the information-theoretic version of the law of large numbers. For a sequence of 'i.i.d.' symbols (independent and identically distributed — each drawn the same way, independently), as the length n grows the per-symbol log-probability converges to the entropy H(X). As a result, almost all of the probability concentrates on a 'typical set' of about 2^{nH} sequences, each of probability near 2^{-nH}. This is the precise reason that H bits per symbol are enough for compression: you only need to give index numbers to the typical set.
depths.deep: The AEP is what makes Shannon's source and channel coding theorems provable: compression hands short codes only to the typical sequences (ignoring the vanishingly rare atypical ones), and channel coding picks codewords so that their typical outputs barely overlap. The exponential gap between the 2^{nH} typical sequences and the |alphabet|^n total possible sequences is the quantitative heart of why information can be compressed at all.

atoms.note: Typical set size ≈ 2^{nH}; total sequence count = |X|^n. Compression works because the typical set is exponentially smaller whenever H < log|X|.

Wikipedia (facts): Asymptotic equipartition property; Typical set

quiz.answer: About 2^{nH} typical sequences, each with probability roughly 2^{-nH}.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Flip a biased coin a million times and the exact sequence you get is almost certainly one of a fairly predictable family — the **typical** outcomes, those with roughly the *expected* mix of heads and tails. There are about $2^{(\text{length}\times\text{entropy})}$ of these typical sequences, and nearly *all* the probability lives among them. This concentration is the secret reason compression works at all.

### Precisely

The **asymptotic equipartition property (AEP)** is the information-theoretic law of large numbers. For **i.i.d.** symbols $X_1,\dots,X_n$ (independent, identically distributed), the per-symbol log-probability converges to the entropy:

$$-\tfrac1n\log_2 p(X_1,\dots,X_n)\to H(X).$$

Consequently, almost all probability concentrates on a **typical set** $A_\epsilon^{(n)}$ of about $2^{nH}$ sequences, each with probability near $2^{-nH}$.

### Worked example

A biased coin, $P(H)=0.9$, entropy $H\approx 0.469$ bits. Over $n=100$ flips there are $2^{100}\approx 10^{30}$ possible sequences, but the *typical* ones — those with about 90 heads and 10 tails — number only about $2^{nH}=2^{46.9}\approx 10^{14}$. That is *vastly* fewer than $10^{30}$, yet they carry essentially all the probability. To compress, you assign short index numbers only to those $\approx 10^{14}$ typical sequences (about $nH\approx 47$ bits each), ignoring the rest. The exponential gap $10^{14}$ vs $10^{30}$ is why compression to $H$ bits/symbol succeeds.

### Why it works

By the law of large numbers, the empirical symbol frequencies converge to the true probabilities, so a long sequence almost surely has the "expected mix" — making its probability close to $2^{-nH}$ and placing it in the typical set. The typical set has size $\approx 2^{nH}$ because each typical sequence has roughly equal probability $2^{-nH}$ and together they sum to $\approx 1$. This near-uniformity over an exponentially small set is the "equipartition."

### Where it connects

The AEP is what makes Shannon's **source coding theorem** and **noisy-channel coding theorem** *provable*: compression indexes only the typical set; channel coding picks codewords whose typical noisy outputs barely overlap. Built on **Shannon entropy** and **probability**, it also underpins **rate–distortion** and **channel capacity**.

### A second angle

The AEP is the rigorous engine behind a slogan worth remembering: **"compress the typical, ignore the rest."** Two complementary facts make it work. First, the typical set has probability approaching 1, so a code that *only* handles typical sequences (and gives up on the rest) succeeds with probability $\to 1$. Second, the typical set has only $\approx 2^{nH}$ members, so indexing it costs $\approx nH$ bits — matching the entropy floor. Conversely, *no* set smaller than $\approx 2^{nH}$ can capture most of the probability, which is the converse half: you cannot beat $H$ bits per symbol. Both the achievability and the impossibility halves of **source coding** flow from this one property.

### Watch out

The AEP is an *asymptotic, high-probability* statement — it holds as $n\to\infty$ and for *most* sequences, not every one. Atypical sequences still exist (an all-heads run is possible), they just become vanishingly improbable. Also, the basic AEP assumes **i.i.d.** symbols; correlated sources have an analogous result (via the entropy *rate*), but the simple $2^{nH}$ count uses independence.
